posts.title: How Hydraulic Cylinders Work: A Practical Guide for Maintenance Teams
posts.metaTitle: How Hydraulic Cylinders Work — A Practical Guide
posts.metaDescription: Learn how hydraulic cylinders convert fluid pressure into linear force, what each component does, and how to calculate force and speed for your application.
posts.excerpt: Hydraulic cylinders turn fluid pressure into controlled, powerful straight-line motion. Understanding what happens inside one makes it far easier to specify, maintain and troubleshoot them.
posts.imageAlt: Close-up of hydraulic cylinder assemblies on industrial machinery
posts.html:
Hydraulic cylinders are the muscles of heavy equipment. They lift crane booms, tip dump bodies, clamp workpieces in presses and steer mining trucks. Despite doing very different jobs, almost every cylinder works on the same simple principle — and once your maintenance team understands that principle, diagnosing problems becomes much more logical.

This guide explains how hydraulic cylinders work, what each component does, and how to estimate the force and speed a cylinder can deliver.

The basic principle: pressure acting on an area

A hydraulic cylinder converts fluid pressure into linear force. Oil from a pump enters the cylinder and pushes against a piston. Because hydraulic oil is almost incompressible, the pressure acts evenly across the whole face of the piston and the piston moves, pushing the rod out.

The relationship is straightforward:

Force = Pressure × Area

Double the pressure and you double the force. Double the piston area and you also double the force. This is why a relatively compact cylinder can move loads of many tonnes: system pressures of 150–250 bar acting on a large bore generate very high forces.

The main components of a hydraulic cylinder

Every cylinder design varies, but you will find these parts in almost all of them:

  • Barrel (tube): the main body. Its inner surface is honed to a fine finish so the piston seals can slide without wearing quickly.
  • Piston: separates the two chambers inside the barrel and carries the piston seals and wear bands.
  • Piston rod: transmits force from the piston to the load. Rods are usually induction-hardened and hard-chrome plated to resist wear, corrosion and impact damage.
  • Gland (head): closes the rod end of the barrel and holds the rod seal, wiper and guide bushing.
  • End cap (base): closes the other end of the barrel and usually includes a mounting.
  • Seals and wear rings: keep oil where it belongs and guide moving parts so metal does not touch metal.
  • Ports: where oil enters and leaves each chamber.
  • Mountings: clevises, trunnions, flanges or eyes that connect the cylinder to the machine.

Single-acting vs double-acting cylinders

Single-acting cylinders use hydraulic pressure in one direction only. The return stroke relies on gravity, the load itself or an internal spring. They are common in jacks, simple lifting devices and some tipping applications.

Double-acting cylinders have ports at both ends, so oil can push the piston in either direction. This gives powered extension and retraction and much better control, which is why most industrial and mobile machines use them.

Push force vs pull force

In a double-acting cylinder, the extend (push) force and the retract (pull) force are different. When extending, pressure acts on the full piston area. When retracting, it acts only on the annulus — the piston area minus the rod area.

Stroke direction Effective area Relative force Relative speed
Extend (push) Full piston area Higher Slower
Retract (pull) Piston area − rod area Lower Faster

This matters when you size a cylinder. If your application needs a high pulling force, you may need a larger bore than a push-only calculation suggests.

Worked example: estimating cylinder force

Consider a cylinder with a 100 mm bore and a 56 mm rod operating at 200 bar.

  1. Piston area = π × (0.1 m)² ÷ 4 ≈ 0.00785 m²
  2. Pressure = 200 bar = 20,000,000 Pa
  3. Push force ≈ 0.00785 × 20,000,000 ≈ 157,000 N, or roughly 16 tonnes-force

For the pull force, subtract the rod area (π × 0.056² ÷ 4 ≈ 0.00246 m²) to get an annulus of about 0.00539 m², which gives roughly 108,000 N — about 11 tonnes-force.

These are theoretical figures. In practice you should allow for friction, pressure losses in hoses and valves, and a sensible safety margin.

How fast will the cylinder move?

Speed depends on how much oil flows into the cylinder:

Speed = Flow ÷ Effective area

With 40 litres per minute flowing into the 100 mm bore cylinder above, the extension speed is about 0.085 m/s, or roughly 85 mm per second. Because the annulus area is smaller, the same flow will retract the rod faster.

This is why some circuits use regeneration, routing oil from the rod side back into the cap side to increase extension speed at the cost of force.

What limits a cylinder's performance?

Several practical factors decide whether a cylinder performs as calculated:

  • Rod buckling: long, slender rods under compression can buckle. Longer strokes need thicker rods or additional guidance.
  • Seal friction and leakage: worn seals reduce efficiency and can cause drift.
  • Side loading: cylinders are designed to push and pull in a straight line. Misalignment loads the guide bushing and wears seals rapidly.
  • Cushioning: without end-of-stroke cushioning, heavy loads slam into the end caps, causing shock and fatigue.
  • Contamination: dirty oil scores the barrel and rod and destroys seals.

Maintenance basics for longer cylinder life

You can extend cylinder life considerably with a few simple habits:

  1. Inspect rods regularly for scratches, pitting and chrome damage. A damaged rod will quickly destroy new seals.
  2. Check for external leaks at the gland and ports and investigate the cause rather than just topping up oil.
  3. Watch for drift. A load that creeps down under pressure often points to internal leakage across the piston seal, although valves can also be responsible.
  4. Keep the oil clean with proper filtration and sealed reservoirs.
  5. Check mountings and pins for wear that allows misalignment.
  6. Protect exposed rods on equipment that stands idle in harsh environments.

When to repair and when to replace

Many cylinder faults can be repaired: seals can be replaced, rods re-chromed or remanufactured, and barrels re-honed within limits. Replacement becomes the better option when the barrel is bulged or worn beyond its tolerance, the rod is bent, or the design no longer suits the application.

If you are unsure, our engineers can inspect a cylinder and give you an honest repair-or-replace recommendation. Explore our hydraulic cylinders, or send us the details for a quotation.

Key takeaways

  • Hydraulic cylinders convert pressure into force using Force = Pressure × Area.
  • Push force is higher than pull force because the rod reduces the effective area on the return stroke.
  • Speed depends on oil flow and effective area.
  • Clean oil, good alignment and undamaged rods are the foundation of long cylinder life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my cylinder extend slower than it retracts?

Because the effective area is different on each side of the piston. When extending, oil fills the full bore area; when retracting, it fills only the annulus — the bore area minus the rod area. The same pump flow therefore fills the smaller annulus faster, so the rod retracts more quickly. This is normal behaviour. If the difference seems larger than expected, or extension has slowed over time, check for pump wear, internal leakage or flow control settings rather than assuming the cylinder is at fault.

Can I increase a cylinder's force by raising the pressure?

In theory, yes — force rises in proportion to pressure. In practice you must stay within the rated pressure of every component in the circuit: the cylinder, hoses, valves and pump. Raising the relief setting beyond these ratings risks seal extrusion, burst hoses, cracked welds and serious injury. If you need more force, the safer route is usually a larger bore cylinder or a design review by an engineer who can confirm the structure and mountings can also carry the higher load.

What is the difference between bore, rod and stroke?

The bore is the inside diameter of the barrel, which determines the piston area and therefore the pushing force. The rod is the diameter of the piston rod, which affects pulling force, buckling strength and retract speed. The stroke is the distance the rod travels between fully retracted and fully extended. These three figures, together with the mountings and working pressure, are the core of any cylinder specification and are the first things a manufacturer will ask for.

How often should hydraulic cylinders be inspected?

Operators should check for leaks, rod damage and unusual movement as part of daily or pre-use checks. A more detailed inspection of rods, mountings, pins and hoses fits naturally into monthly or quarterly maintenance, depending on duty. Cylinders on critical or safety-related equipment, such as cranes, should also be covered by the equipment's periodic thorough examination. The right frequency depends on operating hours, environment and the consequences of failure, so adjust it based on what your inspections find.

posts.title: Tie-Rod vs Welded Hydraulic Cylinders: Which Should You Choose?
posts.metaTitle: Tie-Rod vs Welded Hydraulic Cylinders: Which to Choose?
posts.metaDescription: Compare tie-rod and welded hydraulic cylinders on strength, size, serviceability and cost, and learn which design suits industrial or mobile applications.
posts.excerpt: Tie-rod and welded cylinders can look similar on a drawing, but they behave very differently in service. Here is how to choose the right construction for your machine.
posts.imageAlt: Technician working on precision hydraulic machinery
posts.html:
When you specify a new hydraulic cylinder, one of the first decisions is the type of construction. The two most common designs are tie-rod and welded cylinders. Both convert hydraulic pressure into linear force in the same way, but the way they are built affects their size, strength, serviceability and cost.

This article compares the two designs and explains where each one makes most sense.

What is a tie-rod cylinder?

A tie-rod cylinder holds its end caps onto the barrel using high-strength threaded steel rods that run along the outside of the barrel. Nuts on the ends of the tie rods clamp the assembly together.

Tie-rod cylinders are very common in industrial applications such as machine tools, presses, production lines and material handling equipment. Many are built to recognised dimensional standards, which makes interchangeability easier.

Advantages of tie-rod cylinders

  • Easy to service: remove the tie-rod nuts and the cylinder comes apart, so seals can be replaced quickly.
  • Standardised dimensions: many sizes follow industry standards, which simplifies replacement.
  • Cost-effective for standard bores and strokes at moderate pressures.

Limitations of tie-rod cylinders

  • Larger outer dimensions: the tie rods add width, which can be a problem where space is tight.
  • Pressure limits: under high or shock loads, tie rods can stretch, which may lead to leakage at the end caps.
  • Long strokes: very long tie rods can whip or need intermediate supports.
  • Dirt traps: exposed tie rods collect debris in dirty environments.

What is a welded cylinder?

A welded cylinder has its end cap welded directly to the barrel. The gland at the rod end is usually threaded or retained with a wire ring or bolted flange so the cylinder can still be dismantled for repair.

Welded cylinders dominate mobile hydraulics — cranes, excavators, tippers, agricultural machinery and mining equipment — and are widely used in heavy industrial machinery.

Advantages of welded cylinders

  • Compact: no external tie rods, so the cylinder is narrower for the same bore.
  • Robust: better suited to high pressures, shock loads and harsh environments.
  • Flexible design: mountings, ports and bores can be customised to fit the machine.
  • Long strokes: no tie rods to stretch or support.

Limitations of welded cylinders

  • Repair takes more specialist work: glands can be very tight after years in service and need proper tooling to remove.
  • Usually custom-made: less dimensional standardisation, so replacements are often manufactured to drawing or sample.

Side-by-side comparison

Factor Tie-rod cylinder Welded cylinder
Typical use Industrial, factory automation Mobile, heavy industrial
Pressure and shock tolerance Moderate High
Envelope size Larger Compact
Serviceability Very easy Good, with proper tooling
Standardisation Often standardised Usually custom
Harsh or dirty environments Fair Very good
Long strokes Limited Well suited

How to choose the right design

Ask these questions when specifying a cylinder:

  1. What is the working pressure and are there shock loads? High pressure or impact usually points towards a welded design.
  2. How much space is available? If width is limited, a welded cylinder is often the only option.
  3. Where will it operate? Outdoor, dusty or wet environments favour welded construction without exposed tie rods.
  4. How important is fast maintenance? On a production line with spare cylinders on the shelf, a standard tie-rod design can be swapped and resealed quickly.
  5. Does it need to match an existing standard? If you are replacing an existing standard tie-rod cylinder, staying with the same type avoids machine modifications.

What about other designs?

Tie-rod and welded are not the only options:

  • Telescopic cylinders use nested stages to achieve a long stroke from a short retracted length, typically in tippers and dump bodies.
  • Mill-type cylinders use bolted flanges and heavy construction for steel mills and severe industrial service.
  • Compact or short-stroke cylinders suit clamping and fixturing.

Repairing or replacing an existing cylinder

If you are replacing a cylinder, start by recording the bore, rod diameter, stroke, retracted length, mounting type, port sizes and working pressure. Photographs of the nameplate, mountings and ports help a manufacturer understand the application. If the cylinder has failed in service, tell your supplier how it failed — the cause may change the specification.

We manufacture both welded and tie-rod style cylinders to drawing or sample. Learn more about our hydraulic cylinders or our custom hydraulic systems, and request a quote with your requirements.

Summary

  • Choose tie-rod cylinders for standard industrial applications where serviceability and standard dimensions matter.
  • Choose welded cylinders for mobile, high-pressure, shock-loaded or space-limited applications.
  • Whatever the design, accurate dimensions and honest information about the operating conditions are the key to a cylinder that lasts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I replace a tie-rod cylinder with a welded cylinder?

Often, yes — provided the replacement matches the stroke, retracted length, mountings, port positions and pressure rating. A welded cylinder is usually more compact, so it can fit in the same space. Check that the mounting dimensions are identical or that adapters are acceptable, and confirm that the welded design is serviceable enough for your maintenance approach. If the original tie-rod cylinder followed a dimensional standard, discuss the change with your supplier so future replacements remain straightforward.

Why do tie-rod cylinders sometimes leak at the end caps?

Under high pressure or shock loading, the tie rods stretch slightly. This can allow the end caps to separate microscopically from the barrel, letting the static seals extrude or leak. Correct tie-rod torque, proper static seals and keeping pressure peaks within the design rating all help. If leakage keeps returning, the application may simply be too severe for a tie-rod design, and a welded or mill-type cylinder could be the better long-term choice.

Are welded cylinders harder to repair?

They require more specialist tooling but are very repairable. Glands may be threaded, retained by wire rings or bolted, and years of service can make them tight to remove. An experienced repair shop has the equipment to dismantle them without damage, inspect every component, re-seal, and pressure test. The main difference for maintenance teams is that welded cylinders are less suited to quick resealing on site, so holding a reconditioned spare is often the best strategy for critical machines.

Which design is more cost-effective?

For standard industrial applications at moderate pressure, catalogue tie-rod cylinders are usually the most economical option, particularly in common sizes. For mobile, high-pressure or space-limited applications, welded cylinders give better value because they last longer in those conditions. Consider total cost: a cheaper cylinder that leaks or fails repeatedly costs more in downtime and repairs than a slightly more expensive design suited to the duty.

posts.title: Telescopic Hydraulic Cylinders Explained: Design, Uses and Care
posts.metaTitle: Telescopic Hydraulic Cylinders: Design, Uses and Care
posts.metaDescription: How telescopic hydraulic cylinders achieve long strokes from a short body, where they are used, and the maintenance practices that keep multi-stage cylinders reliable.
posts.excerpt: Telescopic cylinders deliver a very long stroke from a compact body. That makes them essential for tippers and lifting equipment, but their multi-stage design brings specific maintenance needs.
posts.imageAlt: Machinist working on a steel component in a heavy engineering workshop
posts.html:
Some applications need a very long stroke but have little space to mount a cylinder. A dump truck body, for example, must tip steeply, yet the cylinder has to fit under the body when it is lowered. The answer is the telescopic hydraulic cylinder.

This article explains how telescopic cylinders work, where they are used and how to keep them in good condition.

How a telescopic cylinder works

A telescopic cylinder contains a series of nested tubes, called stages, each sliding inside the next. When oil enters the base, the largest stage extends first, followed by progressively smaller stages. When fully extended, the cylinder can be several times longer than its retracted length.

Because each stage has a different effective area, the cylinder behaves differently through its stroke:

  • The largest stage extends first with the highest force and the lowest speed.
  • Smaller stages follow, extending faster but with less force for the same pressure.

This suits tipping applications well. The most force is needed at the start of the lift, when the load is heaviest and the geometry is least favourable.

Single-acting vs double-acting telescopic cylinders

Single-acting telescopic cylinders extend hydraulically and retract under gravity. They are by far the most common type, especially in tippers, trailers and dump bodies.

Double-acting telescopic cylinders can be powered in both directions. They are used where gravity cannot be relied on to retract the cylinder — for example in horizontal applications, push-off trailers or some refuse vehicles. They are more complex and need careful design of the internal oil paths.

Typical applications

  • Tipper trucks and dump trailers
  • Agricultural trailers
  • Refuse collection vehicles
  • Mining and quarry haul equipment
  • Some lifting platforms and specialised cranes
  • Roll-off container systems

Design considerations

Telescopic cylinders need careful engineering:

  1. Stability at full extension: an extended telescopic cylinder is long and slender. The design must consider buckling, mounting geometry and side loads from uneven loading.
  2. Stage overlap: each stage needs enough overlap with the next to resist bending. Too little overlap leads to wear and seal failure.
  3. Stop rings and cushioning: stages must stop positively at the end of their travel without shock damage.
  4. Sealing: every stage has its own seals, so there are more potential leak paths than in a standard cylinder.
  5. Mountings: trunnion and eye mountings must allow the cylinder to follow the arc of the tipping body without binding.

Common problems with telescopic cylinders

Symptom Possible causes
Stages extend out of sequence Internal leakage, contamination, damaged stop rings or uneven wear
Jerky movement Air in the system, worn bearings or contamination
External leaks between stages Worn or damaged stage seals, scored stage surfaces
Body creeps down Internal leakage, valve problems or worn seals
Bent stages Side loading from uneven loads or tipping on slopes

Safety first: side loads and tipping on slopes

Many telescopic cylinder failures are not caused by the cylinder at all. Tipping on uneven ground, sticky loads that do not slide out, or uneven loading can put large side loads on an extended cylinder. Operators should tip only on firm, level ground and make sure loads discharge freely. Never work under a raised body unless it is supported by a suitable mechanical prop.

Maintenance practices that extend life

  • Inspect every stage for scoring, dents and chrome damage when the cylinder is extended for checks.
  • Keep stages clean. Mud and grit on the stages are dragged past the wipers and seals.
  • Lubricate mounting points as specified so the cylinder can pivot freely.
  • Check for leaks at each stage seal and the bleed points.
  • Bleed air from the system as recommended by the manufacturer.
  • Maintain clean oil — telescopic cylinders are particularly sensitive to contamination because of their many sliding surfaces.

Repair and reconditioning

Telescopic cylinders can usually be reconditioned. Typical work includes resealing every stage, polishing or re-plating damaged stages, replacing bearings and stop rings, and pressure testing the complete cylinder. Bent stages normally need replacing rather than straightening.

When ordering a replacement or repair, provide the number of stages, retracted and extended lengths, the largest stage diameter, mounting details and operating pressure.

Find out more about our hydraulic cylinders, or contact our team to discuss a telescopic cylinder repair.

Key points

  • Telescopic cylinders provide long strokes from short retracted lengths using nested stages.
  • The largest stage gives the most force and extends first.
  • Stability, stage overlap and side loading are the main design and operating concerns.
  • Clean oil, clean stages and careful operation make the biggest difference to service life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do telescopic cylinders extend in stages?

The stage with the largest effective area needs the lowest pressure to move, so it extends first. Each smaller stage needs progressively higher pressure, so they follow in sequence. On retraction under gravity, the order is generally reversed. If stages extend out of sequence, the cause may be friction from wear or contamination, damaged stop rings, or internal leakage, and the cylinder should be inspected before it causes uneven loading or damage.

Can a telescopic cylinder be repaired if one stage is bent?

A bent stage normally needs replacing rather than straightening, because straightening rarely restores the precise geometry and surface finish needed for sealing. The rest of the cylinder can usually be reconditioned with new seals, bearings and stop rings. It is equally important to find out why the stage bent — side loading from tipping on uneven ground or sticky loads is a common cause — otherwise the repaired cylinder may fail the same way.

How do I bleed air from a telescopic cylinder?

Follow the equipment manufacturer's procedure. Typically, the cylinder is extended slowly through several full cycles at low load, and bleed screws, where fitted, are opened carefully to release air. Air causes jerky, spongy movement and can damage seals, so it is worth bleeding thoroughly after any repair or hose change. Always make sure the load body is safely supported and that nobody is in the danger zone during bleeding.

What information do I need to order a replacement telescopic cylinder?

Record the number of stages, the retracted and fully extended lengths, the diameter of the largest stage, mounting types and dimensions at both ends, port size and position, working pressure, and the body or load it lifts. Photographs of the mountings and any nameplate are very helpful. If the original failed, explain how, so the manufacturer can consider improvements such as heavier stages or better bearings.

posts.title: 9 Common Causes of Hydraulic Cylinder Failure (and How to Prevent Them)
posts.metaTitle: 9 Causes of Hydraulic Cylinder Failure & Prevention
posts.metaDescription: The nine most common causes of hydraulic cylinder failure — from contamination and side loading to rod damage — with practical steps to prevent each one.
posts.excerpt: Most hydraulic cylinder failures are not random. They follow predictable patterns — and once you know what to look for, most of them can be prevented.
posts.imageAlt: Technician inspecting precision hydraulic machinery on a production floor
posts.html:
A failed hydraulic cylinder can stop a crane, a press line or a fleet of mobile machines. The repair cost is usually small compared with the cost of the downtime. The good news is that cylinders rarely fail without a reason, and the same causes appear again and again.

Here are the nine most common causes of hydraulic cylinder failure, the signs to look for, and how to prevent each one.

1. Contaminated hydraulic fluid

Contamination is the single biggest cause of hydraulic component failure. Hard particles act like grinding paste between the rod and seals, and between the piston and barrel. Water causes corrosion and degrades the oil.

Signs: scored rods and barrels, rapid seal wear, cloudy or dark oil.

Prevention: use the correct filtration, change filters on schedule, keep reservoir breathers in good condition, cap open hoses and ports during maintenance, and take periodic oil samples.

2. Side loading and misalignment

Cylinders are designed to push and pull in a straight line. When the load is offset or the mountings are misaligned, the rod is forced against the guide bushing on one side.

Signs: uneven wear on one side of the rod or bushing, oval wear patterns, leakage that returns quickly after resealing.

Prevention: check mounting alignment, use spherical bearings or self-aligning mountings where movement is expected, and replace worn pins and bushes before they allow excessive play.

3. Damaged piston rods

The rod is exposed to the environment every time it extends. Impacts from debris, weld spatter or careless handling dent or scratch the chrome. Every extension then drags the damage through the rod seal.

Signs: visible scratches, pits or flaking chrome; a rod seal that leaks soon after replacement.

Prevention: fit rod guards or bellows in harsh environments, protect rods during nearby welding, and inspect rods during routine checks. Light damage can sometimes be polished; deeper damage needs re-chroming or a new rod.

4. Wrong or worn seals

Seals must suit the pressure, temperature, speed and fluid. A seal that is not compatible with the fluid can swell or harden. A seal designed for lower pressure can extrude into the clearance gap.

Signs: leaks, drift, nibbled or extruded seal edges, hardened or cracked seals.

Prevention: use quality seal kits matched to the actual operating conditions, and replace all seals together during a rebuild rather than only the one that leaked.

5. Excessive heat

High oil temperature thins the fluid, increases internal leakage and shortens seal life dramatically. Many elastomer seals degrade quickly once temperatures rise above their rated limit.

Signs: hard, brittle or discoloured seals; sluggish performance on hot days or after long cycles.

Prevention: keep coolers clean, check relief valve settings, avoid running the system over relief, and investigate why oil is getting hot instead of just tolerating it.

6. Pressure spikes and shock loads

Sudden stops, dropped loads and fast valve shifts create pressure spikes far above normal working pressure. Over time these fatigue welds, threads and mountings.

Signs: cracks at welds or ports, loosened glands, damaged end caps, bent rods.

Prevention: use end-of-stroke cushioning where needed, set relief valves correctly, and train operators to avoid shock loading.

7. Rod buckling

Long-stroke cylinders under compression can buckle if the rod is too slender for the load, especially when the cylinder is extended and mounted with pivots at both ends.

Signs: a visibly bent rod, binding, and seal leakage at the gland.

Prevention: check buckling calculations during design, use larger rod diameters or stop tubes for long strokes, and do not exceed the rated load.

8. Corrosion

Moisture in the oil corrodes the barrel and piston from the inside. Outside, salt, chemicals and humidity attack the rod surface, especially on equipment that stands idle with rods extended.

Signs: rust spots or pitting on the rod, pitting inside the barrel found during repair.

Prevention: store equipment with rods retracted where possible, remove water from the oil, specify suitable rod coatings for marine or chemical environments and apply protective products to exposed rods.

9. Poor installation and maintenance practices

Many failures begin on the workshop bench: damaged seals during assembly, dirty components, incorrect torque on gland threads, or air left in the system.

Signs: failures shortly after repair or installation.

Prevention: assemble in clean conditions, use the correct installation tools, follow torque specifications, bleed air properly and pressure test after repair.

A quick diagnostic table

Symptom Most likely causes
External leak at rod seal Rod damage, worn or wrong seal, side load
Load drifts under pressure Piston seal bypass, valve leakage
Jerky movement Air in oil, stick-slip from worn seals, contamination
Rod scored along its length Contamination, damaged wiper
Bent rod Buckling, side load, impact
Repeated failure after rebuild Root cause not fixed, alignment, installation errors

Treat the cause, not just the symptom

When a cylinder fails, ask why before ordering seals. A cylinder resealed without correcting misalignment or contamination will often fail again within weeks. A good repair shop should report what it found inside the cylinder — scored barrels, damaged seals, contamination — so you can fix the underlying problem.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most common cause of hydraulic cylinder failure?

Contamination is the most common underlying cause across hydraulic systems in general. Hard particles score rods and barrels and wear seals, while water causes corrosion. Many failures that appear to be "seal problems" actually start with dirt entering past a worn wiper or during maintenance. Good filtration, sealed reservoirs, clean maintenance practices and healthy wipers prevent a large share of cylinder failures.

How can I tell if side loading is damaging my cylinder?

Look for uneven wear: an oval-shaped wear pattern on the rod or guide bushing, wear concentrated on one side of the piston wear rings, or seals that start leaking soon after replacement. Visually, you may notice the cylinder flexing or mountings showing uneven wear. Check alignment between the mounting points through the full stroke, and consider spherical bearings where some misalignment is unavoidable.

Should I replace all seals or just the leaking one?

Replace the complete seal set. Seals in a cylinder age together, and if one has failed the others are usually near the end of their life too. Dismantling a cylinder is the expensive part of the job, so fitting a full kit avoids a second repair a few weeks later. While the cylinder is apart, inspect the rod, barrel and wear rings, because damaged surfaces will quickly destroy new seals.

When is a cylinder failure a safety issue?

Any cylinder that supports or controls a load — on cranes, lifting platforms, presses or tipping bodies — becomes a safety issue if it can drift, drop or fail suddenly. External leaks of high-pressure oil can also cause injection injuries and fire risks near hot surfaces. Take such equipment out of service until it is repaired, support loads mechanically before working on them, and follow the equipment's inspection requirements after repair.

posts.title: Hydraulic Cylinder Seal Types Explained: How to Choose the Right Seal Kit
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Cylinder Seal Types: Choosing the Right Kit
posts.metaDescription: Understand rod seals, piston seals, wipers, wear rings and static seals, the common materials, and how pressure, speed and temperature affect seal selection.
posts.excerpt: A hydraulic cylinder is only as reliable as its seals. This guide explains each seal's job, common materials and the factors that decide which seal kit you need.
posts.imageAlt: Assorted precision-machined spare parts and fasteners
posts.html:
Seals are small, inexpensive parts, yet they decide whether a hydraulic cylinder holds its load or leaks oil across the workshop floor. Choosing the wrong seal can turn a routine repair into a repeat failure. This guide explains the different hydraulic cylinder seal types, what each one does, and how to choose the right seal kit.

The seals inside a typical cylinder

A standard double-acting cylinder contains several types of seal, each with a specific role.

Rod seal

The rod seal sits in the gland and prevents oil escaping along the piston rod. It is the most critical seal for preventing external leakage. It must seal at full system pressure while the rod moves in and out, and it must allow a very thin oil film to lubricate the rod without leaving visible leakage.

Wiper (scraper)

The wiper sits at the outer end of the gland. It does not hold pressure. Its job is to scrape dirt, dust and moisture off the rod as it retracts, so contamination does not reach the rod seal. A worn wiper is one of the most common reasons rod seals fail early.

Piston seal

The piston seal stops oil passing from one side of the piston to the other. If it wears or is damaged, oil bypasses the piston, the cylinder loses force and loads can drift. Piston seals may be single-acting (sealing pressure from one side) or double-acting (sealing in both directions).

Wear rings (guide rings)

Wear rings are fitted on the piston and in the gland. They keep metal parts apart and absorb side loads. They are not designed to seal, but without them the piston would contact the barrel and the rod would contact the gland, causing scoring.

Static seals

O-rings and back-up rings seal joints that do not move, such as between the gland and the barrel or between the piston and the rod. Back-up rings prevent O-rings from extruding into clearance gaps at high pressure.

Buffer seals

In higher-pressure or heavy-duty cylinders, a buffer seal is fitted ahead of the rod seal. It absorbs pressure peaks and protects the main rod seal, which then operates under lower, steadier pressure.

Common seal materials

Material Strengths Typical limitations
Polyurethane (PU) Excellent wear and extrusion resistance, common in mobile hydraulics Limited at high temperatures and with some water-based fluids
Nitrile rubber (NBR) Good general-purpose material for mineral oils, widely used for O-rings Moderate temperature range, less wear-resistant than PU
Fluoroelastomer (FKM) High temperature and chemical resistance Higher cost, less suited to low temperatures
PTFE compounds Very low friction, high speed capability, no stick-slip Usually needs an energiser ring; careful installation required
Polyacetal / filled nylons Used for wear rings and back-up rings Not sealing materials on their own

Always confirm material compatibility with the actual hydraulic fluid. Fire-resistant and biodegradable fluids can be incompatible with materials that work well with mineral oil.

How to choose the right seal kit

1. Pressure

Higher pressures increase the risk of extrusion, where the seal is forced into the clearance gap between moving parts. Harder materials, back-up rings and smaller clearances help.

2. Speed

Fast-moving rods generate heat at the seal lip. PTFE-based seals are often used at higher speeds because of their low friction.

3. Temperature

Consider both oil temperature and ambient temperature. Equipment in a foundry or steel plant needs very different seals from equipment working outdoors in cold climates.

4. Fluid type

Mineral oil, water-glycol, phosphate esters and biodegradable fluids each require compatible materials.

5. Environment

Dusty and muddy environments demand robust double-lip wipers. Corrosive environments may need special rod finishes alongside the seals.

6. Groove dimensions

A seal must match the groove it fits into. Replacing a seal with a "close enough" profile is a common cause of repeat leaks. If you do not have the original part numbers, measure the groove dimensions carefully or let the repairer measure them.

Installation matters as much as selection

Even the right seal will fail if installed badly. Good practice includes:

  • cleaning all components thoroughly before assembly;
  • checking rods and barrels for burrs, sharp edges and damage;
  • using installation tools and sleeves to protect seal lips from threads and edges;
  • lubricating seals with clean system fluid before assembly;
  • never twisting O-rings or overstretching seals;
  • replacing the complete seal set rather than individual seals.

When seals keep failing

If seals fail repeatedly, the seal is rarely the root cause. Look for scored rods or barrels, misalignment, contamination, excessive temperature or incorrect groove dimensions. A professional repair should identify these issues rather than simply fitting another seal kit.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does a wiper seal do if it does not seal pressure?

The wiper protects the rod seal. As the rod retracts, the wiper scrapes off dust, mud, water and debris that would otherwise be dragged into the gland. A worn or damaged wiper is one of the most common reasons rod seals fail early, especially on mobile and outdoor equipment. Heavy-duty double-lip wipers or metal-cased scrapers are available for very dirty environments.

Are polyurethane or PTFE seals better?

Neither is better in every case. Polyurethane offers excellent wear and extrusion resistance and is very common in mobile hydraulics. PTFE-based seals have very low friction and suit high speeds and applications where stick-slip must be avoided, but they need careful installation and usually an energiser. The right choice depends on pressure, speed, temperature, fluid and environment — which is why seal selection should be based on actual operating conditions.

Why do new seals sometimes leak immediately after a rebuild?

Common causes include seals damaged during installation by sharp edges or threads, a scratched rod or barrel, incorrect groove dimensions, the wrong seal profile, or contamination left inside the cylinder. Occasionally a seal is installed the wrong way round. Proper tools, deburred components, careful cleaning and a pressure test after assembly catch most of these problems before the cylinder returns to service.

How long should hydraulic seals last?

There is no single figure. Seal life depends on operating hours, pressure, speed, temperature, oil cleanliness, rod condition and alignment. In clean, well-maintained systems seals can last many years; in contaminated or overheated systems they may fail within months. Rather than relying on time, monitor leakage and drift and use those observations, plus findings from previous repairs, to plan resealing.

posts.title: How to Measure a Hydraulic Cylinder for Replacement
posts.metaTitle: How to Measure a Hydraulic Cylinder for Replacement
posts.metaDescription: A step-by-step guide to measuring bore, rod, stroke, retracted length, mountings and ports so your replacement hydraulic cylinder fits first time.
posts.excerpt: Ordering a replacement cylinder without accurate measurements is the fastest way to waste time and money. Use this checklist to record everything a manufacturer needs.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer drafting mechanical component drawings at a workbench
posts.html:
When a hydraulic cylinder fails and the original drawings are missing, the replacement has to be built from measurements. Getting them right first time avoids delays, modifications and a second order. This guide walks you through every measurement a manufacturer needs.

Before you start: safety

Never measure a cylinder that is still connected to a pressurised system. Lower or support the load mechanically, relieve system pressure, and disconnect the hydraulic lines with suitable caps on hoses and ports. Cylinders can contain trapped pressure, so follow your site's isolation procedures.

Tools you will need

  • Vernier caliper (and ideally an internal caliper or bore gauge)
  • Steel tape measure
  • Thread gauges for ports
  • A camera to photograph mountings, ports and nameplates
  • A notepad or measurement sheet

1. Check for a nameplate or part number

Many cylinders carry a stamped part number, serial number or manufacturer's plate. Photograph it before cleaning. If the machine manufacturer is known, their part number can save a lot of measuring.

2. Bore diameter

The bore is the internal diameter of the barrel. It cannot be measured directly without dismantling, so measure the outside diameter of the barrel and estimate wall thickness, or measure the bore during disassembly if the cylinder is being repaired. Tell the manufacturer which measurement you have taken.

3. Rod diameter

Measure the piston rod with a caliper at several points along its length. Wear and chrome damage can affect readings, so record the largest consistent figure. Common rod sizes follow standard increments, which helps confirm your measurement.

4. Stroke

Stroke is the distance the rod travels from fully retracted to fully extended. Measure the exposed rod length when fully retracted and again when fully extended; the difference is the stroke. If the cylinder cannot be cycled, the stroke can be determined during dismantling.

5. Retracted and extended lengths

These are measured between the centres of the mounting points — for example, pin centre to pin centre. Record:

  • Retracted length (closed centres)
  • Extended length (open centres)

These two dimensions are critical because the cylinder must fit the machine geometry exactly.

6. Mounting types and dimensions

Identify the mounting at each end and record its dimensions:

Mounting What to measure
Clevis Pin diameter, slot width, clevis depth
Eye / spherical bearing Pin diameter, eye width, bearing type
Trunnion Trunnion diameter, length, position along the barrel
Flange Flange thickness, bolt pattern, bolt sizes, pilot diameter
Tang or lug Thickness, hole size, distance to centre

Note whether eyes contain plain bushes or spherical bearings, and measure any grease nipple positions.

7. Port details

Record the type, size and position of each port:

  • thread type and size (BSP, NPT, metric, SAE O-ring boss) or flange type;
  • port orientation relative to the mountings;
  • distance from the port centre to the end of the cylinder.

Photographs taken from several angles help the manufacturer understand port orientation.

8. Operating conditions

Measurements describe the geometry; operating conditions decide the design. Tell the manufacturer:

  • working pressure and maximum pressure;
  • whether the cylinder pushes, pulls or both;
  • the load and any shock loading;
  • operating speed and cycles per day;
  • fluid type and temperature range;
  • environment: outdoor, marine, dusty, hot or corrosive.

9. Why the original cylinder failed

If the cylinder failed, describe how. A bent rod might point to buckling or side loads; repeated leaks may point to misalignment. A replacement made to the same dimensions will fail the same way if the cause is not addressed.

A simple measurement checklist

  1. Part number / photos of nameplate
  2. Bore (or barrel outside diameter)
  3. Rod diameter
  4. Stroke
  5. Retracted and extended centres
  6. Mounting types and dimensions at both ends
  7. Port types, sizes, positions and orientation
  8. Working pressure, load and speed
  9. Fluid type, temperature and environment
  10. Failure description and quantity required

When measuring is difficult

Sometimes the easiest route is to send the cylinder, or the worn parts, to a manufacturer who can reverse-engineer it, produce a drawing for your approval and manufacture an exact replacement — often with improvements to address the original failure.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I measure bore size without dismantling the cylinder?

Not exactly. You can measure the outside diameter of the barrel and estimate the bore from typical wall thicknesses, but this is only an estimate. Many bore and rod sizes follow standard increments, which helps narrow it down. For an accurate replacement, tell the manufacturer that you measured the outside diameter, or allow them to dismantle the cylinder and measure the bore directly during inspection.

What is the difference between stroke and closed length?

Stroke is how far the rod moves. Closed (retracted) length is the distance between the mounting centres when the cylinder is fully retracted. Both are needed: the stroke defines the motion, and the closed length defines whether the cylinder fits the machine geometry. The extended length should equal the closed length plus the stroke, which is a useful check on your measurements.

How do I identify port thread types?

Use thread gauges and calipers to measure the outside diameter and thread pitch, and look for features such as an O-ring face or chamfer. Common types include BSP, metric, NPT and SAE O-ring boss, and some cylinders use flange ports instead. Photograph the ports and note their orientation relative to the mountings. If you are unsure, send photos and measurements to the manufacturer.

Is it better to send the old cylinder to the manufacturer?

If downtime allows, yes. With the cylinder in hand, the manufacturer can measure every dimension accurately, inspect the failure, check the materials and recommend improvements. This removes the risk of measurement errors. If the machine cannot wait, send detailed measurements and photos for a replacement, then send the old cylinder afterwards so the drawing can be confirmed and kept on file.

Send your measurements and photos through our quote request form, or learn more about our hydraulic cylinders.

posts.title: Repair or Replace? Deciding What to Do With a Damaged Hydraulic Cylinder
posts.metaTitle: Repair or Replace a Hydraulic Cylinder? A Decision Guide
posts.metaDescription: How to decide whether a damaged hydraulic cylinder should be repaired or replaced, based on rod and barrel condition, cost, lead time and the cause of failure.
posts.excerpt: A leaking or damaged cylinder does not always need replacing. Here is how to weigh repair against replacement using condition, cost, downtime and root cause.
posts.imageAlt: Machinist grinding a steel part in a fabrication workshop
posts.html:
When a hydraulic cylinder starts leaking or loses performance, maintenance teams face a familiar question: should we repair it or buy a new one? The right answer depends on the condition of the main components, the cost and lead time of each option, and — most importantly — why the cylinder failed in the first place.

What a cylinder repair usually involves

A professional repair is more than replacing seals. A typical rebuild includes:

  1. Dismantling and cleaning all components.
  2. Inspection of the rod, barrel, piston, gland and mountings, with measurements against tolerances.
  3. Repairs such as polishing, re-chroming or replacing the rod, honing the barrel, and replacing bushes or bearings.
  4. Resealing with a complete, correctly specified seal kit.
  5. Assembly and pressure testing to confirm there is no internal or external leakage.
  6. A findings report explaining what failed and why.

When repair makes sense

Repair is usually the better option when:

  • the barrel bore is within tolerance or can be honed without exceeding it;
  • the rod is straight, with damage limited to light scratches or chrome wear that can be polished or re-plated;
  • the cylinder is a custom or obsolete design with a long lead time for a new unit;
  • the mountings and welds are sound;
  • the failure was caused by a correctable issue, such as worn seals or contamination.

Repair is often faster than ordering a new custom cylinder and keeps the original geometry, which avoids machine modifications.

When replacement is the better option

Replacement is usually more sensible when:

  • the barrel is bulged, cracked or worn beyond honing limits;
  • the rod is bent or the base material is damaged under the chrome;
  • welds or mounting points are cracked or fatigued;
  • the cylinder has been repaired several times and keeps failing;
  • the original design was undersized for the application;
  • a standard cylinder is readily available at a lower cost than the repair.

Comparing cost honestly

Look beyond the purchase price. Consider:

Factor Repair Replacement
Direct cost Usually lower for large or custom cylinders Can be lower for small standard cylinders
Lead time Often days Days for stock items, weeks for custom units
Fit Original geometry retained May need modifications if not identical
Reliability Good if root cause is fixed Good, and a chance to improve the design
Documentation Findings report New drawings and test certificate

The cost of downtime often outweighs the difference between the two options. If a crane or production line is stopped, the fastest reliable solution is usually the cheapest overall.

Always find the root cause

Whichever option you choose, ask why the cylinder failed. Common causes include contamination, misalignment, rod damage, excessive heat and pressure spikes. Repairing or replacing a cylinder without fixing the cause simply resets the clock to the next failure.

A good repair report should tell you, for example, that the rod was scored by contamination, or that uneven bushing wear indicates side loading. That information lets you fix the system, not just the cylinder.

Consider an upgrade

A failure is also an opportunity to improve. During repair or replacement you can:

  • increase rod diameter to resist buckling;
  • specify harder or thicker rod coatings for harsh environments;
  • upgrade seals for higher temperatures or speeds;
  • add cushioning to reduce shock;
  • change mountings to spherical bearings to accommodate misalignment.

Keep a spare for critical equipment

For cylinders whose failure would stop production, consider holding a reconditioned spare. When a cylinder fails, swap in the spare immediately and repair the failed unit without time pressure.

Getting a reliable recommendation

The most reliable way to decide is to have the cylinder inspected and measured. We provide honest repair-or-replace recommendations with a written findings report. Explore our hydraulic cylinder services or request an inspection quote.

Summary

  • Repair when the barrel and rod are within limits and the design suits the application.
  • Replace when major components are bent, cracked or worn beyond tolerance, or the design is inadequate.
  • Factor in downtime, lead time and reliability, not just price.
  • Always fix the root cause, and consider upgrades while the cylinder is apart.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does a cylinder repair take compared with a new cylinder?

Repairs are often quicker, especially for custom or large cylinders, because the main structure already exists. Typical repair time depends on what is found: resealing is fast, while re-chroming a rod or honing a barrel adds processing time. New custom cylinders require materials, machining, welding and testing, which usually takes longer. Ask your supplier for both options and their realistic timelines when deciding.

Is a repaired cylinder as reliable as a new one?

A professionally repaired cylinder — with components inspected and measured, worn parts restored or replaced, new seals fitted and a pressure test performed — can perform reliably for a long time. Reliability depends on the quality of the repair and on fixing the root cause of the failure. A quick reseal without inspection or testing is far less reliable.

What should a repair findings report include?

It should describe the condition of the rod, barrel, piston, gland, seals and mountings, the measurements taken, what was replaced or repaired, the likely cause of failure, and the test results. Photographs of damage are valuable. This information helps you correct problems in the machine, such as misalignment or contamination, and provides a record for future maintenance.

When does it make sense to upgrade during a repair?

Upgrade when the failure points to a design weakness or a change in duty: a bent rod suggests a larger rod diameter, recurring corrosion suggests a better rod coating, and overheating seals suggest a higher-temperature material. Because the cylinder is already apart, upgrades during repair are often inexpensive compared with the benefit of longer service life.

posts.title: Hard Chrome Plating for Piston Rods: Why It Matters and When to Upgrade
posts.metaTitle: Hard Chrome Plating for Hydraulic Piston Rods
posts.metaDescription: Why hydraulic piston rods are induction hardened and hard-chrome plated, what affects coating life, how to spot rod damage and when to consider alternatives.
posts.excerpt: The surface of a piston rod decides how long the seals last and how well the cylinder resists corrosion. Here is what hard chrome plating does and how to protect it.
posts.imageAlt: Polished hydraulic components on heavy machinery
posts.html:
Every time a hydraulic cylinder extends, its piston rod leaves the protection of the barrel and meets dust, moisture and impacts. When it retracts, the rod passes back through the wiper and rod seal. The condition of the rod surface therefore controls two things: how long the seals last and how well the rod resists corrosion and damage.

That is why most hydraulic piston rods are induction hardened and hard-chrome plated.

What hard chrome plating does

Hard chrome is an electroplated layer of chromium applied to the polished rod. It provides:

  • High surface hardness, resisting scratches and wear from seals and contaminants.
  • Corrosion resistance, protecting the steel underneath from moisture and chemicals.
  • A smooth, low-friction surface that allows seals to slide with minimal wear.
  • Good oil retention characteristics when finished correctly, helping to lubricate the seal contact.

Why induction hardening comes first

Chrome is hard but thin. If the steel underneath is soft, an impact can dent the base metal and crack the chrome above it. Induction hardening hardens the outer layer of the steel rod before plating, providing a strong foundation that supports the chrome and resists dents. The combination of a hardened case and hard chrome is standard for demanding mobile and industrial applications.

Surface finish matters

The finish of the rod after plating and polishing is carefully controlled. Too rough, and the surface acts like a file on the seals. Too smooth, and it may not retain enough lubricating film, causing friction and stick-slip. Rod manufacturers and cylinder builders work to specified roughness ranges recommended by seal manufacturers.

Common causes of chrome damage

Damage Typical cause
Scratches along the rod Contamination, failed wiper, debris
Dents and chips Impact from rocks, tools or handling
Pitting and rust spots Moisture, salt, chemicals, long idle periods
Flaking chrome Impact damage to an unhardened base, poor plating adhesion
Weld spatter burns Welding nearby without protecting the rod

How rod damage destroys seals

A rod seal is designed to slide over a smooth surface. A single nick or pit drags across the seal lip thousands of times, cutting it and creating a leak path. Replacing the seal without repairing the rod will result in another leak, often within days. This is why rod inspection is part of every proper cylinder repair.

Repair options for damaged rods

  • Polishing: removes light surface marks when the chrome is intact.
  • Re-chroming: the old chrome is removed, the rod is ground, re-plated and polished back to size. Suitable when the base material is undamaged.
  • New rod: necessary when the rod is bent, deeply pitted, cracked, or the base metal is damaged.

Protecting rods in service

  1. Retract rods when equipment is idle, especially outdoors.
  2. Use rod boots or guards in heavy-debris environments such as mining and demolition.
  3. Protect rods during welding on or near the machine.
  4. Keep wipers in good condition so dirt does not reach the seals.
  5. Clean exposed rods on equipment that works in mud, cement or chemical environments.
  6. Use suitable rod coatings where corrosion is severe.

Alternatives for harsh environments

In very corrosive environments — marine, offshore, chemical plants — standard hard chrome may not be enough. Options include thicker or multi-layer chrome, nickel-chrome systems, stainless steel rods, and thermal spray or laser-clad coatings. These options cost more but can dramatically extend service life where corrosion is the main failure mode.

The bottom line

The rod surface is one of the most important parts of a hydraulic cylinder. Specifying the right base material, hardening and plating, and protecting the rod in service, prevents the majority of rod seal leaks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a scratched piston rod be polished instead of re-chromed?

Light surface marks that have not penetrated the chrome can sometimes be polished out. Deeper scratches, pits or areas where the chrome is chipped or worn through cannot be fixed by polishing, because the protective layer is already compromised. In those cases the rod should be re-chromed or replaced. Fitting new seals over a damaged rod will lead to repeat leaks.

Why is induction hardening done before chrome plating?

Chrome is hard but thin. If the steel underneath is soft, an impact can dent the base material and crack the chrome. Induction hardening gives the rod a hard outer case that supports the chrome and resists dents. Together, the hardened case and chrome layer provide much better protection than chrome on a soft base.

What causes rust spots on chrome rods?

Chrome plating contains microscopic cracks or porosity. In humid, salty or chemical environments, moisture can reach the steel through these paths and cause pitting, especially when rods stay extended while equipment is idle. Retracting rods during storage, cleaning off salt and chemicals, applying protective products and specifying upgraded coatings for harsh environments all reduce corrosion.

Are there alternatives to hard chrome?

Yes. Options include nickel-chrome systems, stainless steel rods, thermal spray coatings and laser cladding. These are typically used in marine, offshore, chemical and other highly corrosive environments. They usually cost more than standard chrome, so they are best reserved for applications where corrosion is the main reason rods fail. Discuss compatibility with seals and surface finish requirements with your cylinder manufacturer.

We manufacture rods with induction hardening and hard chrome plating as standard, and can advise on upgraded coatings for harsh environments. See our hydraulic cylinders or ask an engineer.

posts.title: Hydraulic Cylinder Drift: How to Diagnose Internal and External Leakage
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Cylinder Drift: Diagnosing the Real Cause
posts.metaDescription: Why loads creep down when a hydraulic cylinder should hold them, how to tell piston seal bypass from valve leakage, and how to test safely.
posts.excerpt: A load that slowly creeps down is a common complaint — and the cylinder is not always to blame. Here is a methodical way to find the real cause of drift.
posts.imageAlt: Technician diagnosing hydraulic machinery
posts.html:
"The boom won't hold" or "the platform creeps down overnight" — cylinder drift is one of the most common hydraulic complaints. It is also one of the most frequently misdiagnosed. Many cylinders are resealed when the real problem is a valve, and some valves are replaced when the piston seal was at fault.

This guide explains what causes drift and how to diagnose it methodically and safely.

What is cylinder drift?

Drift is unwanted movement of a cylinder when the control valve is in neutral and the cylinder should be holding position. It usually shows up as a load slowly lowering, or a cylinder slowly extending or retracting.

Drift happens when oil escapes from the chamber that is holding the load. That oil can escape through three main routes:

  1. Across the piston seal inside the cylinder (internal leakage).
  2. Through the control valve or load-holding valve back to tank.
  3. Externally, through a leaking fitting, hose or rod seal.

External leakage: the easy one

Start with the obvious. Inspect the cylinder, hoses and fittings for visible oil. A rod seal leak or a weeping fitting on the loaded side can cause drift. External leaks are also a safety and environmental hazard, so they should be fixed regardless.

Internal piston seal leakage

If the piston seal is worn or damaged, oil passes from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side of the piston. In a double-acting cylinder, this lets the load move as oil transfers between chambers.

Typical causes include worn or damaged piston seals, a scored barrel, a loose piston nut or a cracked piston.

Valve leakage

Spool-type directional control valves are not leak-tight by design. A small clearance between the spool and the body allows some leakage, which increases as the valve wears. If the circuit relies on the spool to hold a load, some drift is expected over time.

This is why load-holding circuits use pilot-operated check valves or counterbalance valves mounted close to the cylinder. If these valves are contaminated, incorrectly adjusted or worn, they leak and allow drift.

A safe, methodical diagnosis

Safety first: always support loads mechanically before working on a hydraulic circuit. Never disconnect hoses from a cylinder holding a load. Relieve pressure and follow your site's isolation procedures.

Step 1: Observe the drift

Note how fast the load drifts, in which direction, and whether it changes with temperature. Drift that increases as oil gets hot often indicates internal leakage in valves or worn seals, because hot oil is thinner.

Step 2: Check the load-holding valves

If the cylinder has counterbalance or pilot-operated check valves, check their settings and condition. Contamination on a valve seat is a common cause and may be cured by cleaning.

Step 3: Isolate the cylinder from the valve

With the load safely supported or the cylinder unloaded, isolation tests can separate cylinder leakage from valve leakage. One common workshop method is to fully extend or retract the cylinder against its stop, then check whether oil flows from the opposite port when pressure is applied. A steady flow indicates oil passing the piston seal.

Because these tests involve pressurised components, they should only be performed by trained personnel following the equipment manufacturer's procedures.

Step 4: Bench test if necessary

The most reliable test is on a test bench, where the cylinder can be pressurised at each end and leakage measured directly. This is standard during professional cylinder repair.

Interpreting results

Finding Likely cause Action
Oil flows past piston under pressure Piston seal or barrel damage Repair cylinder
Cylinder holds on bench, drifts on machine Valve leakage Service or replace valves
Drift only when hot Worn seals or valves, oil viscosity Inspect, check cooling
Visible external leak Rod seal or fitting failure Repair leak

Preventing drift

  • Keep oil clean to protect seals and valve seats.
  • Use proper load-holding valves on critical cylinders.
  • Maintain oil temperature within the recommended range.
  • Inspect and replace seals before they fail completely.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is some drift normal?

Some drift can be expected in circuits that rely only on a spool-type directional valve to hold a load, because spool valves have small internal clearances. Applications that must hold loads securely — cranes, lifting platforms and presses — use load-holding valves such as counterbalance or pilot-operated check valves to minimise drift. Any noticeable change in drift rate is a signal to investigate.

Why does drift get worse when the oil is hot?

Hot oil is thinner, so it leaks more easily through worn seals and valve clearances. If drift is acceptable in the morning but worsens after hours of operation, internal leakage in cylinders or valves is likely, and you should also check why the oil is getting hot. Excessive temperatures accelerate seal wear and oil degradation.

Can a contaminated valve cause drift?

Yes. A particle trapped on the seat of a check valve or counterbalance valve can prevent it from closing fully, allowing oil to escape and the load to drift. Sometimes cleaning the valve solves the problem, but the source of contamination should also be addressed with better filtration and clean maintenance practices.

Is it safe to test a cylinder for internal leakage on the machine?

Only if done by trained personnel following the equipment manufacturer's procedures, with loads lowered or mechanically supported and pressures controlled. Disconnecting hoses from a cylinder that is holding a load is dangerous. Where there is any doubt, remove the cylinder and test it on a proper test bench, which also gives a more reliable result.

If you need a cylinder bench-tested to confirm internal leakage, our workshop can test, repair and certify it. See our hydraulic cylinder services or contact us.

posts.title: What Is a Hydraulic Power Pack? Components and How It Works
posts.metaTitle: What Is a Hydraulic Power Pack? Components Explained
posts.metaDescription: A clear explanation of how a hydraulic power pack works, from the reservoir and pump to valves, filters and coolers, and where power units are used.
posts.excerpt: A hydraulic power pack is the heart of a hydraulic system. Here is what each component does and how they work together to deliver controlled power.
posts.imageAlt: Electric motor driving a hydraulic pump with pipework
posts.html:
If hydraulic cylinders are the muscles of a machine, the hydraulic power pack is its heart. Also called a hydraulic power unit (HPU), a power pack stores hydraulic fluid, pressurises it, controls it and sends it to the actuators that do the work.

This guide explains what a hydraulic power pack is, the main components and how they work together.

What does a hydraulic power pack do?

A power pack converts mechanical energy — usually from an electric motor or engine — into hydraulic energy in the form of pressurised fluid flow. That flow is directed by valves to cylinders and hydraulic motors, which convert it back into mechanical work.

Power packs range from small units the size of a shoebox powering a single clamp, to skid-mounted systems with hundreds of litres of oil supplying entire production lines or heavy lifting equipment.

The main components

Reservoir (tank)

The reservoir stores the hydraulic fluid. It does more than hold oil: a well-designed tank allows air bubbles to escape, lets contaminants settle, and helps dissipate heat. Baffles separate the return area from the pump suction to give the oil time to settle.

Electric motor or engine

The prime mover drives the pump. Electric motors are standard for industrial units; diesel or petrol engines are used for mobile and remote applications.

Hydraulic pump

The pump creates flow. Common types are gear pumps (simple and economical), vane pumps (quiet and efficient at medium pressures) and piston pumps (high pressure and variable displacement for efficient control). Pumps create flow; pressure only rises when that flow meets resistance from a load.

Pressure relief valve

The relief valve protects the system by limiting maximum pressure. When pressure reaches the set point, it opens and sends flow back to the tank. It is a critical safety component.

Directional control valves

These valves direct oil to the actuators, controlling whether a cylinder extends, retracts or holds. They can be manually, solenoid or proportionally operated.

Flow and pressure control valves

Flow control valves set actuator speed. Pressure reducing and sequence valves control pressure in parts of the circuit or the order in which operations happen.

Filters

Filters remove particles that would otherwise wear pumps, valves and seals. Power packs typically include suction strainers, pressure filters and/or return line filters, often with clogging indicators.

Cooler

Hydraulic systems generate heat whenever pressure drops without doing useful work. Air-blast or water coolers remove that heat to keep oil within its working temperature range.

Accessories

Level and temperature gauges, breathers, pressure gauges, accumulators, heaters and electrical control panels complete the unit.

How it all works together

  1. The motor drives the pump, which draws oil from the reservoir.
  2. The pump delivers flow into the pressure line.
  3. The relief valve limits the maximum pressure.
  4. Directional valves send flow to the selected actuator.
  5. The actuator moves the load; pressure rises only as much as the load requires.
  6. Return oil flows back through the filter and cooler to the reservoir.

Where hydraulic power packs are used

  • Presses, clamping fixtures and machine tools
  • Crane and hoist hydraulics
  • Material handling and lifting tables
  • Test rigs and special-purpose machines
  • Mobile equipment and remote sites
  • Marine, mining and steel plant equipment

Standard vs custom power packs

Standard compact units suit simple applications such as a single cylinder with basic control. Custom power packs are designed around specific requirements: flow, pressure, duty cycle, multiple circuits, precise control, environmental conditions and space limits.

A well-designed custom unit is sized for the real duty cycle, which avoids overheating, wasted energy and premature wear.

Choosing a power pack

When specifying a power pack, prepare the following information:

  • required flow and maximum pressure for each actuator;
  • duty cycle and number of operations per hour;
  • control method: manual, solenoid, proportional or PLC;
  • available power supply;
  • ambient conditions and installation space;
  • noise limits and maintenance access.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a power pack and a hydraulic power unit?

The terms are used interchangeably. Both describe a self-contained unit that includes a reservoir, a pump driven by a motor or engine, and the valves and accessories needed to supply pressurised oil to actuators. Some people use "power pack" for smaller compact units and "power unit" or "HPU" for larger industrial systems, but there is no strict distinction.

Can one power pack run several machines?

Yes, if it is designed for the combined flow and pressure demand and the circuits are arranged properly with suitable valves. Centralised systems can be efficient, but a failure then affects every connected machine, and long pipe runs add pressure losses. For critical machines, separate units or a central system with redundancy may be more appropriate.

How noisy are hydraulic power packs?

Noise depends on pump type, motor speed, mounting and pressure. Gear pumps are typically louder than vane or internal gear pumps. Noise can be reduced by choosing quieter pump types, using lower motor speeds, isolating vibration with proper mounts and hoses, and fitting acoustic enclosures. Specify noise limits at the enquiry stage if the unit will be near operators.

What maintenance does a power pack need?

Routine tasks include checking oil level and temperature, inspecting for leaks, changing filter elements based on indicators or analysis, cleaning coolers, checking pressures and monitoring pump noise. Periodic oil analysis on larger or critical units helps catch contamination and wear early. A short, consistent maintenance routine prevents most power pack failures.
