posts.title: How to Size a Hydraulic Power Unit for Your Machine
posts.metaTitle: How to Size a Hydraulic Power Unit (HPU) — Step by Step
posts.metaDescription: Step-by-step guidance on sizing a hydraulic power unit: calculating flow, pressure, motor power, reservoir volume and cooling for your duty cycle.
posts.excerpt: An undersized power unit is slow and overheats; an oversized one wastes energy and money. Here is a step-by-step approach to sizing an HPU correctly.
posts.imageAlt: Technician working on an industrial power unit control panel
posts.html:
Getting the size of a hydraulic power unit right is one of the most important decisions in a hydraulic system. Undersize it and the machine is slow and overheats. Oversize it and you pay for energy, space and equipment you do not need. This guide walks through the main sizing steps.

Step 1: Define what the actuators must do

Start with the work, not the pump. For each cylinder or hydraulic motor, list:

  • the force or torque required;
  • the speed required (mm/s or rpm);
  • the stroke or travel;
  • how often it operates (the duty cycle);
  • which actuators operate at the same time.

Step 2: Calculate the required pressure

For a cylinder, the required pressure comes from the force and piston area:

Pressure = Force ÷ Effective area

Add an allowance for friction, pressure losses through valves and hoses, and a margin for control. A common approach is to design so the working pressure sits comfortably below the maximum rating of the components.

Step 3: Calculate the required flow

Flow determines speed:

Flow (L/min) = Effective area (cm²) × Speed (cm/s) × 60 ÷ 1000

For example, a cylinder with an effective area of 78.5 cm² extending at 5 cm/s needs about 23.6 L/min.

If several actuators move at the same time, add their flows together. If they move in sequence, size for the largest single demand — unless an accumulator is used to supply peak demand.

Step 4: Calculate motor power

Hydraulic power depends on pressure and flow:

Power (kW) ≈ Pressure (bar) × Flow (L/min) ÷ 600

This gives hydraulic power at the pump. Divide by the pump's overall efficiency (often in the region of 0.8–0.9 depending on pump type and condition) to estimate the motor power needed.

For example, 200 bar at 24 L/min is about 8 kW of hydraulic power, so a motor of roughly 9–10 kW would be appropriate before considering duty cycle.

Step 5: Consider the duty cycle

Many machines need full pressure and flow only for part of the cycle. Pressure-compensated variable pumps, two-stage pumps (high flow at low pressure, low flow at high pressure) or accumulators can reduce motor size and energy consumption significantly.

Step 6: Size the reservoir

A traditional rule of thumb is a reservoir of around three times the pump flow per minute for industrial systems, but modern designs vary. The reservoir must:

  • hold enough oil to fill all actuators and lines with margin;
  • allow air to separate and contaminants to settle;
  • help dissipate heat;
  • accommodate thermal expansion.

Mobile and space-limited systems often use smaller tanks combined with better filtration and cooling.

Step 7: Plan for heat

Every bar of pressure dropped without doing useful work becomes heat. Relief valve flow, throttling and inefficiencies all generate heat. Estimate heat load from the power lost and compare it with what the tank surface can dissipate. If the difference is significant, add a cooler.

Step 8: Select filtration

Choose filtration based on the most sensitive component in the system. Servo and proportional valves need much finer filtration than simple directional valves. Include clogging indicators so operators know when to change elements.

Step 9: Choose controls

Decide how the system will be controlled: manual levers, solenoid valves controlled by a PLC, or proportional valves for smooth, variable motion. Controls affect the valve stack, electrical panel and filtration requirements.

A sizing summary table

Item What decides it
Pressure Highest force ÷ smallest effective area, plus losses
Flow Speed × effective area, summed for simultaneous moves
Motor power Pressure × flow ÷ efficiency, adjusted for duty cycle
Reservoir Flow rate, system volume, heat dissipation
Cooling Heat generated vs heat dissipated
Filtration Sensitivity of valves and pumps

Get it checked

These calculations give a solid starting point, but every application has details that affect the final design — ambient temperature, noise, space, power supply and maintenance access among them.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if a power unit is undersized?

An undersized unit cannot deliver the required flow or pressure, so actuators move too slowly or cannot reach full force. The pump may run at its limits continuously, the relief valve may open frequently and the oil overheats. Components wear faster and the machine underperforms. Correct sizing based on the actual duty cycle avoids these problems.

Is it better to oversize a power unit to be safe?

Moderate margins are sensible, but significant oversizing wastes energy, increases purchase cost and can cause heat problems if excess flow is dumped over the relief valve. A better approach is accurate sizing with a reasonable allowance for losses and future needs, using variable pumps or accumulators where demand varies.

How does an accumulator reduce power unit size?

If a machine needs high flow only briefly, an accumulator can store oil during low-demand periods and release it during peaks. The pump and motor can then be sized for average demand rather than peak demand. This reduces motor size, energy use and heat. Accumulators must be correctly sized and fitted with appropriate safety blocks.

What information do I need to give a supplier to size a unit?

Provide each actuator's force or torque, speed, stroke and timing, which functions operate simultaneously, the duty cycle, available power supply, control requirements, ambient conditions and space constraints. Drawings of the machine and a description of the cycle help the supplier propose an efficient design rather than a generic unit.

Our engineers size and build hydraulic power packs and custom hydraulic systems for specific duty cycles. Share your requirements and we will recommend a suitable configuration.

posts.title: Hydraulic Fluid Contamination: Sources, Effects and Control
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Fluid Contamination: Sources, Effects, Control
posts.metaDescription: Contamination causes most hydraulic failures. Learn where particles, water and air come from, how they damage components, and how to keep oil clean.
posts.excerpt: Contaminated oil is behind the majority of hydraulic component failures. Understanding where contamination comes from is the first step to controlling it.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer reviewing technical data on a workstation screen
posts.html:
Hydraulic components are built with tight internal clearances, often just a few microns. That precision is what makes them efficient — and what makes them vulnerable to contamination. Most hydraulic failures can be traced back to dirty, wet or aerated oil.

This article explains the types of contamination, where they come from, the damage they cause, and practical ways to control them.

The three main types of contamination

1. Solid particles

Dirt, metal wear particles, rubber from hoses and seals, paint flakes and fibres. Particles are the most common contaminant and the most damaging.

2. Water

Water enters through condensation, leaking coolers, poor storage and washing equipment. It reduces lubrication, promotes rust, accelerates oil degradation and can cause cavitation damage.

3. Air

Air enters through suction leaks, low oil levels, poor return line design and turbulence in the tank. Air causes spongy operation, noise, overheating and oil oxidation.

Where contamination comes from

  • Built-in contamination: debris left from manufacturing, assembly or repairs.
  • Ingressed contamination: dirt entering through breathers, worn wipers, open reservoirs and during maintenance.
  • Generated contamination: wear particles produced by the system itself, which then cause further wear.
  • New oil: new oil is not necessarily clean oil. It can contain particles from storage and transfer.

How contamination damages components

Contaminant Damage mechanism Typical result
Hard particles Abrasive wear, silting, erosion Pump wear, valve sticking, scored cylinders
Water Corrosion, loss of lubrication, additive depletion Rust, bearing failure, sludge
Air Aeration, cavitation, oxidation Noise, heat, darkened oil, erratic motion
Sludge and varnish Deposits on valves Sticking spools, slow response

Wear particles generated by contamination create more wear in a chain reaction. Once this cycle starts, component life drops rapidly.

Measuring cleanliness

Oil cleanliness is commonly reported using the ISO 4406 code, which counts particles above certain sizes in a sample. Each step up in the code represents roughly double the number of particles. Component manufacturers often recommend target cleanliness levels, and more sensitive components such as servo and proportional valves require cleaner oil.

Regular oil analysis can also measure water content, viscosity, wear metals and additive condition — giving early warning before failures happen.

Practical contamination control

Keep dirt out

  • Fit desiccant or high-quality breathers on reservoirs.
  • Keep wipers and rod seals in good condition.
  • Cap hoses and ports whenever lines are opened.
  • Clean around fittings before disconnecting them.

Filter new oil

Transfer new oil through a filter cart rather than pouring it directly into the reservoir. Store drums indoors, on their sides, and sealed.

Remove what gets in

  • Use correctly rated pressure and return filters.
  • Change filter elements based on clogging indicators or oil analysis, not just the calendar.
  • Use offline filtration units for large or critical systems.

Control water and air

  • Fix leaking coolers and seals promptly.
  • Avoid pressure-washing near breathers and seals.
  • Check suction lines for leaks and maintain correct oil levels.
  • Make sure return lines discharge below the oil level.

Clean after repairs

After component replacement or major repairs, flush the system to remove debris before returning it to service. Our power packs and repaired cylinders are cleaned and flushed before dispatch for this reason.

The payoff

Clean oil extends the life of pumps, valves, seals and cylinders and reduces unplanned downtime. For many systems, improving contamination control is one of the lowest-cost reliability improvements available.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does ISO 4406 cleanliness code mean?

It is a standard way of reporting how many particles of certain sizes are present in a fluid sample. The code consists of numbers representing particle counts in size ranges; each step up roughly doubles the particle count. Component manufacturers often specify target codes, and sensitive components require cleaner oil. Oil analysis laboratories report results using this code.

How often should I take oil samples?

It depends on the criticality and size of the system. Critical or high-value systems may be sampled monthly or quarterly, while smaller systems may be sampled less often. Sample consistently from the same point while the system is running, using clean equipment, so results can be compared over time. Trends are more important than single readings.

Is new hydraulic oil clean enough to use directly?

Often not. New oil can contain particles from manufacturing, storage and transfer that exceed the cleanliness levels recommended for hydraulic components. Filtering new oil through a transfer cart when filling or topping up is a simple way to avoid introducing contamination into the system.

How do I know if water is in my hydraulic oil?

Water can make oil look cloudy or milky, though small amounts may be invisible. Oil analysis can measure water content accurately. Signs of water problems include corrosion, sludge, filter blocking and reduced component life. Sources include condensation, leaking coolers, washing equipment and poor storage, so find and fix the source as well as removing the water.

Learn more about our hydraulic power packs with integrated filtration, or ask our engineers about improving your system's cleanliness.

posts.title: Choosing the Right Hydraulic Oil: Viscosity, Additives and Temperature
posts.metaTitle: Choosing the Right Hydraulic Oil — Viscosity & Additives
posts.metaDescription: How to choose hydraulic oil by viscosity grade, additive package and operating temperature, and when to consider fire-resistant or biodegradable fluids.
posts.excerpt: Hydraulic oil transmits power, lubricates, cools and protects. Choosing the right grade and type is one of the simplest ways to improve system reliability.
posts.imageAlt: Industrial pump and pipework in a hydraulic plant room
posts.html:
Hydraulic oil is often treated as a consumable that simply needs topping up. In reality it is a working component of the system. It transmits power, lubricates moving parts, removes heat, protects against corrosion and carries contaminants to the filters. The wrong oil can shorten component life even when everything else is done right.

What hydraulic oil has to do

  • Transmit power with minimal compressibility.
  • Lubricate pumps, motors, valves and seals.
  • Cool the system by carrying heat to the reservoir and cooler.
  • Seal small internal clearances.
  • Protect against rust, corrosion and oxidation.
  • Release air and separate from water quickly.

Viscosity: the most important property

Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flow. Hydraulic oils are classified by ISO viscosity grade (ISO VG), such as VG 32, VG 46 or VG 68. The number refers to viscosity at 40 °C.

  • Too thin: internal leakage increases, lubricating films break down and wear accelerates.
  • Too thick: flow resistance increases, pumps can cavitate on cold starts, and energy is wasted as heat.

Pump manufacturers specify an acceptable viscosity range for operation and for cold starting. The goal is to keep the oil within that range across the whole operating temperature range.

Viscosity index

Viscosity changes with temperature. The viscosity index (VI) describes how much. A high-VI oil changes less between cold and hot conditions. High-VI oils are useful for equipment that works outdoors across wide temperature swings, such as mobile cranes and construction machinery.

Common hydraulic fluid types

Fluid type Typical use Notes
Anti-wear (AW) mineral oil Most industrial and mobile systems Contains anti-wear additives for pumps
High-VI mineral oil Outdoor and mobile equipment Stable viscosity over wide temperatures
Fire-resistant fluids Steel plants, foundries, mining Different types with different seal compatibility
Biodegradable fluids Forestry, marine, environmentally sensitive sites Check compatibility and maintenance needs

Additives

Hydraulic oils contain additive packages designed for specific duties:

  • Anti-wear additives protect pump surfaces under high load.
  • Antioxidants slow oil degradation at high temperatures.
  • Rust and corrosion inhibitors protect metal surfaces.
  • Anti-foam agents help release entrained air.
  • Demulsifiers help water separate from the oil.

Mixing oils with different additive chemistries can cause additive reactions, sludge and filter blocking. Avoid mixing brands or types unless the supplier confirms compatibility.

Matching oil to operating temperature

Consider three temperatures:

  1. Cold start temperature: the oil must be thin enough for the pump to draw it without cavitation.
  2. Normal operating temperature: the oil should stay within the optimum viscosity range.
  3. Maximum temperature: the oil must not become too thin, and high temperatures accelerate oxidation.

If the system regularly runs hot, a heavier grade is not always the answer. The better solution is often to find the source of the heat and improve cooling.

Fire-resistant and special fluids

Where hydraulic leaks could reach ignition sources — foundries, steel mills, die casting and underground mining — fire-resistant fluids may be required. These fluids can require different seals, hoses, filters and maintenance practices. Changing fluid type usually needs a system review and thorough flushing.

Good oil management practices

  • Use the grade specified by the equipment or pump manufacturer.
  • Label containers and top-up points clearly to prevent mixing.
  • Filter new oil before it enters the system.
  • Monitor condition through oil analysis.
  • Change oil based on condition, not just time.
  • Investigate any unusual colour, smell, foaming or cloudiness.

Summary

Choose oil primarily on viscosity for your temperature range, then select the right fluid type and additive package for the application. Keep it clean, dry and within temperature limits, and it will protect every component in the system.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I mix different brands of hydraulic oil?

It is best to avoid mixing. Oils with different additive chemistries can react, causing sludge, foaming or reduced performance. If mixing is unavoidable, check compatibility with the oil suppliers first. Clear labelling of oil types at storage areas and top-up points helps prevent accidental mixing.

Which viscosity grade should I use?

Follow the equipment or pump manufacturer's recommendation, which is based on keeping the oil within an acceptable viscosity range at operating temperature and on cold starts. Common industrial grades include ISO VG 32, 46 and 68. Outdoor equipment with large temperature swings may benefit from a high viscosity index oil.

How often should hydraulic oil be changed?

Ideally based on condition rather than a fixed interval. Oil analysis shows whether the oil is still fit for use by checking contamination, water, oxidation and additive levels. Where analysis is not available, follow the manufacturer's recommended interval and shorten it in harsh or high-temperature conditions.

When should fire-resistant fluids be used?

Fire-resistant fluids are used where a hydraulic leak could reach an ignition source — near furnaces, molten metal, hot surfaces or in underground mining. Switching to a fire-resistant fluid requires checking compatibility of seals, hoses, filters and other materials, and usually requires thorough flushing. A risk assessment should guide the decision.

Our hydraulic power packs are designed with appropriate cooling and filtration for the specified fluid. Contact our engineers for advice on your system.

posts.title: Hydraulic System Overheating: Causes and Practical Fixes
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic System Overheating: Causes & Practical Fixes
posts.metaDescription: Why hydraulic systems overheat, how heat damages oil and seals, and practical fixes from relief valve settings and coolers to circuit design.
posts.excerpt: Overheating is a symptom, not a fault in itself. Find where the system is wasting energy and you will usually find the cause of the heat.
posts.imageAlt: Technician checking an industrial hydraulic power unit
posts.html:
Hot hydraulic oil is a warning sign. High temperatures thin the oil, increase internal leakage, harden seals and accelerate oil degradation. Running hot for long periods significantly shortens the life of pumps, seals and the oil itself.

The key to fixing overheating is understanding where the heat comes from.

Where does the heat come from?

Hydraulic heat is wasted energy. Any time oil flows from high pressure to low pressure without doing useful work, that energy is converted into heat. Common sources include:

  • oil flowing over the relief valve;
  • flow being throttled through flow control valves;
  • internal leakage in worn pumps, motors, valves and cylinders;
  • pressure drops in undersized hoses, pipes and valves;
  • a pump running at full flow when the machine is idle.

Why heat is harmful

  • Viscosity drops, increasing leakage and reducing lubricating film strength.
  • Seals harden, crack and lose their sealing ability.
  • Oil oxidises faster, forming varnish and sludge.
  • Efficiency falls, so the system generates even more heat.

Common causes and fixes

1. Relief valve set too low or system running over relief

If the relief valve opens during normal operation, all excess flow is converted to heat. Check the relief setting against the system requirements and check that other pressure settings, such as pump compensators, are correctly coordinated.

2. Pump running unloaded at full pressure

Fixed-displacement pumps in simple circuits may push full flow over the relief valve when actuators are idle. Options include unloading valves, open-centre valves that return flow to tank at low pressure, or variable-displacement pumps.

3. Worn components

Worn pumps and motors leak internally, converting energy to heat. Rising case drain flow on piston pumps and motors is a useful indicator of wear.

4. Undersized lines and valves

High flow velocities in small hoses and valves create pressure drops and heat. Review line sizes, particularly in return lines and after system modifications that increased flow.

5. Cooling problems

Air-blast coolers clog with dust and debris; water coolers scale up or lose flow. Fans fail, thermostats stick and coolers get bypassed. Clean and inspect coolers regularly.

6. Low oil level or undersized reservoir

A low oil level reduces the time oil spends in the tank and reduces heat dissipation. Systems that have grown over time may have outgrown their reservoir.

7. High ambient temperatures

Units in hot environments — near furnaces, in direct sun or in enclosed spaces — have less temperature difference available to shed heat. Ventilation, relocation or extra cooling may be needed.

A practical troubleshooting sequence

  1. Measure oil temperature at the reservoir and, if possible, across major components using an infrared thermometer.
  2. Check oil level and cooler condition.
  3. Check relief and compensator settings against specifications.
  4. Look for hot spots: a valve or component much hotter than its surroundings is often where energy is being lost.
  5. Check case drain flows on pumps and motors.
  6. Review the circuit for throttling and unnecessary pressure drops.

Design improvements

When overheating is caused by the design rather than a fault, consider:

  • variable-displacement or load-sensing pumps;
  • accumulators to meet peak demand with a smaller pump;
  • larger coolers or adding cooling capacity;
  • better reservoir design;
  • reducing throttling losses with improved valve selection.

Monitor temperature

Fit a temperature gauge or sensor on the reservoir and record readings. A gradual increase over months often indicates wear or cooler fouling, giving you time to act before failures occur.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a normal operating temperature for hydraulic oil?

It depends on the oil, components and application, but many systems are designed to run within a moderate range well below the temperature at which seals and oil degrade rapidly. Check the oil and component manufacturers' recommendations. More important than a single number is consistency: a system that runs hotter than it used to is telling you something has changed.

Can a larger cooler fix overheating?

It can control the symptom, but it does not fix wasted energy. If the system is overheating because oil continuously flows over a relief valve or through worn components, a bigger cooler only removes heat that should not be generated in the first place. Find and fix the source of heat first, then size cooling appropriately.

Why does my system overheat only in summer?

Higher ambient temperatures reduce the temperature difference available for cooling, so the same system sheds less heat. Dust on cooler fins, poor ventilation and direct sunlight make it worse. Clean coolers, improve airflow and check that the system is not wasting energy. If necessary, add cooling capacity for peak conditions.

How do I find where heat is being generated?

An infrared thermometer or thermal camera helps identify hot spots. A valve, motor or pump significantly hotter than nearby components is often where energy is being lost — for example, through internal leakage or continuous relief valve flow. Combining temperature readings with pressure measurements and circuit diagrams usually reveals the cause.

posts.title: Hydraulic Accumulators: Types, Uses and Safety Considerations
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Accumulators: Types, Uses and Safety
posts.metaDescription: How hydraulic accumulators store energy, the differences between bladder, piston and diaphragm types, common applications and essential safety practices.
posts.excerpt: Accumulators store hydraulic energy for later use, smoothing pressure and boosting performance. They also store energy when the system is off — which makes safety essential.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer reviewing hydraulic system documentation
posts.html:
A hydraulic accumulator is a pressure vessel that stores hydraulic fluid under pressure, usually against a compressed gas. When the system needs more flow than the pump can supply, the accumulator releases stored fluid. When demand drops, it refills.

Accumulators can make systems smaller, more efficient and smoother — but they also store energy that remains after the pump stops. Understanding how they work is essential for safe maintenance.

How an accumulator works

Most industrial accumulators are gas-charged. A separating element — a bladder, piston or diaphragm — divides the vessel into a gas side, pre-charged with dry nitrogen, and an oil side connected to the hydraulic system.

As system pressure rises above the pre-charge pressure, oil enters and compresses the gas. When system pressure falls, the compressed gas pushes oil back into the circuit.

Types of accumulators

Type Characteristics Typical uses
Bladder Fast response, good for pulsation damping and energy storage Mobile and industrial systems
Piston Large volumes, higher pressure ratios, tolerant of large shells Heavy industry, large energy storage
Diaphragm Compact, smaller volumes Pulsation damping, small circuits

Common applications

  • Energy storage: supply peak flow so a smaller pump and motor can be used.
  • Emergency power: complete a movement, such as closing a valve or lowering a load safely, if power fails.
  • Pressure maintenance: compensate for leakage and hold pressure for clamping without running the pump continuously.
  • Shock absorption: absorb pressure spikes from fast valve shifts.
  • Pulsation damping: smooth pump flow ripple.
  • Thermal expansion compensation: absorb volume changes in closed circuits.

The importance of pre-charge pressure

The nitrogen pre-charge pressure determines how the accumulator performs. If it is too low, the accumulator delivers less usable volume and the separating element can be damaged. If it is too high, oil may not enter at all.

Pre-charge pressure should be checked regularly with the correct charging and gauging equipment, with the oil side fully depressurised. Loss of pre-charge is a common, easily overlooked cause of poor system performance.

Safety considerations

Accumulators store energy even when the pump is off. Many hydraulic injuries happen because people assume a stopped system is safe.

Always:

  • Discharge the oil side of the accumulator before working on the circuit, using the system's dump or bleed valve, and confirm with a pressure gauge.
  • Use only nitrogen for pre-charging. Never use oxygen or compressed air, which can cause explosions.
  • Use proper charging equipment and follow the manufacturer's procedures.
  • Respect the vessel's pressure rating and local pressure-vessel regulations, including any inspection or certification requirements.
  • Label circuits containing accumulators so maintenance staff are aware of stored energy.
  • Ensure accumulator circuits have a safety block with a relief valve and isolation and bleed valves.

Signs of accumulator problems

  • Pump cycling on and off more frequently than normal.
  • Loss of emergency function or reduced cycle speed.
  • Increased pressure spikes and noise.
  • Pressure dropping quickly when the pump stops.

These often indicate lost pre-charge, a failed bladder or piston seal, or an incorrectly sized accumulator.

Sizing accumulators

Accumulator sizing depends on the volume of oil needed, the minimum and maximum working pressures, the pre-charge pressure and whether gas compression is fast (adiabatic) or slow (isothermal). Correct sizing calculations are important both for performance and safety.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should accumulator pre-charge be checked?

Follow the manufacturer's recommendation, which depends on accumulator type and duty. Many maintenance programmes check pre-charge periodically and after any maintenance on the circuit. Checks must be done with the oil side fully depressurised and using proper charging and gauging equipment. Local regulations may also set inspection requirements for pressure vessels.

Why must accumulators only be charged with nitrogen?

Nitrogen is inert and dry. Oxygen or compressed air mixed with hydraulic oil under pressure can create an explosion risk, and air introduces moisture. Always use dry nitrogen and the correct charging equipment, following the accumulator manufacturer's instructions.

Can an accumulator be dangerous when the machine is off?

Yes. An accumulator can hold pressurised oil after the pump stops, which can move actuators unexpectedly or spray high-pressure oil when a fitting is loosened. Always discharge the oil side and verify zero pressure with a gauge before working on the circuit, and label systems containing accumulators.

What are signs of a failed accumulator?

Signs include the pump cycling on and off more often, loss of emergency functions, more pressure pulsation or shock, and pressure dropping quickly when the pump stops. These may indicate lost pre-charge, a ruptured bladder or worn piston seals. Investigate promptly, as the accumulator may no longer provide the protection or performance the system relies on.

Our engineers include accumulators in hydraulic power packs and custom systems where they improve efficiency or safety, complete with safety blocks. Ask us about your application.

posts.title: Reading a Hydraulic Circuit Diagram: A Beginner's Guide to ISO Symbols
posts.metaTitle: Reading Hydraulic Circuit Diagrams: ISO Symbols Guide
posts.metaDescription: Learn to read hydraulic circuit diagrams, including ISO 1219 symbols for pumps, valves, cylinders and filters, and how to trace a circuit step by step.
posts.excerpt: A hydraulic circuit diagram is the map of a system. Learn to read the symbols and you can troubleshoot faster, communicate clearly and avoid costly mistakes.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer working on technical drawings
posts.html:
A hydraulic circuit diagram shows how the components of a system are connected and how they work together. It does not show where parts are physically located; it shows how oil flows and how the system behaves. For maintenance teams, being able to read a schematic turns troubleshooting from guesswork into logic.

Most modern diagrams use symbols based on the international standard ISO 1219. Once you recognise the basic building blocks, even complex circuits become readable.

Lines

  • Solid lines are working lines: pressure, suction and return.
  • Dashed lines are pilot or control lines that carry signals rather than working flow.
  • Dotted or thin dashed lines often show drain lines.
  • A dot where lines cross means they are connected; lines crossing without a dot are not connected.

Energy conversion symbols

Pumps

A pump is drawn as a circle with a solid triangle pointing outwards, showing that energy leaves the pump as flow. A diagonal arrow through the symbol indicates variable displacement.

Motors

A hydraulic motor is a circle with a solid triangle pointing inwards, because energy enters the motor from the fluid.

Cylinders

Cylinders are drawn as rectangles with a piston and rod. A single-acting cylinder has one port; a double-acting cylinder has two. Cushioning is shown with small rectangles at the ends, sometimes with an arrow for adjustable cushions.

Valve symbols: the "boxes"

Directional control valves are drawn as a row of squares (envelopes). Each square represents one switching position. Arrows inside show flow paths; T-shapes show blocked ports.

  • A 4/3 valve has four ports and three positions.
  • Ports are commonly labelled P (pressure), T (tank), A and B (work ports).
  • The valve is drawn in its normal (unactuated) position, which is the box connected to the lines.

The symbols at the ends of the valve show how it is operated: a lever for manual operation, a box with a diagonal line for a solenoid, a spring for return, and a dashed triangle for pilot operation.

Centre conditions

The middle position of a 3-position valve is very important:

Centre type Behaviour
Closed centre All ports blocked; actuator holds, pump flow must go elsewhere
Open centre Pump flow returns to tank; actuator may move under load
Float centre A and B to tank; actuator can move freely
Tandem centre P to T; A and B blocked — pump unloads and actuator holds

Pressure control valves

Pressure valves are drawn as a single square with an arrow offset from the flow line and a spring. A dashed pilot line shows the pressure being sensed.

  • Relief valve: normally closed; opens to tank when pressure exceeds its setting.
  • Pressure reducing valve: normally open; limits downstream pressure.
  • Sequence valve: opens to allow flow to a second circuit once pressure reaches a set point.
  • Counterbalance valve: holds a load and controls lowering speed.

Flow control and check valves

  • A check valve is a ball against a seat, allowing flow in one direction only.
  • A pilot-operated check valve includes a pilot line that can open it in the reverse direction.
  • A flow control valve shows a restriction, sometimes with a check valve in parallel for free return flow.

Conditioning and accessories

  • Filters are drawn as a diamond with a dashed line across.
  • Coolers are diamonds with outward arrows; heaters have inward arrows.
  • Accumulators are drawn as an oval or capsule shape.
  • Pressure gauges are circles with a pointer.
  • The reservoir is an open rectangle at the bottom of the diagram.

How to read a circuit step by step

  1. Start at the pump and follow the pressure line.
  2. Find the relief valve to understand the maximum system pressure.
  3. Follow each directional valve to its actuator and identify the normal position.
  4. Shift the valve mentally into each position and trace where oil goes.
  5. Trace the return path back through filters and coolers to the tank.
  6. Look for load-holding devices and how they are piloted.
  7. Check pilot and drain lines, which are often where subtle faults hide.

Why schematics matter in troubleshooting

With a schematic, you can identify which valves could cause a symptom, where to fit gauges and how components interact. Without one, it is easy to replace good parts. If your equipment lacks up-to-date diagrams, consider having them prepared — every custom system we supply includes a circuit diagram.

Frequently Asked Questions

What standard do hydraulic symbols follow?

Most modern hydraulic schematics use symbols based on ISO 1219. Older drawings or those from different regions may use slightly different conventions, but the core ideas — circles for pumps and motors, boxes for valve positions, diamonds for filters and coolers — are widely recognised. A legend on the drawing helps interpret any special symbols.

What do P, T, A and B mean on a valve?

P is the pressure port connected to the pump supply, T is the tank or return port, and A and B are the work ports connected to the actuator. Some valves also have drain (L or Y) and pilot (X) ports. Understanding these labels helps you trace where oil flows in each valve position.

Why is the valve drawn in a particular position?

Valves are drawn in their normal (unactuated) position — the position they take when no signal or force is applied. This is the box connected to the circuit lines. To understand other positions, imagine sliding the boxes across so that a different box connects to the lines.

My machine has no circuit diagram. What should I do?

Ask the equipment manufacturer first. If no diagram is available, a hydraulic engineer can survey the system and create one. A current, accurate schematic makes troubleshooting faster, supports safe maintenance and helps when ordering replacement components or planning upgrades.

posts.title: Preventive Maintenance Checklist for Hydraulic Power Units
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Power Unit Maintenance Checklist (Daily–Annual)
posts.metaDescription: A practical daily, weekly, monthly and annual preventive maintenance checklist for hydraulic power units covering oil, filters, leaks, temperatures and safety.
posts.excerpt: A simple, consistent preventive maintenance routine prevents most hydraulic power unit failures. Use this checklist as the starting point for your own.
posts.imageAlt: Technician inspecting an industrial power unit
posts.html:
Hydraulic power units rarely fail suddenly. Most failures are preceded by warning signs — rising temperatures, noise, leaks, slower cycles — that a regular inspection routine would catch. This checklist gives you a practical starting point. Always adapt it to the manufacturer's recommendations and your operating conditions.

Safety note: perform inspections in line with your site's procedures. Before opening any part of the hydraulic system, isolate power, relieve pressure, discharge accumulators and secure suspended loads.

Daily checks (operators)

  • Oil level in the sight glass is within the normal range.
  • Oil temperature is within its normal operating range.
  • No new leaks on hoses, fittings, valves and cylinders.
  • Unusual noise: whining, knocking or rattling from the pump or motor.
  • Filter indicators are not showing a blocked condition.
  • Gauges show normal working pressures.
  • Machine behaviour: no unusual slowness, jerkiness or drift.

Record anything unusual. A simple log makes trends visible.

Weekly checks

  • Inspect hoses for abrasion, cracking, kinks and bulges.
  • Check hose clamps and supports are secure.
  • Clean the air-blast cooler fins in dusty environments.
  • Check the reservoir breather condition.
  • Look at oil appearance in the sight glass: cloudiness may indicate water or air.
  • Check motor and pump mounting bolts and couplings.

Monthly checks

  • Take an oil sample for analysis on critical systems, or at least inspect a sample visually.
  • Measure case drain flow on piston pumps and motors where possible, and compare with previous readings.
  • Check relief valve and pressure settings against the specification.
  • Inspect electrical connections on solenoids and sensors.
  • Check accumulator pre-charge where the schedule requires it, following the correct procedure.
  • Test emergency stop and safety functions.

Quarterly to six-monthly checks

  • Replace filter elements if not already replaced on condition.
  • Clean or check suction strainers.
  • Inspect cylinder rods for damage and corrosion.
  • Check coupling elements between motor and pump for wear.
  • Review temperature and pressure logs for trends.

Annual checks

  • Comprehensive oil analysis and, if required, oil change and reservoir cleaning.
  • Inspect the reservoir interior for sludge, water and debris.
  • Pressure test and inspect hoses; replace hoses according to age, condition and risk.
  • Thermographic survey of motors, pumps, valves and coolers.
  • Verify accumulator certification and inspection requirements under local regulations.
  • Review the spare parts list for critical items.

What to watch for

Observation Possible cause
Rising oil temperature over weeks Cooler fouling, internal wear
Pump noise or whine Cavitation, aeration, low oil, blocked suction
Milky oil Water contamination
Foam in reservoir Air ingress, low level, return line issues
Slow cycle times Pump wear, internal leakage, incorrect settings
Frequent filter changes Contamination source, component wear

Keep records

A maintenance log turns inspections into useful data. Record temperatures, pressures, filter changes, oil analysis results and repairs. Comparing readings over time is often the clearest indication that something is wearing.

Plan spares for critical units

For power units that stop production when they fail, keep critical spares on site: filter elements, seal kits, a spare solenoid coil, hoses and, for the most critical systems, a spare pump.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who should carry out daily checks on a power unit?

Operators are usually best placed to perform simple daily checks: oil level, temperature, visible leaks, unusual noise and filter indicators. They see the machine every day and notice changes. Detailed inspections, adjustments and repairs should be performed by trained maintenance personnel following safe isolation procedures.

Should filters be changed on a schedule or by indicator?

Ideally by condition — when the clogging indicator approaches its limit or oil analysis shows cleanliness drifting from target — with a maximum time interval as a safety net. Changing purely by calendar can waste elements or, worse, leave a blocked filter in bypass for weeks. Always investigate sudden increases in filter change frequency.

Why keep maintenance logs?

Logs reveal trends that single inspections miss: gradual temperature increases, rising case drain flow, more frequent filter changes or longer cycle times. These trends often give months of warning before a failure, allowing repairs to be planned around production rather than forced by breakdowns.

Which spares should be kept for a power unit?

At minimum, filter elements, seal kits for key components and common hoses. For critical units, add a spare solenoid coil, pressure gauges and, where downtime would be very costly, a spare pump or complete motor-pump assembly. Review spares after each breakdown to see what would have shortened the repair.

posts.title: Hydraulic Filtration Explained: Suction, Pressure and Return Filters
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Filtration Explained: Suction, Pressure, Return
posts.metaDescription: Where hydraulic filters go, what micron ratings and beta ratios mean, how to choose filtration levels and when to change filter elements.
posts.excerpt: Filters are your system's main defence against contamination. Understanding where each filter goes and what its rating means helps you protect expensive components.
posts.imageAlt: Hydraulic pump and pipework installation
posts.html:
Contamination is responsible for the majority of hydraulic component failures, and filtration is the primary defence against it. But not all filters do the same job. Where a filter is placed, how fine it is and how it is maintained all affect how well it protects the system.

Why filtration matters

Pumps, valves and motors have internal clearances measured in microns. Particles of a similar size enter those clearances and cause abrasive wear. The wear creates more particles, and the damage accelerates. Effective filtration breaks this cycle.

Filter locations

Suction filters and strainers

Placed on the pump inlet, suction strainers protect the pump from large debris. They are usually coarse, because fine filters on the suction side restrict flow and can cause cavitation. Many modern designs avoid fine suction filtration for this reason and rely on other filters to keep the oil clean.

Pressure filters

Pressure filters sit after the pump and protect sensitive downstream components such as servo and proportional valves. They must withstand full system pressure, so housings are robust. They provide the highest level of protection for specific components.

Return line filters

Return filters clean oil before it goes back into the reservoir. They capture contaminants generated by the system or ingressed through cylinders. They operate at low pressure, making them economical, and they are the most common main filtration point in many systems.

Offline (kidney loop) filtration

An independent pump circulates oil from the reservoir through a filter and back again. Offline filtration can run continuously regardless of machine operation and is very effective for large reservoirs and critical systems. It is also useful for cleaning oil after maintenance.

Breathers

As oil level changes, air moves in and out of the reservoir. A breather filter stops dust entering with that air. Desiccant breathers also remove moisture.

Understanding filter ratings

Micron rating

The micron rating describes the particle size the filter is designed to capture. A smaller number means finer filtration. On its own, however, a micron rating says little about how efficiently the filter captures particles.

Beta ratio

The beta ratio measures efficiency: the number of particles of a given size upstream divided by the number downstream. A higher beta ratio means a more efficient filter at that particle size. Quality filter elements are specified with both a particle size and a beta ratio.

Choosing filtration levels

Select filtration based on the most sensitive component in the system and the target oil cleanliness recommended by its manufacturer. Systems with servo or proportional valves, high pressures or expensive piston pumps require cleaner oil than simple low-pressure circuits.

Component sensitivity Filtration approach
Simple gear pump circuits Return line filtration, good breathers
Piston pumps, high pressure Finer return filtration, possibly pressure filtration
Proportional and servo valves Fine pressure filtration plus return filtration
Large reservoirs, critical systems Add offline filtration

Bypass valves and indicators

Most filters include a bypass valve that opens when the element becomes blocked, preventing the element from collapsing or starving the pump. When it opens, unfiltered oil passes through the system. That is why clogging indicators — visual or electrical — are important. They tell you to change the element before bypass occurs.

When to change filter elements

  • When the clogging indicator shows the element is approaching bypass.
  • When oil analysis shows cleanliness is outside target.
  • According to the manufacturer's maximum interval, even if the indicator has not triggered.
  • After any major component failure or system repair.

Frequent filter blocking is a symptom. It may indicate a failing component generating wear particles, a contamination source, or an incorrect element.

Good filtration practice

  • Use genuine or equivalent-quality elements with documented ratings.
  • Never run without an element installed.
  • Change elements in clean conditions and inspect used elements for debris.
  • Filter new oil before adding it to the system.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I fit a fine filter on the pump suction?

Usually not. Fine filters on the suction side create pressure drop that can starve the pump and cause cavitation, especially with cold oil. Suction strainers are normally coarse to protect against large debris, while fine filtration is placed in the return line, pressure line or an offline loop. Follow the pump manufacturer's inlet requirements.

What is a beta ratio?

The beta ratio describes filter efficiency at a specific particle size: the number of particles upstream divided by the number downstream. A higher ratio means the filter captures a higher proportion of particles of that size. Comparing beta ratios at the same particle size is a better way to compare filters than comparing nominal micron ratings.

What happens when a filter goes into bypass?

When the element becomes clogged, a bypass valve opens to protect the filter and maintain flow. Unfiltered oil then circulates through the system, allowing contamination to reach sensitive components. Clogging indicators warn you before bypass occurs, so elements can be changed in time.

Is offline filtration worth adding?

For large reservoirs, critical systems or systems that struggle to reach target cleanliness, offline (kidney loop) filtration is very effective. It filters continuously, independent of machine operation, and can also remove water with suitable elements. It is often one of the most cost-effective ways to improve component life.

All our hydraulic power packs include filtration matched to the components used, with clogging indicators as standard. Ask our team about upgrading your system's filtration.

posts.title: Gear vs Vane vs Piston Pumps: Choosing the Right Hydraulic Pump
posts.keyword: gear vs vane vs piston pumps
posts.metaTitle: Gear vs Vane vs Piston Pumps: Which Hydraulic Pump?
posts.metaDescription: Compare gear, vane and piston hydraulic pumps on pressure, efficiency, noise, contamination tolerance and cost to choose the right pump for your application.
posts.excerpt: Gear, vane and piston pumps all create flow, but they differ in pressure capability, efficiency, noise and cost. Here is how to choose between them.
posts.imageAlt: Electric motor and pump assembly in an industrial plant
posts.html:
Every hydraulic system starts with a pump. The pump converts mechanical rotation into hydraulic flow, and the type of pump you choose affects efficiency, noise, maintenance and the overall cost of the system. The three most common designs are gear, vane and piston pumps.

A key principle: pumps create flow, not pressure

A hydraulic pump moves a volume of oil for every revolution. Pressure only builds when that flow meets resistance from a load or a valve. This is why pressure ratings describe what a pump can withstand, while displacement describes what it delivers.

Gear pumps

Gear pumps use meshing gears to carry oil from the inlet to the outlet. External gear pumps are the most common; internal gear pumps offer quieter operation.

Strengths

  • Simple, robust and economical.
  • Compact for the flow they deliver.
  • Relatively tolerant of contamination compared with piston pumps.
  • Widely available and easy to replace.

Limitations

  • Fixed displacement only.
  • Efficiency falls as they wear.
  • External gear pumps can be noisy.

Typical uses: mobile equipment, simple industrial power packs, lubrication systems, auxiliary circuits.

Vane pumps

Vane pumps use a rotor with sliding vanes inside a cam ring. As the rotor turns, the vanes trap and carry oil.

Strengths

  • Quiet operation, making them popular in factories.
  • Good efficiency at medium pressures.
  • Variable displacement versions available.
  • Vane wear is partly self-compensating.

Limitations

  • Generally lower maximum pressure than piston pumps.
  • Sensitive to contamination and to viscosity at cold start.

Typical uses: machine tools, plastic injection machines, industrial power units where low noise matters.

Piston pumps

Piston pumps use reciprocating pistons in a rotating cylinder block. Axial piston pumps are the most common in industrial and mobile hydraulics; radial piston pumps are used for very high pressures.

Strengths

  • Highest pressure capability.
  • High volumetric and overall efficiency.
  • Variable displacement with pressure compensation, load sensing and other controls.
  • Excellent energy efficiency in systems with varying demand.

Limitations

  • Higher purchase and repair cost.
  • Require clean oil and correct installation, including case drain lines.

Typical uses: cranes, excavators, presses, heavy industrial systems, high-pressure and energy-efficient circuits.

Side-by-side comparison

Feature Gear Vane Piston
Pressure capability Low–medium/high Medium High
Efficiency Moderate Good Very good
Noise Moderate–high Low Moderate
Contamination tolerance Best Moderate Lowest
Variable displacement No Yes (some) Yes
Initial cost Lowest Medium Highest

How to choose

  1. Pressure requirement: high working pressures point towards piston pumps.
  2. Duty cycle: if demand varies widely, a variable-displacement pump saves energy and reduces heat.
  3. Noise limits: indoor installations near workers may favour vane or internal gear pumps.
  4. Contamination risk: harsh environments with limited maintenance may favour robust gear pumps.
  5. Budget and lifecycle cost: a cheaper pump that wastes energy as heat can cost more over its life.
  6. Mounting and drive: shaft type, flange standard and rotation direction must match.

Replacing an existing pump

When replacing a pump, record the nameplate details, displacement, rotation direction, shaft type, mounting flange and port details. If the original pump failed early, investigate why — contamination, cavitation and incorrect start-up are common causes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which hydraulic pump type is the most efficient?

Piston pumps generally offer the highest volumetric and overall efficiency, especially at high pressures, and variable displacement versions can save significant energy by delivering only the flow the system needs. Vane pumps are efficient at medium pressures. Gear pumps are typically the least efficient, and their efficiency drops further as they wear. For machines that run long hours, the energy cost difference can outweigh the higher purchase price of a piston pump.

Can I replace a gear pump with a piston pump?

Often yes, but it is not a simple swap. A piston pump may need a case drain line, different mounting and shaft details, cleaner oil and different control settings. The circuit may also need changes to take advantage of variable displacement. Have the change reviewed by a hydraulic engineer so the new pump is installed and set up correctly.

Why are gear pumps so common on mobile equipment?

They are compact, robust, relatively tolerant of contamination and inexpensive. On many mobile machines, a gear pump provides adequate performance for auxiliary functions at a low cost, and replacement is quick and easy. More demanding mobile machines, such as excavators and cranes, often use piston pumps for their main functions.

What causes a vane pump to fail early?

Common causes include contamination, which wears the cam ring and vanes; running with oil that is too thick at start-up, which can stop vanes extending properly; cavitation from inlet restrictions; and running at pressures above the pump's rating. Clean oil, correct viscosity and good inlet conditions are the keys to long vane pump life.

How do I identify which pump I have?

Look for a nameplate or part number on the pump body. If it is missing, note the mounting flange, shaft type, port sizes, rotation direction and physical construction, and photograph the pump from several angles. A hydraulic specialist can usually identify the type and displacement from this information, or by inspecting the pump.

posts.title: Hydraulic Pump Cavitation and Aeration: Symptoms and Solutions
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Pump Cavitation & Aeration: Causes and Fixes
posts.metaDescription: How to recognise hydraulic pump cavitation and aeration, why they damage pumps so quickly, and the practical fixes for suction and air ingress problems.
posts.excerpt: A whining pump and foaming oil are warning signs. Cavitation and aeration can destroy a pump quickly — but both are usually preventable.
posts.imageAlt: Technician working on a mechanical drive assembly
posts.html:
Cavitation and aeration are two of the most common causes of hydraulic pump damage. They sound similar — both make the pump noisy — and they are often confused. Understanding the difference helps you fix the real problem quickly.

What is cavitation?

Cavitation occurs when pressure at the pump inlet drops so low that vapour bubbles form in the oil. When these bubbles move into the high-pressure side of the pump, they collapse violently. The implosions erode metal surfaces, creating pitted, sponge-like damage.

What is aeration?

Aeration happens when air enters the oil, usually through a suction leak, a low oil level or poor return line design. The air bubbles compress as they enter the high-pressure side and can cause similar noise, heat and damage to cavitation.

Symptoms

Symptom Cavitation Aeration
Noise Steady high-pitched whine Erratic knocking or rattling
Oil appearance Usually clear Foamy or milky with bubbles
Actuator motion Slow, loss of power Spongy, jerky movement
Temperature Increases Increases, oil oxidises
Pump damage Erosion pitting Erosion, micro-dieseling, scorched oil

Common causes of cavitation

  • Clogged suction strainer or inlet filter.
  • Undersized or long suction line with excessive pressure drop.
  • Oil too thick, especially during cold starts.
  • Pump running too fast for its inlet conditions.
  • Pump mounted too high above the oil level.
  • Collapsed or kinked suction hose.
  • Blocked reservoir breather, creating a vacuum in the tank.

Common causes of aeration

  • Loose suction fittings or damaged hose drawing air in.
  • Low reservoir oil level, allowing vortexing at the suction.
  • Worn pump shaft seal on pumps with inlet pressure below atmospheric.
  • Return lines discharging above the oil surface, creating turbulence.
  • Poor reservoir design with insufficient settling time.
  • Air not bled from the system after maintenance.

How to diagnose

  1. Listen to the pump and note the type of noise.
  2. Check the oil level and look for foam in the reservoir.
  3. Inspect suction components: strainer, hose, clamps and fittings.
  4. Measure inlet vacuum with a suitable gauge where a test point exists. Compare with the pump manufacturer's inlet limits.
  5. Check oil temperature and viscosity, particularly in cold weather.
  6. A classic test for air leaks is to carefully apply clean oil around suction fittings while running; if the noise changes, air is being drawn in at that point. Follow safe procedures when working near rotating equipment.

Solutions

For cavitation

  • Clean or replace the suction strainer.
  • Increase suction line diameter and shorten the line.
  • Use the correct oil viscosity and warm the oil before high-load operation in cold climates.
  • Reduce pump speed if it exceeds inlet limits.
  • Mount the pump below the oil level (flooded inlet) where possible.
  • Make sure the breather is clean and correctly sized.

For aeration

  • Tighten or replace suction fittings and hoses.
  • Maintain the correct oil level.
  • Replace worn shaft seals.
  • Extend return lines below the oil surface and use diffusers.
  • Improve reservoir baffling.
  • Bleed air thoroughly after maintenance.

Why act quickly

Both conditions damage pumps progressively. Erosion debris then contaminates the whole system, damaging valves and cylinders. A pump that has suffered severe cavitation usually needs rebuilding — and if the inlet condition is not corrected, the replacement will suffer the same fate.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I tell cavitation from aeration by sound?

Cavitation usually produces a steady, high-pitched whine that changes with pump speed and inlet conditions. Aeration tends to sound more erratic — a knocking, rattling or "marbles" noise — often accompanied by foam in the reservoir. The sound alone is not conclusive, so check inlet vacuum, oil level, foam and suction fittings to confirm.

Can cold weather cause cavitation?

Yes. Cold oil is much thicker, so the pump has to work harder to draw it through the suction line. The inlet pressure can drop below the pump's limit, causing cavitation. Warming the oil before heavy operation, using an oil grade suited to the climate and ensuring the suction line is generously sized all help.

Is it safe to look for suction leaks with the pump running?

Only with great care and following safe procedures for working near rotating machinery. A common method is applying clean oil around suction fittings and listening for a change in pump noise. Never put hands near couplings or rotating parts, and if in doubt, stop the machine and inspect fittings, hoses and clamps with the system isolated.

Will a cavitated pump need to be replaced?

Not always, but cavitation erodes internal surfaces and can lead to rapid wear. A pump that has suffered significant cavitation should be inspected. Even if it is still working, its efficiency may be reduced. Whatever the outcome, correct the inlet conditions first — otherwise a new or repaired pump will suffer the same damage.

Does aeration affect hydraulic oil?

Yes. Entrained air accelerates oxidation of the oil, causes overheating and can create localised high temperatures that darken and degrade the oil. Aerated oil also makes actuators spongy and less precise. Fixing air leaks, maintaining oil level and improving reservoir design protect both the oil and the components.

posts.title: 8 Warning Signs Your Hydraulic Pump Is Failing
posts.metaTitle: 8 Warning Signs Your Hydraulic Pump Is Failing
posts.metaDescription: Learn the early warning signs of hydraulic pump failure — noise, heat, slow cycles, pressure loss and leaks — and how to respond before a breakdown.
posts.excerpt: Hydraulic pumps usually give plenty of warning before they fail. Recognising the signs early lets you plan a repair instead of reacting to a breakdown.
posts.imageAlt: Technician operating precision machinery
posts.html:
A hydraulic pump rarely fails without warning. Wear develops gradually, and the system tells you about it — if you know what to look for. Spotting these signs early allows you to plan a repair or replacement during scheduled downtime instead of facing an unexpected breakdown.

1. Unusual noise

A healthy pump has a consistent sound. New noises are an early warning:

  • High-pitched whining often points to cavitation.
  • Knocking or rattling can indicate aeration or internal mechanical damage.
  • Grinding may indicate bearing failure.

Noise problems are often caused by inlet conditions rather than the pump itself, so check the suction side before condemning the pump.

2. Slower machine operation

If cylinders and motors move more slowly than before, the pump may be delivering less flow because of internal wear. Worn components allow oil to leak internally from the outlet back to the inlet, so less oil reaches the actuators — especially at high pressure and temperature.

3. Loss of pressure or force

A pump that can no longer build pressure under load may be worn, or a control such as a pressure compensator may be faulty. Remember that a pump creates flow; low pressure can also be caused by a relief valve that is set too low or stuck open. Test methodically before replacing parts.

4. Rising oil temperature

Internal leakage converts energy into heat. A gradual rise in operating temperature over weeks or months is a classic sign of a wearing pump or motor.

5. Increased case drain flow

Piston pumps and motors have a case drain line that returns internal leakage to the tank. As the pump wears, case drain flow increases. Measuring case drain flow periodically and comparing it with baseline readings is one of the most useful condition-monitoring checks for piston units.

6. External leakage

Leaks from the shaft seal, housing joints or ports may indicate seal wear, excessive case pressure, or damage. A leaking shaft seal can also allow air into the pump on some designs.

7. Contaminated oil and metal particles

Metal particles in filters, on magnetic plugs or in oil analysis results can indicate internal wear. Rapidly blocking filters are another clue. Oil analysis showing rising wear metals is an early warning worth acting on.

8. Vibration

Increased vibration can come from worn bearings, misaligned couplings or internal damage. Vibration monitoring on critical units can detect problems long before they are audible.

What to do when you see warning signs

  1. Record the symptom and when it started.
  2. Check the basics: oil level, oil condition, filters, suction line and temperature.
  3. Measure: pressures, flow if possible, case drain flow and temperatures.
  4. Compare with baseline data from when the system was healthy.
  5. Plan the repair before the pump fails completely and contaminates the system.

Why early action saves money

When a pump fails catastrophically, metal debris spreads through valves, cylinders and hoses. Clean-up and secondary damage can cost far more than the pump itself. Repairing or replacing a pump at the first signs of wear avoids this.

Common root causes to fix

Root cause Prevention
Contamination Better filtration, clean oil handling
Cavitation Correct suction design and oil viscosity
Overheating Fix heat sources, maintain coolers
Incorrect start-up Fill and bleed pump case before start
Misalignment Check couplings and mounting

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a hydraulic pump fail suddenly without warning?

Sudden failures do happen — for example, from severe cavitation, running dry or a mechanical break — but most pumps show warning signs first, such as noise, heat, slower cycles or increased case drain flow. Regular observation and simple measurements catch many problems early enough to plan a repair.

What is a healthy case drain flow?

Manufacturers often publish expected leakage values for new pumps, but the most practical approach is to measure case drain flow when the pump is known to be healthy and use that as a baseline. Repeat measurements under the same pressure, speed and temperature conditions. A steady increase indicates wear.

Could low pressure be caused by something other than the pump?

Yes. A relief valve set too low or stuck open, internal leakage in valves or cylinders, or a faulty pressure compensator can all cause low pressure. Remember that pumps create flow; pressure only builds when flow meets resistance. Test systematically before replacing the pump.

How does oil analysis help detect pump wear?

Oil analysis can show increasing levels of wear metals such as iron, copper or other elements used in pump components. Rising particle counts and changes in oil condition can also point to wear or contamination. Analysed regularly, it can give early warning before noise or performance changes appear.

Should I replace the pump or repair it?

Compare the cost and lead time of repair against a new pump, consider the pump's age and availability, and think about efficiency upgrades. For larger and more expensive pumps, professional repair with performance testing is often good value. For small, inexpensive gear pumps, replacement is often simpler.

posts.title: Hydraulic Motors Explained: Types and Selection Criteria
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Motor Types Explained & How to Select One
posts.metaDescription: Learn how hydraulic motors convert flow into torque, the differences between gear, vane, piston and LSHT motors, and how to select one for your load.
posts.excerpt: Hydraulic motors deliver high torque from compact packages. Choosing the right type depends on the speed, torque and duty your application demands.
posts.imageAlt: Technician assembling a heavy mechanical drive
posts.html:
A hydraulic motor is the rotary counterpart of a hydraulic cylinder. Instead of pushing in a straight line, it converts hydraulic flow and pressure into rotation and torque. Hydraulic motors drive winches, slew rings, conveyors, mixers, wheels and tracks — anywhere high torque is needed from a compact unit.

How a hydraulic motor works

Pressurised oil acts on internal elements — gears, vanes or pistons — to create rotation. Two simple relationships describe its performance:

  • Speed depends on flow: the more oil supplied, the faster the motor turns.
  • Torque depends on pressure and displacement: higher pressure or larger displacement gives more torque.

Displacement is the volume of oil required for one revolution. A large-displacement motor turns more slowly for a given flow but produces more torque.

Main types of hydraulic motor

Gear motors

Simple, compact and economical. Suitable for moderate pressures and speeds, such as fans, conveyors and auxiliary drives. Efficiency is lower at low speeds.

Vane motors

Smooth and relatively quiet, with good performance at medium speeds. Used in industrial applications such as machine tools and conveyors.

Axial piston motors

High efficiency and high pressure capability. Available in fixed and variable displacement. Used where efficiency and power density matter, including mobile propulsion and industrial drives.

Low-speed high-torque (LSHT) motors

These include radial piston and orbital (gerotor/geroler) motors. They produce very high torque at low speeds, often eliminating the need for a gearbox. Typical uses include winches, slewing drives, augers, wheel drives and conveyors.

Comparison overview

Type Speed range Torque Efficiency Typical uses
Gear Medium–high Low–medium Moderate Fans, auxiliary drives
Vane Medium Medium Good Industrial drives
Axial piston Wide Medium–high Very good Propulsion, high-power drives
Radial piston (LSHT) Low Very high Very good Winches, heavy drives
Orbital (LSHT) Low–medium High Moderate–good Augers, conveyors, light winches

Selection criteria

1. Torque requirement

Calculate the torque needed to start and run the load, including breakaway torque, acceleration and any shock loads. Starting torque is often significantly higher than running torque.

2. Speed range

Determine minimum and maximum speeds. Some motors run smoothly at very low speeds; others become jerky or inefficient.

3. Pressure and flow available

Match motor displacement to the available pressure and flow from the power unit.

4. Load type

Consider whether the motor must hold a load, reverse frequently, or experience overrunning loads (for example, lowering on a winch). Overrunning loads require counterbalance or brake valves, and holding loads usually need a mechanical brake because hydraulic motors leak internally.

5. Shaft and mounting

Check shaft type, side load capacity, mounting flange and whether the motor will support external radial loads from pulleys or sprockets.

6. Case drain and back pressure

Many motors require a case drain line. Excess back pressure on the return or case can damage shaft seals.

Braking and load holding

Because hydraulic motors have internal leakage, they should not be relied on to hold a suspended load. Winches and hoists use spring-applied, hydraulically released brakes and counterbalance valves to hold and control loads safely.

Signs of motor wear

  • Reduced speed under load.
  • Increased case drain flow.
  • Overheating.
  • Shaft seal leaks.
  • Noise and vibration.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a low-speed high-torque (LSHT) motor?

An LSHT motor is designed to deliver very high torque at low rotational speeds, often eliminating the need for a gearbox. Radial piston and orbital motors are common types. They are used for winches, slewing drives, augers, wheel drives and conveyors, where large torque is needed at modest speeds.

Can a hydraulic motor hold a suspended load?

Not on its own. Hydraulic motors have internal leakage, so a load can slowly rotate the motor and lower over time. Winches and hoists use spring-applied, hydraulically released brakes and counterbalance or brake valves to hold and control loads safely.

Why does my hydraulic motor run slower under load?

As load increases, pressure rises and internal leakage in the motor and pump increases, so less oil does useful work and speed falls. Some speed drop is normal; a growing drop indicates wear. Check case drain flow, oil temperature and pump performance to identify the cause.

Do all hydraulic motors need a case drain?

No. Some motors drain internally to the return port, while others require an external case drain, especially when return line pressure is high or motors are used in series. Always follow the manufacturer's data sheet; incorrect draining can damage shaft seals.

How do I size a hydraulic motor?

Determine the torque required (including starting torque), the speed range, the available pressure and flow, and the type of load. Then select a displacement that delivers the torque at the available pressure and the speed at the available flow, allowing for efficiency losses. Check shaft load limits if pulleys or sprockets apply side loads.
