posts.title: Hydraulic Pump Repair and Reconditioning: What to Expect
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Pump Repair & Reconditioning: What to Expect
posts.metaDescription: What happens during a professional hydraulic pump repair, from inspection and parts replacement to performance testing, and how to decide if repair is worth it.
posts.excerpt: A professionally reconditioned pump can deliver near-new performance at a fraction of the cost. Here is what a proper pump repair involves — and what to ask your repairer.
posts.imageAlt: Precision machinery in a repair workshop
posts.html:
When a hydraulic pump wears out, replacement is not the only option. Many pumps — particularly larger piston pumps — can be reconditioned to perform like new for a lower cost and often with a shorter lead time. But the quality of repair varies widely. Knowing what a proper repair involves helps you choose a repairer and evaluate quotations.

The repair process

1. Initial assessment

The repairer records the pump's details: make, model, part number, displacement, rotation and controls. They note any external damage and, ideally, ask about the failure symptoms and operating conditions.

2. Strip and clean

The pump is fully dismantled. Every part is cleaned so that wear and damage can be properly inspected.

3. Inspection and measurement

Critical components are measured against tolerances. For piston pumps this includes pistons and bores, slippers, swash plate, valve plate, cylinder block, bearings and shaft. Gear pumps are checked for wear on gears, bushings and the housing.

4. Root cause findings

A good repairer explains why the pump failed. Common findings include:

  • Abrasive wear — contamination.
  • Erosion pitting — cavitation or aeration.
  • Scored or burnt surfaces — lack of lubrication, overheating or dry start.
  • Broken parts — pressure spikes or mechanical overload.

5. Quotation

You should receive a quote listing the parts to be replaced or remanufactured, with an option to compare the cost against a new pump.

6. Rebuild

Worn parts are replaced or remanufactured. Precision surfaces such as valve plates can sometimes be lapped. All seals, bearings and wear items are replaced.

7. Performance testing

This step separates professional repairs from basic rebuilds. The pump is run on a test bench to check flow at various pressures, control functions (such as compensator settings), case drain leakage and noise. A test report documents the results.

Repair or replace?

Consider repair when… Consider replacement when…
The housing and major parts are reusable The housing or rotating group is badly damaged
The pump is large or expensive A new pump costs little more than repair
New lead times are long The model is obsolete with no parts available
The application needs an exact match You want to upgrade to a more efficient design

Questions to ask your repairer

  1. Will the pump be performance tested, and will I receive a test report?
  2. What parts will be replaced, and are they genuine or equivalent quality?
  3. Will you tell me the cause of failure?
  4. What warranty applies?
  5. What is the turnaround time?

After the repair: protect your investment

A rebuilt pump will fail again if the underlying cause is not fixed. Before fitting it:

  • clean or flush the system to remove debris from the original failure;
  • replace filter elements;
  • correct suction-side problems if cavitation was found;
  • fill the pump case with clean oil before starting;
  • follow the correct start-up procedure.

Exchange units for critical equipment

For critical machines, consider keeping a reconditioned exchange pump on the shelf. When a pump fails, fit the spare immediately and send the failed pump for repair.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I know if a repaired pump has been tested properly?

Ask for a test report. A proper test measures flow at various pressures, verifies control settings such as compensator pressure, checks case drain leakage and confirms there are no leaks or abnormal noises. A repair shop that cannot provide test data may not have tested the pump under realistic conditions.

Why did my rebuilt pump fail soon after installation?

Common causes include contamination left in the system from the original failure, starting the pump without filling the case, air in the suction line, closed suction valves, incorrect rotation or unresolved cavitation problems. Flushing the system and following the correct start-up procedure prevent most early failures.

Can any pump be repaired?

Most industrial and mobile pumps can be repaired if parts are available and the housing is not damaged. Some low-cost pumps are designed to be replaced rather than repaired. Obsolete pumps can sometimes be repaired using remanufactured or custom-made parts, but the cost should be compared with a modern replacement.

What is an exchange pump?

An exchange pump is a reconditioned unit available immediately in exchange for your failed pump. You fit the exchange unit to restore production quickly, and the failed unit is repaired and returned to stock. Exchange programmes are useful for critical machines with standard pump models.

How long does a pump repair take?

It depends on the pump, the damage found and parts availability. Simple repairs can be quick, while repairs requiring special parts or remanufactured components take longer. Ask for an estimate after inspection, and discuss urgent options if downtime is costly.

We recondition and test hydraulic pumps and motors with a documented findings and test report. Request a repair quote.

posts.title: Calculating Hydraulic Pump Flow and Power: Simple Formulas
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Pump Flow & Power Calculations Made Simple
posts.metaDescription: Simple formulas to calculate hydraulic pump flow, required motor power, cylinder speed and torque, with worked examples for everyday engineering decisions.
posts.excerpt: A handful of simple formulas lets you estimate pump flow, motor power, cylinder speed and torque. Here they are, with worked examples.
posts.imageAlt: Hydraulic pump and drive motor installation
posts.html:
You do not need complex software to make sensible decisions about hydraulic systems. A handful of formulas covers most everyday questions: how much flow a pump delivers, how much power it needs, how fast a cylinder will move and how much torque a motor will produce.

The formulas below use common metric units. Results are theoretical; real systems include losses, so always allow a margin.

1. Pump flow

Flow (L/min) = Displacement (cc/rev) × Speed (rpm) ÷ 1000

Example: a pump with 20 cc/rev displacement driven at 1,450 rpm delivers:

20 × 1,450 ÷ 1000 = 29 L/min (theoretical)

Actual flow is lower due to internal leakage. Volumetric efficiency depends on pump type, condition, pressure and viscosity.

2. Hydraulic power

Power (kW) = Pressure (bar) × Flow (L/min) ÷ 600

Example: 29 L/min at 180 bar:

180 × 29 ÷ 600 = 8.7 kW hydraulic power

3. Drive motor power

Motor power (kW) = Hydraulic power ÷ Overall pump efficiency

With an overall efficiency of around 0.85:

8.7 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 10.2 kW

You would typically select the next standard motor size, considering duty cycle and starting conditions.

4. Pump torque

Torque (Nm) ≈ Displacement (cc/rev) × Pressure (bar) ÷ 62.8

Example: 20 cc/rev at 180 bar:

20 × 180 ÷ 62.8 ≈ 57 Nm (theoretical, before mechanical losses)

This is the torque the drive motor or engine must supply.

5. Cylinder area and force

Area (cm²) = π × Diameter (cm)² ÷ 4

Force (kN) = Pressure (bar) × Area (cm²) ÷ 100

Example: an 80 mm bore cylinder has an area of about 50.3 cm². At 180 bar:

180 × 50.3 ÷ 100 ≈ 90.5 kN (about 9.2 tonnes-force)

6. Cylinder speed

Speed (m/s) = Flow (L/min) ÷ (Area (cm²) × 6)

Example: 29 L/min into the 80 mm cylinder:

29 ÷ (50.3 × 6) ≈ 0.096 m/s, or about 96 mm/s

7. Hydraulic motor speed and torque

Motor speed (rpm) = Flow (L/min) × 1000 ÷ Displacement (cc/rev)

Motor torque (Nm) ≈ Displacement (cc/rev) × Pressure (bar) ÷ 62.8

Example: a 100 cc/rev motor supplied with 29 L/min at 180 bar:

  • Speed = 29 × 1000 ÷ 100 = 290 rpm
  • Torque ≈ 100 × 180 ÷ 62.8 ≈ 287 Nm (before efficiency losses)

8. Heat generated

Any power not converted into useful work becomes heat. If 3 kW is lost through a relief valve and throttling, the system must dissipate 3 kW of heat — through the reservoir and a cooler if needed.

Quick reference table

Quantity Formula
Pump flow (L/min) cc/rev × rpm ÷ 1000
Hydraulic power (kW) bar × L/min ÷ 600
Motor power (kW) Hydraulic kW ÷ efficiency
Torque (Nm) cc/rev × bar ÷ 62.8
Cylinder force (kN) bar × cm² ÷ 100
Cylinder speed (m/s) L/min ÷ (cm² × 6)
Motor speed (rpm) L/min × 1000 ÷ cc/rev

Use the numbers wisely

These calculations are excellent for sanity checks, comparing options and preparing enquiries. Final designs should account for efficiency, pressure losses, duty cycle, temperature and safety factors.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is actual pump flow lower than the calculated flow?

The calculation gives theoretical flow based on displacement and speed. Real pumps have internal leakage that increases with pressure, temperature and wear, so actual flow is lower. Volumetric efficiency describes the ratio of actual to theoretical flow. A drop in actual flow over time is a sign of wear.

How do I convert bar to psi?

One bar is approximately 14.5 psi. For example, 200 bar is roughly 2,900 psi. Keep units consistent when using formulas, as mixing metric and imperial units is a common source of calculation errors.

Why does motor power need to be higher than hydraulic power?

Pumps are not perfectly efficient. Mechanical friction and internal leakage mean some input power is lost as heat. Dividing hydraulic power by overall efficiency gives the shaft power needed from the motor. Additional margin may be needed for starting loads and duty cycle.

How do I calculate cylinder retraction speed?

Use the same speed formula but with the annulus area — the piston area minus the rod area. Because the annulus is smaller, the same flow produces a faster retraction speed. Remember that the oil leaving the cap side during retraction can exceed pump flow, which affects return line and valve sizing.

Can these formulas be used for safety-critical design?

They are useful for estimates and checks, but final designs for safety-critical systems should be prepared by qualified engineers using manufacturer data, appropriate safety factors and applicable standards. Real systems include pressure losses, dynamic loads and efficiency variations that simple formulas do not capture.

posts.title: Variable Displacement Pumps and Energy Efficiency in Hydraulic Systems
posts.metaTitle: Variable Displacement Pumps & Hydraulic Energy Efficiency
posts.metaDescription: How pressure-compensated and load-sensing variable displacement pumps cut energy use and heat in hydraulic systems, and when they are worth the investment.
posts.excerpt: Fixed pumps deliver full flow whether the machine needs it or not. Variable displacement pumps supply only what is required — saving energy and reducing heat.
posts.imageAlt: Industrial hydraulic pump with electric motor
posts.html:
Many hydraulic systems waste a large share of their input power as heat. A common reason is the pump: a fixed-displacement pump delivers the same flow on every revolution, whether the machine needs it or not. When the actuators are idle or moving slowly, the excess flow goes over a relief valve or through throttling valves, turning energy into heat.

Variable displacement pumps solve this by adjusting their output to match demand.

How a variable displacement pump works

Most variable displacement pumps in industrial and mobile systems are axial piston pumps with a movable swash plate. The angle of the swash plate sets the piston stroke — and therefore the flow per revolution. A control system changes the angle in response to system conditions. Some vane pumps also offer variable displacement by shifting the cam ring.

Common control types

Pressure compensation

The pump delivers full flow until system pressure reaches a set level. It then reduces displacement to deliver only enough flow to maintain that pressure. When actuators stop, the pump "destrokes" to almost zero flow while holding pressure. This avoids the heat that would be generated by dumping full flow over a relief valve.

Load sensing

A load-sensing pump monitors the pressure required by the actuator and supplies just enough pressure and flow to meet it, plus a small margin. Load sensing is common in mobile hydraulics such as cranes and excavators, where many functions operate at different pressures and speeds.

Power (horsepower) limiting

The pump limits its output so that pressure × flow does not exceed the available input power. This allows a smaller engine or motor to be used without stalling.

Electronic and proportional control

Electronically controlled pumps adjust displacement in response to signals from a controller, allowing sophisticated energy-saving strategies and precise control.

Where the savings come from

Situation Fixed pump Variable pump
Actuators idle, pressure held Full flow over relief → high heat Near-zero flow, minimal loss
Slow movement needed Excess flow throttled → heat Flow reduced to demand
Low-pressure function Pump works against higher pressure Pressure matched to load (load sensing)

The result is lower electricity or fuel consumption, cooler oil, longer component life and sometimes a smaller cooler and reservoir.

When is a variable pump worth it?

A variable displacement pump costs more than a gear pump. The investment is usually justified when:

  • the system spends a lot of time holding pressure with little flow;
  • demand varies widely through the cycle;
  • the system runs for long hours each day;
  • overheating is a recurring problem;
  • the power supply or engine size is limited.

For a simple machine that runs occasionally at constant demand, a fixed pump may remain the most economical choice.

Other ways to improve efficiency

  • Accumulators supply peak flow so a smaller pump can run at a steadier load.
  • Variable speed drives on electric motors adjust pump speed to demand, an increasingly popular option for fixed and variable pumps alike.
  • Unloading circuits send fixed-pump flow to tank at low pressure when idle.
  • Correct line sizing reduces pressure losses.
  • Regular maintenance prevents wear-related leakage and efficiency loss.

Setting up variable pumps correctly

Variable pumps rely on correctly adjusted controls. Compensator and load-sensing settings must be coordinated with relief valve settings. Incorrect settings can cause instability, noise or excessive heat. Settings should be checked during commissioning and after maintenance.

Retrofitting older systems

Older machines with fixed pumps can often be upgraded with a variable pump or a variable speed drive. The energy savings on high-utilisation machines can be significant, and the reduction in heat often improves reliability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a pressure-compensated pump?

A pressure-compensated pump delivers full flow until system pressure reaches a set value, then reduces displacement to maintain that pressure with only the flow required. When actuators stop, the pump delivers little flow while holding pressure, saving energy compared with a fixed pump dumping flow over a relief valve.

Is load sensing worth it on industrial machines?

Load sensing is very common in mobile hydraulics and can benefit industrial machines with multiple functions operating at different pressures. It adjusts pump pressure to just above the highest load demand. The benefit depends on the circuit and duty cycle; an engineering review can estimate savings.

Can a variable speed drive replace a variable pump?

In some applications, yes. Variable speed drives adjust the electric motor speed to match demand, reducing energy use even with a fixed pump. Combining a variable speed drive with a variable pump is also possible. The best choice depends on the duty cycle, response requirements and budget.

Why is my variable pump unstable or noisy?

Instability can result from incorrect compensator or load-sensing settings, poor coordination with relief valves, air in the system, or wear in the pump control. Check settings against specifications and ensure the system is properly bled. Persistent problems may need a pump inspection.

posts.title: How to Start Up a New or Rebuilt Hydraulic Pump Correctly
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Pump Start-Up Procedure: Avoid Early Failure
posts.metaDescription: A step-by-step start-up procedure for new and rebuilt hydraulic pumps: cleaning, filling the case, checking rotation, bleeding air and initial running.
posts.excerpt: Many new and rebuilt pumps are damaged in their first minutes of running. A careful start-up procedure prevents most of these avoidable failures.
posts.imageAlt: Technician installing a mechanical drive assembly
posts.html:
It is surprisingly common for a brand-new or freshly rebuilt hydraulic pump to fail within hours of installation. The cause is rarely a manufacturing defect. More often the pump was started dry, the system was dirty, or air was trapped inside. A careful start-up procedure costs a few extra minutes and protects a significant investment.

Always follow the pump manufacturer's specific instructions; the steps below summarise good general practice.

Before installation

1. Find out why the old pump failed

If contamination, cavitation or overheating destroyed the previous pump, the new one will suffer the same fate unless the cause is corrected.

2. Clean the system

After a pump failure, debris spreads through the circuit. Flush the system, clean the reservoir, replace filter elements and check that hoses and valves are free of debris.

3. Check the specification

Confirm the replacement pump matches the original: displacement, rotation direction, shaft type, mounting flange, port sizes and controls.

Installation

4. Align the drive

Check coupling alignment between the motor or engine and the pump. Misalignment overloads shaft bearings and seals. Use the correct coupling and do not force the pump onto the shaft.

5. Check the suction line

Make sure the suction line is clean, correctly sized, free of air leaks and that any isolation valve is fully open. Starting a pump with a closed suction valve can destroy it in seconds.

6. Connect the case drain correctly

On piston pumps and motors, the case drain line must run back to the tank with minimal restriction and terminate below the oil level. The highest drain port is usually used so the case stays full of oil.

Filling and priming

7. Fill the pump case

For pumps with a case drain, fill the case with clean hydraulic oil through the uppermost drain port before starting. Running a piston pump with a dry case quickly damages bearings and sliding surfaces.

8. Fill the reservoir with filtered oil

Use the correct grade, filtered through a transfer cart.

9. Prime the suction side

Ensure the pump inlet is flooded with oil. Pumps mounted above the oil level may need priming according to the manufacturer's instructions.

First start

10. Set controls to minimum

Set relief valves and compensators to low values where possible, and place directional valves in a position that allows flow back to tank at low pressure.

11. Check rotation

Briefly jog the motor to confirm the correct direction of rotation. Running a pump backwards can damage it quickly and will not produce flow.

12. Start and run at low pressure

Start the pump and run it unloaded for a few minutes. Watch for:

  • flow returning to tank;
  • unusual noise;
  • leaks;
  • rising temperature at the case.

13. Bleed air

Cycle actuators slowly through their full stroke several times at low pressure to purge air. Bleed points on cylinders and high points in the circuit help remove trapped air. Top up the reservoir as air is expelled.

Bringing up to pressure

14. Gradually increase pressure

Increase relief and compensator settings in steps to the specified values, using calibrated gauges.

15. Check operation

Confirm actuator speeds, pressures and temperatures. Check case drain flow on piston pumps to establish a baseline for future monitoring.

16. Recheck after initial running

After the first hours of operation, check for leaks, re-check filter indicators (new pumps and cleaned systems can release debris), confirm oil level and temperature, and re-tighten fittings if required.

Quick checklist

Step Done?
Root cause of previous failure corrected ☐
System flushed, filters replaced ☐
Correct pump, rotation and mounting ☐
Suction valve open, suction line sound ☐
Case filled with clean oil ☐
Rotation verified ☐
Started at low pressure, air bled ☐
Pressures set and verified ☐
Baseline readings recorded ☐

Frequently Asked Questions

Why must the pump case be filled before start-up?

Piston pumps rely on oil in the case to lubricate bearings and sliding surfaces. Starting with a dry case can cause immediate damage. Filling the case through the uppermost drain port before start-up ensures lubrication from the first revolution.

How do I check the pump's rotation direction?

Check the arrow on the pump body or the manufacturer's data, then briefly jog the motor and observe the shaft or coupling direction. Running a pump in the wrong direction can damage it and will not produce flow. Electric motors can be reversed by changing phase connections, done by a qualified electrician.

Why should a new pump be started at low pressure?

Starting at low pressure allows air to be purged, lets you check for leaks and noise, and ensures components are lubricated before full load is applied. Gradually increasing pressure to the set values reduces the risk of damage during commissioning.

What should I record after commissioning a pump?

Record pressure settings, operating temperature, cycle times and — for piston pumps — case drain flow. These baseline readings make future troubleshooting easier and help identify wear trends early.

posts.title: Hydraulic Motor Case Drain: Why It Matters and What It Tells You
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Motor Case Drain: Why It Matters
posts.metaDescription: What the case drain on a hydraulic motor or pump does, why restrictions cause seal failures, and how measuring case drain flow helps predict wear.
posts.excerpt: The case drain is a small line with a big job. It protects shaft seals and, when measured, gives an early warning of wear in pumps and motors.
posts.imageAlt: Precision hydraulic machinery in operation
posts.html:
Look at a piston pump or many hydraulic motors and you will see a small hose running back to the tank, separate from the main supply and return lines. That is the case drain. It is easy to overlook, but it plays an important role in protecting the unit — and it can tell you a lot about the unit's condition.

What is case drain flow?

Hydraulic pumps and motors rely on small internal clearances lubricated by oil. Some oil inevitably leaks past pistons, slippers and valve plates into the housing (the case). This internal leakage lubricates and cools the rotating group.

The leaked oil must be returned to the reservoir. The case drain line provides that path at low pressure.

Why the case drain must be unrestricted

The shaft seal of a pump or motor is designed for low case pressure. If the case drain is blocked, restricted or connected into a pressurised return line, case pressure rises. The results can include:

  • blown shaft seals and external leakage;
  • damaged internal components forced apart by case pressure;
  • overheating because oil is not circulating through the case.

Common mistakes include using undersized drain hoses, connecting the drain into a common return line with high back pressure, routing the drain through a filter that becomes blocked, or fitting quick couplers that do not connect properly.

Installation best practice

  • Use the correct hose size recommended by the manufacturer.
  • Route the drain directly to the tank, ending below the oil level.
  • Use the uppermost drain port so the case remains full of oil.
  • Avoid unnecessary fittings and restrictions.
  • If a case drain filter is required, size it generously and monitor it.
  • Fill the case with clean oil before first start.

Case drain flow as a health indicator

As a pump or motor wears, internal clearances increase and more oil leaks into the case. Rising case drain flow is one of the earliest and most reliable signs of wear in piston units.

How to measure it

With suitable flow meters or by timing flow into a measuring container under controlled conditions, case drain flow can be measured at a known pressure, speed and temperature. Measurements must be taken safely by trained personnel, following the manufacturer's guidance — case drain oil can be hot and under pressure if restricted.

Interpreting results

Manufacturers often provide expected case drain values for new units. More useful in practice is trending: record a baseline when the unit is healthy and compare measurements over time under the same conditions.

Trend Interpretation
Stable over time Normal wear, unit healthy
Gradual increase Progressive wear — plan repair
Sudden increase Internal damage — investigate promptly
Very high flow with heat and noise Imminent failure likely

Case drain and temperature

The case of a healthy pump runs slightly warmer than the reservoir. A case that runs much hotter than usual suggests increased internal leakage, poor case flushing or restricted drain flow.

Do all hydraulic motors have case drains?

Not all. Gear motors and some orbital motors drain internally to the return port, while others have an optional external drain that becomes necessary when return line pressure is high — for example, when motors are connected in series. Always check the manufacturer's data sheet.

Summary

  • The case drain removes internal leakage and protects shaft seals.
  • Never restrict or pressurise the case drain.
  • Measuring and trending case drain flow is a simple, powerful condition-monitoring tool.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if the case drain is connected to the return line?

If the return line has significant back pressure, the motor's case pressure rises. This can blow shaft seals and damage internal components. Case drains should generally run directly to the tank with minimal restriction, unless the manufacturer specifically allows a different arrangement.

Can I put a filter on the case drain line?

Sometimes, but only if it is sized generously and monitored, because a blocked filter would raise case pressure. Many systems avoid case drain filters for this reason. Follow the component manufacturer's guidance.

How often should case drain flow be measured?

For critical piston pumps and motors, periodic measurement — for example during scheduled maintenance — provides valuable trend data. Measure under consistent conditions of pressure, speed and temperature so results can be compared accurately.

Why is my motor's shaft seal leaking?

Common causes include excessive case pressure from restricted drains, worn seals, shaft damage, or misalignment and side loads on the shaft. Check the case drain first, as replacing the seal without solving high case pressure will lead to repeat failures.

Does a hot motor case always mean the motor is worn?

Not always. A hot case may result from restricted drain flow, poor case flushing, high system temperatures or heavy duty. However, a case that runs significantly hotter than before, combined with increasing case drain flow, strongly suggests internal wear.

posts.title: Essential Crane Spare Parts Every Maintenance Team Should Stock
posts.metaTitle: Essential Crane Spare Parts to Keep in Stock
posts.metaDescription: Which crane spare parts to keep on the shelf, how to prioritise them by criticality and lead time, and how to build a practical spares strategy.
posts.excerpt: The right spares on the shelf turn a crane breakdown from a multi-day shutdown into a short repair. Here is how to decide what to stock.
posts.imageAlt: Assorted crane spare parts and fasteners
posts.html:
When an overhead crane stops, production often stops with it. The difference between a two-hour repair and a two-week shutdown is frequently whether the right spare part is available. Yet holding every possible part is expensive. A sensible spares strategy focuses on parts that are critical, likely to wear and slow to obtain.

How to prioritise crane spares

Score each potential spare on three questions:

  1. Criticality: if this part fails, does the crane stop or become unsafe?
  2. Failure likelihood: is this a wear part, or one that fails occasionally?
  3. Lead time: how quickly can a replacement be obtained or manufactured?

Parts that score high on all three belong on the shelf.

Commonly stocked crane spare parts

Hoist components

  • Wire rope of the correct construction and length (or a supplier able to deliver quickly).
  • Brake linings, pads or complete brake units for hoist brakes.
  • Limit switches for upper and lower hoist limits.
  • Hook latches and safety catches.
  • Sheave bearings and, for high-duty cranes, spare sheaves.

Travel components

  • Crane wheels, or matched wheel sets for critical cranes.
  • Wheel bearings and bearing housings.
  • Couplings and coupling elements for travel drives.
  • Travel brake components.

Electrical components

  • Contactors and relays used in crane control panels.
  • Pendant or radio remote controls and spare batteries.
  • Fuses and protection devices.
  • Festoon trolleys or conductor bar collectors.
  • Motor brake coils and rectifiers.

Mechanical fasteners and consumables

  • Bolts, pins and retaining devices specified for crane use.
  • Lubricants specified by the crane manufacturer.
  • Buffers and end stops.

Wear parts vs insurance spares

Wear parts — brake linings, collectors, rope, wheel bearings — are consumed at a predictable rate. Stock levels can be based on usage history.

Insurance spares — gearboxes, motors, complete wheel assemblies — rarely fail, but when they do, lead times can be long. For critical cranes, holding one insurance spare can be cheaper than a single extended shutdown.

When original parts are obsolete

Many cranes outlive their manufacturer's parts support. When original spares are no longer available, components such as wheels, pins, sheaves, couplings and drums can often be reverse-engineered from the worn part and manufactured to drawing. Doing this proactively — before the part fails — removes a major risk.

Build a spares register

A simple register makes your strategy work:

Field Example
Crane / location Bay 3 EOT, 20 t
Component Long travel wheel, driven
Drawing / part number Supplier part no. or in-house drawing
Quantity on hand / minimum 2 / 2
Lead time 6 weeks (manufactured)
Supplier Approved manufacturer
Last used Date and reason

Store spares correctly

  • Protect machined surfaces from corrosion with suitable preservatives.
  • Store wire rope off the floor in a dry place.
  • Keep brake linings and rubber parts away from heat, sunlight and ozone.
  • Rotate stock where shelf life matters.
  • Label parts clearly with crane, location and part details.

Review regularly

Review the register after every breakdown and at least annually. Add parts that caused unplanned downtime, adjust quantities based on usage, and remove items for equipment that has been retired.

Getting parts manufactured

Frequently Asked Questions

How many spare wheels should I keep for a crane?

It depends on the crane's criticality, duty and lead time for replacements. For critical cranes with long lead times, many maintenance teams hold at least a matched set of driven wheels, or complete wheel assemblies, so a worn set can be replaced during a short shutdown. For less critical cranes, a supplier who can manufacture quickly may be enough.

Should I keep wire rope in stock?

For cranes where rope replacement is planned or rope damage would stop production, keeping a correctly specified rope — or having a supplier who can deliver quickly — is sensible. Store rope correctly: off the floor, in a dry area and protected from damage. Always confirm rope specification against the crane manufacturer's requirements.

How do I handle obsolete crane parts?

Identify obsolete parts before they fail. Mechanical components such as wheels, pins, sheaves and couplings can often be reverse-engineered and manufactured to approved drawings. Electrical and control components may need modern equivalents or upgrades. Planning ahead avoids emergency shutdowns.

How do I justify spare parts costs to management?

Compare the cost of holding the spare with the cost of downtime if the part fails and must be sourced. For critical equipment, a single avoided shutdown can pay for spares many times over. Use breakdown history and lead times to support your case.

How should brake linings be stored?

Keep them in a cool, dry place away from oil, grease, direct sunlight and heat. Store them in original packaging, labelled with the crane and brake type. Contaminated linings lose friction and should not be fitted.

posts.title: EOT Crane Maintenance Checklist: Daily, Monthly and Annual Checks
posts.metaTitle: EOT Crane Maintenance Checklist: Daily to Annual
posts.metaDescription: A practical EOT overhead crane maintenance checklist covering daily pre-use checks, monthly inspections and annual thorough examinations.
posts.excerpt: Overhead cranes need structured inspection at different intervals. Use this checklist as a starting point for a practical, safety-focused maintenance routine.
posts.imageAlt: Gantry cranes operating at an industrial port
posts.html:
Electric overhead travelling (EOT) cranes are central to many factories, workshops and warehouses. Regular inspection keeps them safe and reliable, and in many countries periodic thorough examination by a competent person is a legal requirement.

This checklist is a practical starting point. Always follow the crane manufacturer's instructions and the regulations that apply in your country, and ensure inspections are carried out by suitably trained and competent people.

Safety first: before any inspection or maintenance, isolate and lock off the crane's electrical supply, prevent other cranes on the same runway from approaching, and use safe access equipment and fall protection.

Daily (pre-use) checks — operator

Before each shift, the operator should check:

  • Controls: pendant or remote buttons operate correctly and return to neutral; emergency stop works.
  • Hoist limits: upper limit switch stops the hook safely.
  • Brakes: hoist and travel brakes hold and stop smoothly without excessive drift.
  • Hook: no visible damage, deformation or cracks; safety latch is present and works.
  • Wire rope: no obvious kinks, broken wires, crushing or birdcaging along visible lengths.
  • Unusual noise or movement: grinding, squealing or jerky travel.
  • Warning devices: horns and lights work.
  • Area: runway clear of obstructions.

Any defect should be reported and the crane taken out of service if safety is affected.

Monthly inspection — maintenance team

  • Wire rope: detailed inspection for wear, corrosion, broken wires and lubrication.
  • Sheaves and drum: groove wear, rope seating, bearing noise.
  • Brakes: lining wear, air gap adjustment, holding performance.
  • Hook block: bearing rotation, wear at the hook saddle and shank.
  • Wheels and rails: flange wear, tread wear, rail condition and fastenings.
  • Gearboxes: oil levels, leaks, noise and temperature.
  • Couplings: wear of flexible elements and alignment.
  • Electrical: collectors, festoon cables, panel components and terminations.
  • Lubrication: in line with the manufacturer's schedule.
  • Bolts and fastenings: end trucks, girder connections and trolley frames.
  • Buffers and end stops: secure and undamaged.

Annual (or statutory) thorough examination

A competent person carries out a thorough examination covering the structure, mechanisms, safety devices and documentation, typically including:

  • structural inspection of girders, end carriages and connections for cracks and deformation;
  • detailed inspection of hoist drum, rope anchorages and reeving;
  • verification of limit switches, overload protection and emergency stops;
  • inspection of wheels, axles and bearings;
  • brake performance verification;
  • review of maintenance records;
  • load testing where required by regulations or after major repairs.

Record keeping

Keep a log for each crane with inspection dates, findings, repairs, parts replaced and examination certificates. Records demonstrate compliance and reveal trends, such as accelerating wheel wear that may indicate alignment problems.

Common findings and what they mean

Finding Possible cause
Rapid wheel flange wear Rail misalignment, crane skewing
Brake slip or long stopping distance Worn linings, incorrect adjustment, contamination
Rope wear on one side Sheave misalignment, worn grooves
Hot gearbox Low oil, wrong oil, bearing wear
Trolley noise Worn wheels, bearings or rail joints

Parts and repairs

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is allowed to carry out the thorough examination of a crane?

Thorough examinations are typically carried out by a competent person with appropriate training, knowledge and experience, as defined by local regulations. Requirements vary between countries, so check the regulations that apply to your site and use qualified inspectors.

How often do overhead cranes need a thorough examination?

Intervals are set by local regulations and the crane's use, and may be more frequent for heavy-duty cranes or cranes lifting people. Many regions require periodic examinations at defined intervals and after significant repairs or modifications. Your crane inspector or local regulations will specify the exact requirements.

What should operators do if they find a defect?

Report it immediately using your site's reporting procedure and, if the defect affects safety, take the crane out of service and prevent its use until it is repaired. Operators should never attempt repairs they are not authorised or trained to carry out.

Do I need to load test a crane after repairs?

Load testing may be required after major repairs, modifications or replacement of load-bearing components, depending on regulations and the nature of the work. A competent person should decide whether a load test is needed.

What records should be kept for each crane?

Keep inspection reports, thorough examination certificates, maintenance and repair records, parts replaced, load test certificates and any modifications. Good records demonstrate compliance and help identify recurring problems.

posts.title: Crane Wire Rope Sheaves: Inspection, Wear and Replacement
posts.metaTitle: Crane Sheave Inspection, Wear and Replacement Guide
posts.metaDescription: How to inspect crane sheaves for groove wear, corrugation, flange damage and bearing problems, and why worn sheaves destroy wire rope.
posts.excerpt: Worn sheaves quietly destroy wire rope. Regular sheave inspection protects your ropes, your crane and your people.
posts.imageAlt: Technician working on a heavy mechanical assembly
posts.html:
Sheaves guide the wire rope through a crane's hoist system. Every lift bends the rope around each sheave, and the condition of the sheave groove directly affects how long the rope lasts. A worn or damaged sheave can ruin a new rope in a fraction of its normal life — so sheave inspection belongs in every crane maintenance routine.

Why sheave condition matters

A wire rope is designed to sit in a groove that supports it around roughly a third of its circumference. When the groove is the correct size and smooth, load is spread evenly across the rope's wires.

When the groove wears, two things happen:

  • A groove that is too narrow pinches the rope, crushing it and causing internal wire breaks.
  • A groove that is too wide or corrugated fails to support the rope, letting it flatten and wear unevenly.

What to inspect

Groove diameter and profile

Use a sheave groove gauge suited to the rope diameter. The gauge should fit the groove bottom correctly. Grooves that are undersize, oversize or misshapen need attention.

Corrugation

A worn rope can imprint its strand pattern into the groove, leaving corrugations. A new rope running in a corrugated groove will be damaged quickly. Corrugated sheaves must be machined (if within limits) or replaced.

Flanges

Check sheave flanges for chips, cracks and wear. Damaged flanges can allow the rope to jump the sheave — a serious hazard.

Bearings

The sheave should rotate freely and quietly without wobble. Seized or rough bearings make the rope slide across the groove, causing rapid wear on both rope and sheave.

Alignment

Sheaves should be aligned with the rope path. Misalignment makes the rope rub against the flange and twist as it runs.

Cracks

Look for cracks in the hub, spokes and web, particularly on cast sheaves and after shock loading.

Common sheave problems and causes

Problem Typical causes
Undersize groove Wear from rope, wrong sheave for rope size
Corrugated groove Long use with worn rope
Flange wear on one side Misalignment, fleet angle problems
Rough rotation Bearing failure, lack of lubrication
Cracks Overload, shock loads, fatigue

Sheave replacement or repair

Lightly worn grooves can sometimes be re-machined to the correct profile, provided enough material remains and the sheave design allows it. Sheaves with cracks, excessive groove wear, damaged flanges or worn bores should be replaced.

Replacement sheaves must match:

  • the rope diameter and groove profile;
  • the pitch diameter required by the crane design;
  • bore and bearing arrangement;
  • material and hardness requirements.

Replace ropes and sheaves together when needed

When replacing a wire rope, inspect every sheave and the drum. Fitting a new rope on worn sheaves is a false economy, because the rope will start wearing immediately.

Inspection frequency

Sheaves are typically checked during monthly crane inspections and in detail during the periodic thorough examination. High-duty cranes, such as those in steel plants or ports, may need more frequent checks.

Safety reminder

Sheave inspection involves working at height near the hoist mechanism. Isolate the crane, secure the load block, and use appropriate access equipment.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a sheave gauge?

A sheave gauge is a template shaped to the correct groove profile for a specific rope diameter. Placed in the groove, it shows whether the groove has worn too narrow, too wide or into an incorrect shape. Gauges are a simple, effective tool for routine sheave inspection.

Can I re-machine a worn sheave groove?

Sometimes. If enough material remains and the sheave design allows, grooves can be re-machined to the correct profile. However, re-machining reduces material thickness and changes pitch diameter slightly, so limits must be respected. Cracked or heavily worn sheaves should be replaced.

Why does a new wire rope wear quickly?

A common reason is fitting a new rope onto worn or corrugated sheaves and drums. The damaged groove profile crushes or abrades the new rope. Inspect and, if necessary, replace sheaves and check the drum whenever a rope is replaced.

What does a noisy sheave indicate?

Noise often indicates worn or poorly lubricated bearings. A sheave that does not rotate freely forces the rope to slide across the groove, causing rapid wear of both rope and sheave. Investigate and repair promptly.

Can I use a different sheave from another crane?

Only if it matches the required rope diameter, groove profile, pitch diameter, bore, bearing arrangement and material specification for your crane. Using an incorrect sheave can damage the rope and compromise safety. Check with the crane manufacturer or a qualified engineer.

posts.title: Crane Brake Maintenance: Keeping Lifting Equipment Safe
posts.metaTitle: Crane Brake Maintenance: Inspection and Adjustment
posts.metaDescription: How crane hoist and travel brakes work, the most common brake problems, and a practical maintenance routine to keep lifting equipment stopping safely.
posts.excerpt: Brakes are among the most safety-critical components on a crane. Here is how they work, what goes wrong and how to keep them in top condition.
posts.imageAlt: Heavy-duty cranes at an industrial port
posts.html:
On any crane, the brakes stand between a controlled lift and a dropped load. Hoist brakes must hold the full rated load securely, and travel brakes must stop the crane and trolley smoothly without skidding or shock. Regular brake maintenance is essential for both safety and reliability.

Types of crane brakes

Electromagnetic disc brakes

Common on modern hoist and travel motors. A spring applies the brake; an electromagnet releases it when power is applied. If power fails, the brake applies automatically — a fail-safe design.

Electro-hydraulic thruster drum brakes

Found on many larger industrial cranes. Springs apply brake shoes to a drum, and an electro-hydraulic thruster lifts them off when energised.

Mechanical load brakes

Some hoists include a mechanical load brake in the gearbox that controls lowering speed, in addition to the motor brake.

Common brake problems

Problem Possible causes
Load drifts or slips Worn linings, incorrect air gap, contamination by oil or grease
Brake does not release fully Coil fault, rectifier failure, thruster failure, incorrect adjustment
Overheating Brake dragging, excessive inching, incorrect adjustment
Long stopping distance Worn linings, weak springs, glazed surfaces
Noise or chatter Uneven wear, loose components, damaged disc or drum
Delayed application Control circuit problems, rectifier issues

Inspection and maintenance routine

Always isolate the crane, secure loads and follow lock-out procedures before working on brakes.

Regular checks

  • Holding test: during pre-use checks, confirm the hoist holds a load without creeping.
  • Stopping performance: watch for increasing stopping distances on travel motions.
  • Noise and smell: burning smells or squeals indicate dragging or overheating.

Periodic maintenance

  • Measure lining wear and replace before the minimum thickness is reached.
  • Check and adjust the air gap on electromagnetic brakes to the manufacturer's specification. As linings wear, the air gap increases and the brake may fail to release properly or apply slowly.
  • Inspect discs and drums for scoring, cracks, heat checking and glazing.
  • Check springs for corrosion, cracks and correct tension.
  • Inspect pins and linkages on drum brakes for wear and free movement.
  • Check thrusters for oil level and leaks.
  • Test electrical components such as coils, rectifiers and connections.
  • Keep brakes clean and dry, free from oil, grease and dust.

Lining replacement

Replace linings in sets so braking is even. Use linings specified for the brake model and duty. After replacement, adjust air gaps and run in according to the manufacturer's procedure, then test holding and stopping performance.

Why brakes fail early

  • Excessive inching (frequent short movements) generates heat and wear.
  • Wrong adjustment causes drag or poor holding.
  • Oil contamination from leaking gearboxes reduces friction dramatically.
  • Overloading the crane strains brakes beyond their design.

Addressing these causes extends brake life significantly.

Brake testing after maintenance

After any brake work, test performance before returning the crane to service: confirm holding with a test load, check stopping distances and verify that the brake applies when power is removed. Major repairs or modifications may require examination by a competent person under local regulations.

Spare parts

Brake linings, coils, rectifiers and springs are worth keeping in stock for critical cranes. Where original parts are no longer available, brake components such as drums, discs and linkages can often be manufactured to drawing or sample.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I know when brake linings need replacing?

Measure lining thickness and compare it with the manufacturer's minimum. Signs of worn linings include longer stopping distances, load drift, noise and the need for frequent adjustment. Replace linings in sets so braking remains even.

What is the air gap on an electromagnetic brake?

The air gap is the clearance between the armature and the magnet body when the brake is applied. As linings wear, the gap increases. If it becomes too large, the magnet may not release the brake fully or may release slowly. Adjust the gap according to the manufacturer's specification during maintenance.

Why is oil on a brake dangerous?

Oil or grease on brake surfaces drastically reduces friction, allowing loads to slip or crane travel to overrun. Find and fix the source, such as a leaking gearbox seal, and replace contaminated linings — cleaning is rarely sufficient.

Can brakes overheat?

Yes. Frequent inching, dragging brakes, incorrect adjustment and heavy duty can cause overheating, which glazes linings and reduces braking performance. Investigate the cause and adjust operating practices or brake sizing if necessary.

What should be tested after brake maintenance?

Test that the brake holds the rated load without slipping, that it applies when power is removed and releases fully when energised, and that stopping performance is normal. Follow your site's procedures and any regulatory requirements before returning the crane to service.

posts.title: Understanding Crane Duty Classification and Why It Matters for Parts
posts.metaTitle: Crane Duty Classification Explained (FEM / ISO / CMAA)
posts.metaDescription: What crane duty classes mean, how load spectrum and usage determine them, and why the duty class matters when buying replacement crane parts.
posts.excerpt: Two cranes with the same capacity can need very different components. Duty classification explains why — and why it matters when ordering spares.
posts.imageAlt: Mechanical crane components and fasteners
posts.html:
A 10-tonne crane in a maintenance workshop and a 10-tonne crane in a steel mill have the same rated capacity, but they live very different lives. The workshop crane might lift its full load a few times a week. The steel mill crane may lift heavy loads continuously, around the clock. Their components must be designed differently — and that is what duty classification describes.

What is crane duty classification?

Duty classification groups cranes and their mechanisms according to how hard they work. Several standards systems are used internationally, including ISO 4301, FEM rules widely used in Europe, and CMAA specifications in North America. Each system uses its own class designations, but they consider similar factors.

The two main factors

1. Load spectrum

How often does the crane lift loads close to its rated capacity? A crane that regularly lifts near-maximum loads has a heavier load spectrum than one that mostly lifts light loads.

2. Usage (class of utilisation)

How many working cycles or operating hours will the crane accumulate over its design life? More cycles mean more fatigue on structures and more wear on mechanisms.

Combining load spectrum and usage gives a duty class for the crane as a whole and for individual mechanisms such as the hoist, trolley travel and long travel.

Why it matters for components

Components on higher-duty cranes need:

  • larger safety factors against fatigue;
  • larger or harder wheels to handle repeated rolling loads;
  • larger sheave and drum diameters relative to rope size to reduce rope fatigue;
  • heavier-duty gearboxes, bearings and brakes;
  • motors rated for higher starts per hour and duty.

A part that performs well on a light-duty crane may wear out rapidly on a heavy-duty crane.

Typical applications by duty level

Duty level Typical applications
Light Maintenance workshops, powerhouses, standby cranes
Moderate General manufacturing, assembly, warehouses
Heavy Fabrication shops, steel stockyards, busy production lines
Severe Steel mills, foundries, container ports, continuous process plants

When duty class changes over time

Many cranes are installed for one duty and later used for another. Production increases, shift patterns change and loads become heavier. Signs that a crane is working beyond its original duty include:

  • rapidly wearing wheels, rope or brakes;
  • overheating motors and gearboxes;
  • fatigue cracks in structures;
  • frequent breakdowns despite good maintenance.

If this happens, review the crane's duty against its current use. Upgrading components — or the crane — may be necessary.

Ordering replacement parts

When ordering replacement wheels, sheaves, drums, pins or gear components, tell your supplier:

  • the crane capacity and span;
  • the duty class or a description of how the crane is used;
  • operating hours or cycles per day;
  • environmental conditions such as heat or dust;
  • any history of premature wear.

This information allows the manufacturer to select appropriate materials, heat treatment and dimensions — and possibly suggest improvements, such as harder wheel treads for heavy-duty cranes.

Duty classification and compliance

Duty classification is part of crane design and is defined by the crane manufacturer and applicable standards. Changes to a crane's rated capacity, duty or structure should be assessed by qualified engineers and may require re-certification under local regulations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where can I find my crane's duty classification?

It is often stated in the crane's documentation, nameplate or design data from the manufacturer. If it is not available, a crane engineer can assess the crane and its usage. Knowing the duty class helps when specifying replacement parts.

Can I change my crane's duty classification?

Using a crane more intensively than its design classification can lead to accelerated wear and fatigue. Upgrading components may increase capability, but changes to duty, capacity or structure should be assessed by qualified crane engineers and may require re-certification.

Why do crane wheels wear faster on heavy-duty cranes?

Heavy-duty cranes complete more load cycles with heavier loads, increasing contact stress and rolling wear. Wheels for these cranes need appropriate materials, heat treatment and sometimes larger diameters to achieve acceptable life.

Do duty classes differ between standards?

Yes. Different standards systems use different designations and categories, but they consider similar factors such as load spectrum and usage. When comparing cranes or components, make sure you compare classifications from the same system or convert carefully.

How does duty affect replacement part specification?

Higher duty requires stronger materials, better heat treatment, larger safety margins and more robust designs. Informing your supplier of the crane's duty and usage allows them to specify parts that last.

posts.title: Reverse Engineering Obsolete Crane Parts: How It Works
posts.metaTitle: Reverse Engineering Obsolete Crane Parts: How It Works
posts.metaDescription: How reverse engineering recreates obsolete or unavailable crane parts from worn samples: measurement, material analysis, drawing approval and manufacture.
posts.excerpt: When the original manufacturer can no longer supply a part, reverse engineering can keep your crane running — often with a better part than the original.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer drafting component drawings
posts.html:
Cranes often outlive the companies that built them. Twenty or thirty years after installation, a failed wheel, coupling or gear may have no available replacement. Drawings may be lost and the original manufacturer may no longer exist. Reverse engineering offers a reliable way to recreate the part.

What is reverse engineering?

Reverse engineering is the process of measuring and analysing an existing part to create a drawing and specification, then manufacturing a replacement. For crane parts, it typically applies to:

  • wheels, axles and bearing housings;
  • pins, bushes and shafts;
  • sheaves and drums;
  • couplings and gear components;
  • brake drums and linkages;
  • brackets and fabricated components.

The reverse engineering process

1. Collect the part and information

The worn or failed part is the starting point. Information about the crane — capacity, duty, mating parts and failure history — is equally important, because the replacement must work in the real application.

2. Clean and inspect

The part is cleaned and inspected for wear patterns, cracks and damage. Wear patterns often reveal problems such as misalignment that should be corrected in the new design.

3. Measure

Dimensions are measured using calipers, micrometers, bore gauges and other tools. Where surfaces are worn, the original dimensions must be determined by measuring unworn areas, considering mating parts and applying engineering judgement.

4. Identify material and heat treatment

Hardness testing and, where needed, material analysis help determine the original material and heat treatment. This is particularly important for wheels, shafts and gears, where hardness affects wear life and strength.

5. Create the drawing

A detailed drawing is produced with dimensions, tolerances, material, heat treatment and surface finish requirements.

6. Customer approval

The customer reviews and approves the drawing before manufacture. This step ensures nothing important has been missed and gives the customer a drawing for future orders.

7. Manufacture and inspect

The part is manufactured and inspected against the drawing, with a dimensional and hardness report supplied.

Opportunities to improve

Reverse engineering is not only about copying. It is an opportunity to:

  • specify a harder or tougher material where wear was excessive;
  • improve heat treatment for longer life;
  • correct design weaknesses revealed by the failure;
  • standardise dimensions to match readily available bearings and seals.

How to get the best result

Do Avoid
Send the actual worn part if possible Relying only on photos for complex parts
Provide mating part details Sending parts without context
Describe how the part failed Assuming the original design was ideal
Keep the approved drawing on file Losing the drawing again

Plan before parts fail

The best time to reverse-engineer a critical part is before it fails. During planned maintenance, identify components with no available spares, measure them and create drawings. You can then order spares in advance and avoid emergency shutdowns.

Safety and compliance

Load-bearing crane components must be designed and manufactured to appropriate engineering standards. Replacement parts should match or exceed the original specification, and significant changes should be reviewed by qualified engineers.

Frequently Asked Questions

How accurate is reverse engineering from a worn part?

Accuracy depends on the condition of the part and the expertise of the engineers. Worn surfaces must be reconstructed using unworn areas, mating parts and engineering judgement. Providing mating parts or dimensions and an unworn sample, if available, improves accuracy.

Will I own the drawing created by reverse engineering?

This depends on your agreement with the supplier. Many customers request the approved drawing as part of the order so they can reorder in future. Discuss ownership and confidentiality before work begins.

Can reverse-engineered parts be better than the original?

Yes. Reverse engineering offers the opportunity to improve materials, heat treatment and design details based on how the original failed. Any changes to load-bearing parts should be reviewed by qualified engineers.

How long does reverse engineering take?

Simple parts can be measured and drawn quickly, while complex assemblies with many interfaces take longer. Customer approval time also affects the schedule. Planning reverse engineering before failure avoids urgent pressure.

What parts are not suitable for reverse engineering?

Certified lifting components such as hooks, and some safety-critical or proprietary electronic components, are usually better replaced with certified or OEM equivalents. Discuss suitability with your supplier.

posts.title: Crane Hooks and Load Blocks: Inspection Basics
posts.metaTitle: Crane Hook & Load Block Inspection Basics
posts.metaDescription: What to look for when inspecting crane hooks and load blocks: throat opening, wear, twisting, cracks, latches, swivels and sheaves — and when to remove from service.
posts.excerpt: The hook is the last link between the crane and the load. Knowing what to inspect — and when to take a hook out of service — is basic lifting safety.
posts.imageAlt: Container cranes lifting loads at a port
posts.html:
The hook and load block carry every load the crane lifts. They are subject to wear from slings, impact from loads and fatigue from repeated lifting. Because a hook failure can drop a load, hook and block inspection is a core part of every crane inspection routine.

This guide covers the basics. Always follow the hook manufacturer's criteria, applicable standards and your local regulations, and ensure inspections are performed by trained, competent personnel.

Parts of a hook and load block

  • Hook: the forged hook body, including the saddle (bowl), throat, tip and shank.
  • Safety latch: closes the hook throat to prevent slings slipping off.
  • Hook nut and thrust bearing: secure the hook and allow rotation.
  • Block frame and side plates: hold the sheaves and hook assembly.
  • Sheaves: guide the wire rope.
  • Swivel: allows the hook to rotate under load (on many blocks).

What to inspect on the hook

Throat opening

An increase in throat opening indicates the hook has been overloaded or bent. Many inspection programmes measure the throat opening against a reference value recorded when the hook was new, or between marks punched on the hook. A significant increase means the hook must be removed from service.

Wear in the saddle

Slings wear the bowl of the hook over time. Wear beyond the manufacturer's limit reduces strength.

Twisting

A hook twisted from its original plane has been overloaded or side-loaded and must be removed from service.

Cracks, nicks and gouges

Look for cracks, especially at the saddle and shank. Nicks and gouges create stress concentrations. Non-destructive testing, such as magnetic particle inspection, may be required during periodic examinations.

Latch

The safety latch must be present, undamaged and close the throat properly. A missing or damaged latch should be replaced before use.

Shank and threads

Check the shank for bending and the threaded area for corrosion and damage. The hook nut and its locking device must be secure.

What to inspect on the load block

  • Sheaves: groove wear, flange damage and free rotation.
  • Side plates: cracks, bending and corrosion.
  • Fasteners: tightness and locking devices.
  • Swivel and thrust bearing: smooth rotation without roughness or excessive play.
  • Rope guards: present and correctly positioned to keep the rope in the sheave grooves.
  • Capacity marking: clearly legible.

Remove from service if…

Condition Action
Throat opening increased beyond limit Remove from service
Hook twisted from its plane Remove from service
Cracks found Remove from service
Saddle wear beyond manufacturer's limit Remove from service
Latch missing or not working Repair before use
Rough or seized swivel Repair before use

Never weld, heat, straighten or grind a damaged hook. Heating and welding can destroy the material properties of a forged hook. Damaged hooks must be replaced with correctly rated parts.

Inspection frequency

  • Pre-use: visual check by the operator for obvious damage and latch function.
  • Frequent inspections: more detailed checks at intervals based on usage.
  • Periodic thorough examination: by a competent person, including measurements and, where required, NDT.

Good lifting practice protects hooks

  • Never side-load or tip-load a hook.
  • Seat slings in the saddle of the hook, not on the tip.
  • Never exceed the rated capacity.
  • Avoid shock loading.
  • Use suitable shackles or master links for multiple slings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why must damaged hooks never be welded?

Hooks are forged and heat-treated to achieve specific strength and toughness. Welding or heating changes the material properties and can create hidden weaknesses or cracks. Damaged hooks must be replaced with correctly rated components.

How is throat opening measured?

Many inspection programmes record a reference measurement between two points on the hook, sometimes marked with punch marks, when the hook is new. Later measurements are compared with this reference. An increase beyond the allowed limit indicates overload or damage, and the hook must be removed from service.

What is the purpose of the hook latch?

The latch closes the throat opening to help prevent slings and rigging from slipping off the hook. It is not designed to carry load. A missing or damaged latch should be replaced before the hook is used.

Do load blocks need NDT inspection?

Non-destructive testing may be required during periodic thorough examinations, particularly for high-duty cranes or after incidents. The competent person conducting the examination determines whether NDT is needed.

What causes hook swivel bearings to fail?

Lack of lubrication, contamination and overload are common causes. A rough or seized swivel prevents the hook from rotating freely, which can twist ropes and slings. Inspect and lubricate swivels as part of routine maintenance.

posts.title: Reducing Crane Downtime with a Planned Maintenance Approach
posts.metaTitle: How to Reduce Crane Downtime with Planned Maintenance
posts.metaDescription: Practical strategies to reduce overhead crane downtime: criticality ranking, condition monitoring, spare parts planning, operator training and root cause analysis.
posts.excerpt: Most crane breakdowns are predictable. A planned maintenance approach turns surprises into scheduled jobs — and keeps production moving.
posts.imageAlt: Maintenance technician working on crane drive components
posts.html:
When a production crane breaks down, the cost goes far beyond the repair. Production stops, deliveries slip and people stand idle. Yet most crane failures are preceded by warning signs. A planned maintenance approach catches those signs early and turns emergencies into scheduled work.

Step 1: Rank your cranes by criticality

Not every crane deserves the same attention. Rank each crane by:

  • impact on production if it stops;
  • availability of alternatives (another crane or forklift);
  • safety consequences of failure;
  • utilisation and duty.

Focus your maintenance effort and spares budget on the cranes that matter most.

Step 2: Move from reactive to planned work

Approach Description Result
Reactive Fix when it breaks Unplanned downtime, high cost
Preventive Fixed-interval inspections and replacements Fewer failures, some unnecessary work
Condition-based Act on measured condition Work done when needed
Proactive Remove root causes Fewer failures over time

Most sites benefit from a combination: preventive inspections for safety-critical items, condition monitoring for expensive components, and root cause analysis for repeat failures.

Step 3: Monitor condition

Simple measurements reveal developing problems:

  • wheel and rail wear measurements over time;
  • brake lining thickness and air gap;
  • gearbox oil analysis for wear metals;
  • thermography of motors, panels and gearboxes;
  • vibration checks on high-duty drives;
  • wire rope inspection records.

Trends matter more than single readings. A wheel that loses flange thickness twice as fast as last year indicates an alignment problem.

Step 4: Plan spares

The fastest repair is useless if the part takes six weeks to arrive. For each critical crane:

  • identify parts with long lead times;
  • hold critical spares on site;
  • reverse-engineer obsolete parts before they fail;
  • keep approved drawings for manufactured parts.

Step 5: Train operators

Operators are the first line of defence. Good practices include:

  • thorough pre-use checks and prompt defect reporting;
  • smooth operation without excessive inching or plugging;
  • avoiding side pulls and shock loading;
  • respecting rated capacities.

Poor operating practice accelerates wear on brakes, wheels, ropes and structures.

Step 6: Investigate repeat failures

If the same part fails repeatedly, replacing it again is not the solution. Ask:

  • Is the part correct for the crane's duty?
  • Is there misalignment, overload or contamination?
  • Has the crane's usage changed?
  • Could a better material or design last longer?

Document findings and implement corrective action.

Step 7: Schedule work around production

Plan major work — wheel replacements, rope changes, gearbox overhauls — during planned shutdowns. With parts ready and procedures prepared, jobs that might take days in an emergency can be completed in hours.

Step 8: Keep good records

A maintenance management system or even a well-kept spreadsheet should record inspections, findings, repairs, parts used and downtime for each crane. Records reveal which cranes and components cause most downtime and where investment will pay back fastest.

A simple improvement plan

  1. List cranes and rank criticality.
  2. Review the last year's breakdowns and their causes.
  3. Build a critical spares list and fill the gaps.
  4. Introduce condition checks on wheels, brakes and gearboxes.
  5. Review results quarterly and adjust.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the biggest cause of crane downtime?

It varies by site, but common causes include brake problems, electrical faults, wheel and rail wear, rope damage and waiting for spare parts. Analysing your own breakdown records is the best way to identify the main causes at your site.

How can condition monitoring reduce downtime?

By measuring wear and performance regularly — wheel wear, brake lining thickness, gearbox oil condition, temperatures — you can detect problems before they cause failures and schedule repairs during planned maintenance.

Is preventive maintenance always better than reactive maintenance?

For critical equipment, planned maintenance is usually far more cost-effective because it avoids unplanned shutdowns. For non-critical equipment with readily available parts, running to failure may sometimes be acceptable. The key is matching the strategy to criticality.

How does operator training reduce downtime?

Trained operators avoid harsh operation, side pulls and overloading, report defects early and perform effective pre-use checks. These behaviours reduce wear and catch problems before they become breakdowns.

How often should a spares list be reviewed?

At least annually and after every significant breakdown. Reviewing ensures spares match current equipment, adds parts that caused downtime and removes obsolete items.

posts.title: Gantry vs Overhead Cranes: Components and Maintenance Differences
posts.metaTitle: Gantry vs Overhead Cranes: Components & Maintenance
posts.metaDescription: How gantry and overhead (EOT) cranes differ in structure, travel systems and environment, and what those differences mean for maintenance and spare parts.
posts.excerpt: Gantry and overhead cranes share hoists and trolleys but differ in structure, travel systems and environment — and that changes how you maintain them.
posts.imageAlt: Aerial view of a port with gantry cranes
posts.html:
Overhead (EOT) cranes and gantry cranes both lift and move loads using a hoist and trolley. The difference is how the crane is supported. That difference affects the structure, the travel system, the working environment — and the maintenance each crane needs.

The basic difference

Overhead cranes run on rails mounted on runway beams, usually supported by the building structure or dedicated columns. The bridge spans the bay above the working area.

Gantry cranes have legs that run on rails at ground level (or on wheels or tyres). They are used outdoors, in yards, ports and areas where a building structure is not available. Semi-gantry cranes combine one gantry leg with a runway on the other side.

Component comparison

Area Overhead crane Gantry crane
Support Runway beams on building or columns Legs on ground rails or tyres
Travel wheels At bridge ends, on elevated rails At leg bases, on ground rails
Environment Usually indoors Often outdoors
Exposure Dust, heat in some industries Weather, wind, corrosion, debris
Power supply Conductor bars or festoon Cable reels, festoons, conductor bars
Typical issues Runway alignment, skewing Rail settlement, wind effects, corrosion

Maintenance differences

Travel system

On overhead cranes, runway alignment depends on the building structure. Settlement, thermal movement and damage can misalign rails, leading to wheel flange wear and skewing.

On gantry cranes, ground rails can settle or shift with foundations. Debris on rails, corrosion and heavy traffic crossings add wear. Rail sweepers and guards are particularly important on gantry cranes.

Environment and corrosion

Outdoor gantry cranes face rain, sun, salt and temperature swings. Maintenance plans should include:

  • corrosion inspection and protective coating repairs;
  • drainage of water traps in the structure;
  • weatherproofing of electrical enclosures;
  • lubricants suitable for outdoor temperatures.

Wind

Outdoor cranes must be protected against wind. Storm brakes, rail clamps, anchors and wind speed alarms are essential safety systems. Inspect and test them regularly, and train operators to secure the crane when wind limits are approached.

Power supply

Cable reels and festoon systems on gantry cranes are exposed to weather and mechanical damage. Check cables, slip rings and reel mechanisms regularly.

Structure

Gantry crane legs and connections carry varying loads as the trolley moves. Periodic structural inspection for cracks and corrosion, especially at welded connections, is essential.

Shared maintenance areas

Both crane types share hoists, trolleys, brakes, ropes, hooks and controls. The same inspection principles apply: wire rope and sheave checks, brake maintenance, limit switch testing and hook inspection.

Spare parts considerations

Outdoor gantry cranes may need:

  • wheels with tougher, more wear-resistant treads;
  • sealed bearings to keep out water and dust;
  • corrosion-resistant fasteners and coatings;
  • spare cable reel components.

Port gantry cranes and container cranes, which operate continuously, typically fall into higher duty classes and benefit from critical spares held on site.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do gantry cranes need more maintenance than overhead cranes?

Outdoor gantry cranes often need more attention to corrosion, weather protection, wind safety systems and power supply cables. The core hoist and trolley maintenance is similar. The overall effort depends on duty, environment and crane design.

What is a storm brake or rail clamp?

These devices secure outdoor cranes against being moved by strong winds. They must be inspected and tested regularly, and operators must know when and how to secure the crane when wind speeds increase.

Why do gantry crane rails need regular inspection?

Ground-level rails can be affected by foundation settlement, traffic crossing, debris and corrosion. Misaligned or damaged rails cause wheel wear and skewing. Regular inspection and cleaning protect wheels and travel drives.

Are different wheels needed for outdoor cranes?

Outdoor cranes may benefit from wheels with improved sealing for bearings, corrosion protection and materials suited to the duty. Specify environmental conditions when ordering replacement wheels.

What is a semi-gantry crane?

A semi-gantry crane has one leg running on a ground rail and the other end supported on an elevated runway, often on a building. It combines characteristics of gantry and overhead cranes, and maintenance must address both travel systems.
