posts.title: Crane Wheel Wear: Causes, Inspection and Replacement
posts.metaTitle: Crane Wheel Wear: Causes, Inspection & Replacement
posts.metaDescription: Why crane wheels wear, how to inspect tread and flange wear, what different wear patterns reveal, and when to replace crane wheels.
posts.excerpt: Crane wheels wear for reasons — and the wear pattern tells you what those reasons are. Read the pattern and you can fix the cause, not just the wheel.
posts.imageAlt: Port cranes operating on rails
posts.html:
Crane wheels carry the full weight of the crane and its load, rolling back and forth thousands of times a day on busy cranes. Some wear is inevitable. But wheels that wear quickly or unevenly are telling you something about the crane, the rails or how the crane is used.

How crane wheels wear

Wheels wear in two main areas:

  • Tread wear: the rolling surface that contacts the rail head.
  • Flange wear: the raised edges that guide the wheel along the rail.

A small amount of tread wear over a long period is normal. Rapid flange wear is almost always a sign of an underlying problem.

What wear patterns reveal

Wear pattern Likely cause
Heavy flange wear on one side of all wheels Crane skewing or runway misalignment
Flange wear on diagonally opposite wheels Wheel misalignment or skewing
Uneven tread wear across width Wheel not perpendicular to rail, rail head wear
Flat spots on tread Wheel sliding or skidding, brake problems
Spalling or flaking of tread Overload, insufficient hardness, fatigue
Different diameters on driven wheels Unequal wear causing skewing (cause and effect)
Rapid tread wear Wheel too soft for duty, overload, poor rail condition

Common causes of excessive wear

Misalignment

Wheels that are not square to the rail or not parallel to each other try to "steer" the crane, forcing the flanges against the rail. End carriages damaged by collisions are a common source of misalignment.

Runway problems

Rails that are out of straightness, out of level, wrong gauge or poorly fastened push the crane sideways. Building settlement and thermal movement can alter runway geometry over time.

Crane skewing

If one side of the bridge travels faster than the other, the crane skews. Unequal driven wheel diameters, unbalanced drives or slipping brakes can cause skewing.

Material and hardness

Wheels must be hard enough for their load and duty. Too soft, and treads and flanges wear rapidly. Correct heat treatment provides a hard, wear-resistant surface with a tough core.

Operating practice

Frequent plugging (reversing under power), harsh acceleration and braking, and collisions with end stops accelerate wear and damage.

How to inspect crane wheels

Always isolate the crane and use safe access before inspection.

  1. Visual inspection: look for flange wear, tread damage, cracks, spalling and flat spots.
  2. Measure flange thickness with a gauge and compare against limits.
  3. Measure tread diameter and compare driven wheels on each side.
  4. Check bearings: listen for noise and check for play and heat.
  5. Check alignment: wheel squareness and parallelism, ideally by survey during major maintenance.
  6. Inspect the rail: head wear, alignment, joints and fixings.

When to replace

Replace wheels when:

  • flange thickness falls below the manufacturer's limit;
  • tread wear exceeds allowable limits or creates diameter differences between driven wheels;
  • cracks or significant spalling are found;
  • bearings and axles are damaged beyond repair.

Driven wheels on the same rail line should be kept closely matched in diameter. Replacing them in matched pairs prevents new skewing problems.

Fix the cause, then replace the wheel

Fitting new wheels on a misaligned crane or runway will repeat the problem — often faster, because new wheels have sharper flanges that bite into the rail. Before replacing wheels:

  • survey runway alignment if wear is severe;
  • check end carriage squareness;
  • check drive balance and brakes;
  • review operating practices.

Specifying replacement wheels

Provide: tread diameter, width, flange type (single or double), rail type, bore and keyway or axle details, hardness requirements, crane capacity, and duty. Photos of the worn wheel and wear pattern help the manufacturer recommend improvements.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I measure crane wheel flange wear?

Use a flange wear gauge or calipers to measure flange thickness at a consistent height on the flange, and compare it with the minimum value given by the crane or wheel manufacturer. Measure every wheel and record results so you can compare wear rates over time. Measurements must be taken with the crane isolated and with safe access to the wheels.

Is some flange wear normal?

A small amount of flange contact is normal, particularly when the crane starts, stops or travels over rail joints. Heavy, rapid or one-sided flange wear is not normal and usually points to misalignment, skewing, runway problems or unequal wheel diameters. Investigate the cause before replacing the wheels.

Why do crane wheels get flat spots?

Flat spots form when a wheel slides along the rail instead of rolling. Typical causes include brakes that lock the wheels, sudden stops, drive problems or seized bearings. Flat spots cause impact loads and noise every revolution, so worn wheels should be replaced and the cause corrected.

Can crane wheels be re-machined?

In some cases, worn treads can be re-machined if enough material and hardened depth remain and the wheel design allows. However, re-machining changes the diameter, which matters for driven wheels that must be matched. Surface-hardened wheels may lose their hardened layer. Often replacement is the more reliable solution.

How long should crane wheels last?

Wheel life depends on load, duty class, wheel material and hardness, rail condition and alignment. In good conditions wheels can last many years; on misaligned cranes they may wear out in months. Tracking wear rates is the best way to predict replacement and detect problems.

posts.title: Single vs Double Flange Crane Wheels: Which Do You Need?
posts.keyword: single vs double flange crane wheels
posts.metaTitle: Single vs Double Flange Crane Wheels Explained
posts.metaDescription: The differences between single-flange, double-flange and flangeless crane wheels, where each is used, and how to choose the right profile.
posts.excerpt: Wheel flanges keep a crane on its rails. Choosing between single and double flanges depends on the crane type, guidance system and rail layout.
posts.imageAlt: Container cranes on rails at a port
posts.html:
Crane wheels do more than carry load. Their flanges guide the crane along its rails and prevent derailment. Crane wheels are usually supplied in three basic profiles: double flange, single flange and flangeless. Each suits different applications.

Double-flange wheels

Double-flange wheels have a flange on each side of the tread, capturing the rail head between them.

Advantages

  • Positive guidance in both directions.
  • Lower risk of derailment.
  • The most common choice for overhead crane bridges and many trolleys.

Considerations

  • The gap between flanges (clearance to the rail head) must suit the rail and allow for thermal movement and runway tolerances.
  • If the runway is misaligned, flanges may bind and wear quickly.

Single-flange wheels

Single-flange wheels have one flange, normally on the outside or inside of the rail depending on the design.

Typical uses

  • Some underhung and top-running trolleys.
  • Gantry cranes and transfer cars where guidance is provided on one side.
  • Applications where one rail is the guide rail and the other allows lateral float.

Considerations

  • Guidance relies on correct installation and rail layout.
  • Lateral forces must be managed by the design.

Flangeless wheels

Flangeless wheels have a plain tread and rely on separate guide rollers for guidance.

Typical uses

  • Large spans where thermal expansion and runway tolerances would otherwise cause flange wear.
  • Cranes with horizontal guide roller systems.
  • Some heavy-duty process cranes.

Considerations

  • Guide rollers must be maintained and correctly adjusted.

Tread shape: cylindrical or tapered

Tread profile also matters. Cylindrical treads are common on many industrial cranes. Tapered treads are used on some drive arrangements to help the crane self-centre and reduce skewing, provided they are used with the appropriate rail head profile and drive configuration. Mixing tread types incorrectly can cause tracking problems.

Choosing the right profile

Consideration Points towards
Standard overhead crane bridge Double flange
Wide span, large thermal movement Flangeless with guide rollers, or larger flange clearance
Guide rail on one side only Single flange on guide side
Transfer car on floor rails Double or single flange depending on layout
History of severe flange wear Review alignment, consider guide rollers

Flange clearance

The clearance between the flange and the rail head is important. Too tight and flanges bind and wear; too loose and the crane can skew more before being corrected. Clearance is set by the crane designer based on span, rail size and runway tolerances.

Replacing wheels: match the original — or improve it

When ordering replacements:

  1. Confirm the flange type and positions.
  2. Measure tread width and flange-to-flange distance.
  3. Record the rail type and head width.
  4. Note tread profile (cylindrical or tapered).
  5. Describe any wear problems with the existing wheels.

If wheels have worn rapidly, discuss the wear pattern with the manufacturer. Improved hardness or a different flange arrangement — combined with alignment correction — may extend life considerably.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is flange clearance and why does it matter?

Flange clearance is the space between the wheel flanges and the rail head. It allows for runway tolerances and thermal movement. Too little clearance causes binding and rapid wear; too much allows excessive skewing before correction. The correct clearance is set by the crane design.

Can I convert double-flange wheels to flangeless with guide rollers?

It is possible on some cranes, but it is a design change that affects how lateral forces are transferred to the structure. It should be engineered by qualified crane specialists, considering the end carriage design, runway and guide roller mounting.

Why do some cranes use tapered treads?

Tapered treads, used with appropriate rail heads and drive arrangements, can help the crane self-centre and reduce skewing. They must be used as designed; mixing tapered and cylindrical treads incorrectly can create tracking problems.

Are single-flange wheels less safe?

Not when used correctly. Single-flange wheels are used where the design provides guidance on one side, such as a guide rail. Safety depends on the overall design, installation and maintenance rather than the number of flanges alone.

What information do I need to order replacement wheels?

Provide the tread diameter, tread width, flange type and dimensions, rail type, bore and axle or bearing details, hardness requirements, crane capacity and duty, and drawings or photos of the existing wheel. Mention any wear problems so improvements can be considered.

posts.title: Crane Wheel Materials and Heat Treatment Explained
posts.metaTitle: Crane Wheel Materials and Heat Treatment Explained
posts.metaDescription: Forged vs cast crane wheels, common steel types, induction vs through hardening, and how hardness affects wheel and rail life.
posts.excerpt: The material and heat treatment of a crane wheel decide how long it lasts. Here is what buyers should know before ordering replacement wheels.
posts.imageAlt: Steel component being machined and finished
posts.html:
Two crane wheels can look identical and still have very different service lives. The difference lies in the material and heat treatment. Understanding these factors helps you specify replacement wheels that last, without damaging the rails they run on.

The demands on a crane wheel

A crane wheel must:

  • carry high contact stresses where the tread meets the rail;
  • resist wear from rolling and sliding;
  • resist fatigue from millions of load cycles;
  • withstand impacts and occasional shock loads;
  • remain tough enough not to crack.

These requirements pull in different directions. A very hard material resists wear but can be brittle. A tough material resists cracking but wears faster. Heat treatment gives the best of both: a hard surface with a tough core.

Material options

Forged steel

Forging refines the grain structure of the steel and minimises internal defects. Forged wheels are widely used for heavy-duty applications because of their strength and consistency.

Cast steel

Cast wheels can be economical for larger wheels and complex shapes. Casting quality must be carefully controlled to avoid porosity and inclusions.

Rolled or machined from bar

Smaller wheels are often machined from solid bar or forged blanks.

Common steels for crane wheels are medium-carbon and alloy steels that respond well to heat treatment. The exact grade depends on wheel size, load and duty.

Heat treatment methods

Through hardening

The entire wheel is heat-treated to a uniform hardness. This gives consistent properties but limits the maximum hardness that can be used without making the wheel brittle.

Induction hardening of the tread

The tread and flanges are heated by induction and quenched, producing a hard, wear-resistant surface layer while the core remains tougher. The depth of hardening is important: it must be deep enough to support contact stresses and allow for wear.

Flame hardening

Similar in principle to induction hardening, using a flame to heat the surface. Used for some larger wheels.

Hardness and rail compatibility

Wheel hardness should be matched to the rail. If the wheel is much harder than the rail, the rail wears quickly; if it is much softer, the wheel wears quickly. Rails are expensive and disruptive to replace, so wheel specifications usually aim for a balanced relationship with the rail material.

Typical choices by duty

Duty Typical approach
Light-duty cranes Through-hardened or normalised steel
Moderate-duty cranes Through-hardened or induction-hardened tread
Heavy and severe duty Forged alloy steel with induction-hardened tread and flanges

These are general guides; final specifications should consider load, wheel diameter, speed, rail type and environment.

Quality checks to expect

When buying replacement wheels, ask for:

  • hardness test results on the tread (and sometimes the flange);
  • hardness depth information for surface-hardened wheels where required;
  • dimensional inspection report covering diameter, width, bore and flange dimensions;
  • material certificates where available.

Signs the material or treatment is wrong

  • Rapid, smooth tread wear: wheel too soft.
  • Cracking or spalling: overload, insufficient case depth or brittle material.
  • Rapid rail wear: wheel much harder than the rail.

Getting the specification right

Provide the manufacturer with crane capacity, wheel load, duty, rail type, speed and the history of the existing wheels. With this information, material and heat treatment can be optimised for long life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are forged wheels better than cast wheels?

Forged wheels generally have a more refined grain structure and fewer internal defects, making them a common choice for heavy-duty cranes. High-quality cast wheels can perform well, especially for large sizes, provided casting quality is controlled. The best choice depends on size, duty and cost.

What hardness should crane wheels have?

There is no single answer. Hardness should suit the wheel load, duty and rail material. Very hard wheels can accelerate rail wear, while soft wheels wear quickly. Wheel manufacturers and crane designers select hardness to balance wheel and rail life.

What does case depth mean for induction-hardened wheels?

Case depth is the depth of the hardened layer below the surface. It must be deep enough to support contact stresses and to allow for normal wear over the wheel's life. If the case is too shallow, the hardened layer can wear through or crack.

How can I verify wheel hardness?

Request a hardness test report from the manufacturer. For critical wheels, you can also specify testing of sample parts or sections to confirm hardened depth. Portable hardness testers can check surface hardness on site.

Why did my new wheels crack?

Cracking can result from excessive hardness with insufficient toughness, poor heat treatment, material defects, sharp design features or severe impact loads. A failure investigation, including material and hardness checks, helps identify the cause.

posts.title: Crane Skewing and Rail Alignment Problems: Causes and Solutions
posts.metaTitle: Crane Skewing & Rail Alignment Problems: Causes, Fixes
posts.metaDescription: Why overhead cranes skew and crab along their runway, how rail misalignment and wheel differences cause it, and the steps to diagnose and correct it.
posts.excerpt: A crane that crabs along its runway wears out wheels and rails at an alarming rate. Here is how to find and fix the causes of skewing.
posts.imageAlt: Warehouse with high-bay racking and lifting equipment
posts.html:
A healthy overhead crane travels straight down its runway with its bridge square to the rails. A skewing crane travels slightly diagonally, "crabbing" as it goes, with wheel flanges grinding against the rails. Skewing causes rapid wheel and rail wear, noise, structural stress and, in severe cases, derailment risk.

Signs your crane is skewing

  • Heavy flange wear on wheels, often on diagonally opposite corners.
  • Shiny wear marks on the side of the rail heads.
  • Squealing or grinding during travel.
  • The crane "walks" to one side or the bridge is visibly out of square.
  • Uneven wear on end stops and buffers.

Common causes

1. Unequal wheel diameters

If driven wheels on one side are smaller than on the other, that side travels a shorter distance per revolution. The crane gradually skews. This is often both a cause and a result of skewing — wear creates diameter differences, which increases skew, which increases wear.

2. Drive imbalance

On cranes with separate drives on each end truck, differences in motor speed, brake timing or gear ratios make one side lead the other.

3. Runway misalignment

Rails that are not straight, not parallel, at the wrong gauge or at different elevations force the crane sideways. Causes include building settlement, damaged runway beams, loose rail clips and poor original installation.

4. Damaged or out-of-square end carriages

Collisions with end stops or other cranes can bend end carriages or shift wheel blocks, putting wheels out of alignment.

5. Brake problems

A travel brake that drags or releases late on one side causes uneven travel and skewing, especially during starting and stopping.

6. Operating practice

Aggressive acceleration and frequent reversing under power exaggerate skewing tendencies.

How to diagnose

Safety first: isolate the crane and use proper access and fall protection for all inspections.

  1. Inspect wear patterns on all wheels and rails, noting which flanges are worn and on which side.
  2. Measure driven wheel diameters and compare.
  3. Check drives and brakes for equal performance on both sides.
  4. Check end carriage squareness and wheel alignment.
  5. Commission a runway survey to measure rail straightness, span, elevation and joints along the full length.

A runway survey gives objective data and is the foundation for correcting serious alignment problems.

Solutions

Cause Solution
Unequal driven wheel diameters Replace driven wheels in matched sets
Drive imbalance Check and match drives, brakes and controls
Runway misalignment Realign rails, repair runway beams, replace clips
Bent end carriages Repair or replace, re-square wheels
Brake issues Adjust or repair brakes, balance timing
Operating practice Operator training, soft-start drives

Variable speed drives help

Modern variable frequency drives (VFDs) provide smooth acceleration and deceleration, reducing skewing forces. They are a common upgrade for older cranes with direct-on-line or resistance-controlled travel motors.

Guide rollers for long spans

For wide-span cranes or runways with thermal movement, horizontal guide rollers can take guidance forces off the wheel flanges. This is a design change that should be engineered by qualified crane specialists.

Do it in the right order

Replacing worn wheels without correcting the runway or drives will lead to the same wear again. A sensible sequence is: survey → correct runway and end carriages → balance drives → fit matched new wheels → monitor wear.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I know if my crane is skewing?

Common signs include heavy flange wear on diagonally opposite wheels, wear marks on the side of the rail heads, squealing during travel and visible crabbing of the bridge. Measuring wheel diameters and checking drive performance helps confirm the cause.

What is a runway survey?

A runway survey measures rail straightness, span (gauge), elevation and joint condition along the full length of the runway. It provides objective data to identify misalignment and plan corrections.

Can variable frequency drives reduce skewing?

Yes. VFDs provide smooth acceleration and deceleration and can balance drives more effectively than older control systems, reducing skewing forces. They work best combined with proper alignment and matched wheels.

Should I replace wheels before fixing alignment?

No. Fix alignment, runway and drive issues first, then fit new wheels. Otherwise the new wheels will wear quickly in the same way as the old ones.

Can building settlement affect crane rails?

Yes. Settlement, thermal movement and structural changes can shift runway beams and rails over time. Periodic surveys, especially after building work, help detect these changes.

posts.title: End Carriage Assemblies: Components, Wear and Upgrades
posts.metaTitle: Crane End Carriage Assemblies: Components and Upgrades
posts.metaDescription: What a crane end carriage contains, how its components wear, how to inspect them, and when to upgrade to complete replacement assemblies.
posts.excerpt: End carriages carry the crane bridge and house the wheels and drives. Keeping them in good condition is central to smooth, safe crane travel.
posts.imageAlt: Technician assembling heavy wheel and bearing components
posts.html:
The end carriage — also called an end truck — sits at each end of an overhead crane's bridge. It carries the bridge girders, houses the travel wheels and supports the long travel drives. Every movement of the crane along its runway depends on the condition of the end carriages.

Main components

  • Frame: a fabricated box or channel structure connecting to the bridge girders.
  • Wheels: driven and idler wheels that run on the runway rails.
  • Axles and bearings: support the wheels and allow rotation.
  • Bearing housings or wheel blocks: hold bearings and wheels in alignment.
  • Drive units: geared motors or motors with gearboxes driving the wheels.
  • Brakes: often integrated with drive motors.
  • Buffers: absorb impacts at the end of travel.
  • Rail sweepers and guards: clear debris from the rail and protect against wheel failures.

How end carriages wear

Wheels

Tread and flange wear is the most common issue. Rapid wear usually indicates alignment or skewing problems.

Bearings

Bearings wear from load, contamination and inadequate lubrication. Failing bearings produce noise, heat and play, and eventually allow wheels to tilt.

Bearing housings and axles

Worn bores and axle seats let wheels move out of alignment. Fretting where bearings sit on axles is a common long-term problem.

Frames

Collisions with end stops or other cranes can bend frames and disturb wheel alignment. Fatigue cracks may develop at welded connections on heavily used cranes.

Drives

Gearbox wear, coupling wear and brake issues affect travel performance.

Inspection checklist

Isolate the crane and use safe access for all inspections.

  • Wheel flange and tread wear.
  • Bearing noise, temperature and play.
  • Wheel alignment and squareness.
  • Frame condition: cracks, bending, corrosion.
  • Bolted connections to the girders.
  • Drive gearbox oil levels and leaks.
  • Brake condition and adjustment.
  • Buffers and rail sweepers present and undamaged.

Repair or replace the whole assembly?

Individual wheels and bearings can be replaced when the frame and housings are sound. However, a complete replacement or remanufactured assembly may be better when:

  • housings and axle seats are worn, making alignment difficult;
  • frames are bent or cracked;
  • the crane is being upgraded with new drives;
  • multiple components are near the end of their life;
  • downtime must be minimised — a complete assembly can be pre-built and installed quickly.

Common upgrades

Upgrade Benefit
Hardened forged wheels Longer wheel life on heavy-duty cranes
Modern wheel blocks with cartridge bearings Easier alignment and maintenance
Variable frequency drives Smoother travel, less skewing and wear
Improved buffers Reduced impact damage
Rail sweepers and safety lugs Protection against debris and wheel failure

Pre-assembled wheel sets save downtime

Supplying wheels pre-assembled with axles, bearings and housings means maintenance teams can swap complete units during a short shutdown rather than pressing bearings on site.

Information needed for replacement assemblies

  • Crane capacity, span and duty.
  • Wheel diameter, flange type and rail size.
  • Wheelbase and mounting interface to the bridge.
  • Drive type and arrangement.
  • Photos and dimensions of the existing end carriage.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an end carriage and an end truck?

They are the same component. Both terms describe the assembly at each end of the bridge that carries the wheels and connects to the girders. Terminology varies by region and manufacturer.

When should end carriages be replaced rather than repaired?

Consider replacement when frames are bent or cracked, bearing housings are badly worn, multiple components are near end of life, or when upgrading drives and wheels. Replacement can also reduce downtime if the new assembly is prepared in advance.

Can I upgrade end carriages on an old crane?

Yes, many older cranes are upgraded with modern end carriages, wheel blocks and drives. The upgrade must suit the crane's structure, span, capacity and runway, and should be engineered by qualified crane specialists.

What are rail sweepers for?

Rail sweepers clear debris from the rail ahead of the wheels, preventing wheel damage and derailment risk. They should be present, correctly adjusted and in good condition.

Why do bearing housings wear?

Wear can result from fretting, incorrect fits, contamination, overload and impacts. Worn housings allow bearings and wheels to move out of alignment, accelerating wheel wear.

posts.title: Crane Wheel Bearings: Selection and Maintenance
posts.metaTitle: Crane Wheel Bearings: Selection and Maintenance Guide
posts.metaDescription: Choosing and maintaining crane wheel bearings: bearing types, lubrication, sealing, warning signs of failure and best practices for replacement.
posts.excerpt: Wheel bearings support every tonne a crane carries. Correct selection, lubrication and sealing make the difference between years of service and early failure.
posts.imageAlt: Heavy cranes in operation at a port terminal
posts.html:
Crane wheel bearings carry the crane's weight and every load it lifts, while allowing wheels to roll smoothly. A failed wheel bearing can cause wheel misalignment, skewing, overheating and, in the worst cases, wheel seizure. Good bearing selection and maintenance are essential for reliable crane travel.

Common bearing types

Spherical roller bearings

Widely used in crane wheel blocks because they handle high radial loads, tolerate some misalignment and carry moderate axial loads from guidance forces.

Tapered roller bearings

Handle combined radial and axial loads well and are used in some wheel designs, usually in pairs with careful adjustment.

Cylindrical roller bearings

High radial load capacity; often used in combination with other bearings that take axial loads.

Deep groove ball bearings

Used for lighter-duty wheels and trolleys.

The right choice depends on wheel load, speed, axial forces, misalignment and space.

Lubrication

Most crane wheel bearings are grease-lubricated. Good practice includes:

  • using the grease type specified by the bearing or crane manufacturer;
  • following re-lubrication intervals based on duty and environment;
  • not over-greasing, which can cause overheating and seal damage;
  • using clean grease and clean grease guns to avoid introducing contamination;
  • ensuring grease reaches the bearing through clear lubrication paths.

High-temperature environments, such as steel plants, need greases suitable for elevated temperatures.

Sealing

Seals keep grease in and contamination out. Dust, scale, water and process debris are the enemies of bearings. Inspect seals for damage and replace them when bearings are serviced. Outdoor and dusty environments benefit from improved sealing arrangements.

Warning signs of bearing failure

Sign What it may indicate
Noise (rumbling, grinding, clicking) Wear, damage, contamination
Heat at the wheel block Lubrication problems, overload, failure
Wheel wobble or axial play Bearing wear or loose fit
Grease leaking or discoloured Seal failure, overheating
Uneven wheel wear Misalignment caused by bearing wear

Thermal imaging during operation is an easy way to spot bearings running hotter than their neighbours.

Why bearings fail early

  • Poor lubrication: too little, too much or the wrong grease.
  • Contamination: dust, water and process debris.
  • Incorrect fitting: damage during installation, wrong fits on shafts and housings.
  • Misalignment: bent axles or worn housings.
  • Overload and shock: collisions and harsh operation.

Best practices for replacement

  1. Replace bearings using proper tools — induction heaters and pullers rather than hammers and flames.
  2. Check shaft and housing fits and repair worn seats.
  3. Clean all components before assembly.
  4. Fit new seals with new bearings.
  5. Pack with the correct grease quantity.
  6. Check alignment after reassembly.

Consider pre-assembled wheel blocks

Supplying wheels as pre-assembled units with bearings, axles and housings ensures correct fits and clean assembly in a workshop, and shortens downtime on site.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should crane wheel bearings be greased?

Follow the bearing or crane manufacturer's recommended interval, then adjust it for your duty and environment. Cranes running multiple shifts, in hot areas such as steel plants, or in dusty and wet conditions usually need more frequent lubrication than a lightly used workshop crane. Use the specified grease, a clean grease gun and the correct quantity — over-greasing pushes out seals and causes bearings to run hot, while under-greasing leads to wear. Recording each lubrication task makes it easy to confirm that critical cranes are not missed.

Can I mix different types of grease?

Avoid it unless compatibility has been confirmed. Greases use different thickeners and base oils, and incompatible greases can soften and run out of the bearing or harden into a paste that no longer lubricates. If you need to change grease type, purge the old grease thoroughly according to the manufacturer's guidance and label lubrication points clearly so the same product is used every time.

How can I detect bearing problems before they fail?

Listen for rumbling, grinding or clicking as the crane travels, and check wheel blocks with an infrared thermometer or thermal camera — a bearing running noticeably hotter than its neighbours is a warning sign. During inspections, check for wheel wobble, axial play, leaking or discoloured grease and damaged seals. Catching these signs early allows bearings to be replaced during planned maintenance rather than after a seizure damages the axle or housing.

Why do newly replaced bearings sometimes fail quickly?

The most common causes are installation damage from hammering, worn or incorrectly sized shaft and housing seats, dirt introduced during assembly, the wrong grease or quantity, and misalignment from worn housings or bent axles. Using induction heaters and proper pullers, checking fits, working in clean conditions and replacing seals with every bearing change prevent most early failures. Pre-assembled wheel blocks built in a workshop avoid many of these risks.

Are sealed bearings better for outdoor cranes?

For outdoor and dusty applications, better sealing usually pays off. Water, dust and scale are the main enemies of crane wheel bearings, and effective seals keep grease in and contamination out. The best arrangement depends on speed, temperature and maintenance access, so describe the environment when ordering wheels or assemblies and ask the supplier to recommend suitable sealing.

posts.title: Rail Wear and Its Effect on Crane Wheels
posts.metaTitle: Crane Rail Wear and Its Effect on Crane Wheels
posts.metaDescription: How crane rail head wear, joints, fixings and alignment affect wheel life, what to inspect on runway rails, and when rail repair or replacement is needed.
posts.excerpt: Wheels and rails wear as a pair. Ignoring the rail when replacing wheels is one of the most common — and expensive — maintenance mistakes.
posts.imageAlt: Aerial view of rail-mounted port cranes
posts.html:
Crane wheels and rails work as a system. The rail supports and guides the wheel; the wheel loads and wears the rail. When rails wear or move out of alignment, wheels wear faster — and when wheels are misaligned, rails suffer. Effective maintenance treats them together.

How crane rails wear

Head wear

The top of the rail head wears from rolling contact. Uneven head wear changes the contact between wheel and rail, concentrating stress and accelerating wheel tread wear.

Side wear

Wheel flanges rubbing against the side of the rail head create side wear. This is a clear sign of misalignment or crane skewing.

Joint problems

Rail joints that are uneven, open or poorly supported create impacts each time a wheel passes. Impacts damage wheel treads, bearings and the crane structure.

Fixing failures

Loose or broken rail clips and bolts allow rails to move sideways or rock, causing misalignment and noise.

Corrosion and contamination

Outdoor rails corrode; process debris and spillage on rails can cause wheels to slip or climb.

How rail problems affect wheels

Rail problem Effect on wheels
Misaligned or out-of-gauge rails Rapid flange wear, skewing
Uneven head wear Uneven tread wear, spalling
Stepped or open joints Impact damage, bearing wear
Loose fixings Lateral movement, flange wear
Debris on rails Tread damage, risk of climbing
Rail harder or softer than wheel Accelerated wear of the softer component

What to inspect

Isolate cranes and use proper access and fall protection before inspecting runways.

  • Rail head profile: look for uneven wear, flattening and side wear.
  • Joints: check alignment, gaps, steps and joint bars or welds.
  • Clips and fixings: check for missing, loose or broken components.
  • Pads and bedding: where elastomeric pads are used, check for deterioration.
  • Alignment and gauge: visually, and by periodic runway survey.
  • End stops: secure and undamaged.
  • Cleanliness: remove debris and spillage.

Runway surveys

A runway survey measures rail straightness, span (gauge), elevation and joint condition along the full runway. Surveys are recommended:

  • when wheel wear is excessive or uneven;
  • after building modifications or settlement;
  • after crane collisions;
  • as part of long-term asset management for high-duty cranes.

Survey results show exactly where correction is needed, avoiding guesswork.

Repair options

  • Re-fastening and shimming to correct alignment and level.
  • Replacing clips and pads.
  • Grinding or welding joints to remove steps.
  • Replacing sections of badly worn rail.
  • Full rail replacement where wear is widespread.

Match wheel and rail properties

Wheel hardness and profile should be compatible with the rail. Very hard wheels on softer rails wear the rails; soft wheels on hard rails wear quickly themselves. When replacing either, consider the other.

Coordinate wheel and rail work

When planning wheel replacement:

  1. Inspect the rails and review the runway survey.
  2. Correct alignment and rail defects.
  3. Fit wheels in matched sets.
  4. Monitor wheel wear after the work to confirm the problem is solved.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I know when crane rails need replacing?

Look for severe head wear, significant side wear from flange contact, cracks, damaged or stepped joints that cannot be repaired, and loose or broken fixings that keep recurring. A runway inspection or survey shows whether problems are local — fixable with re-fastening, shimming or joint repairs — or widespread enough to justify replacement. Because rail replacement is disruptive, plan it together with wheel replacement and any runway beam repairs.

Can worn rails damage brand-new wheels?

Yes. Uneven rail heads concentrate contact stresses on part of the tread, stepped joints create impacts, and misaligned rails push flanges into the rail sides. New wheels on a poor runway can wear out much faster than the wheels they replaced. Inspect and correct rail problems before or at the same time as fitting new wheels.

What do rail clips do and why do they fail?

Rail clips hold the rail to the runway beam while allowing controlled thermal movement. They fail through vibration, corrosion, impact and incorrect installation. Loose or missing clips allow rails to move sideways and rock under load, causing misalignment, noise and wear. Check clips during routine crane inspections and replace damaged ones promptly.

Should crane wheels be harder than the rails?

Wheel and rail hardness should be balanced so neither wears excessively. If wheels are much harder than the rails, the rails wear faster — and rails are usually more expensive and disruptive to replace. If wheels are much softer, they wear quickly. Tell your wheel supplier the rail type and condition so they can recommend suitable hardness.

How often should crane runways be surveyed?

Many sites survey runways when wheel wear becomes excessive, after building modifications or settlement, after crane collisions, and at intervals for high-duty cranes. A baseline survey when a crane is new or after major repairs makes later comparisons much more useful.

posts.title: Why Crane Wheels Should Be Replaced in Matched Pairs
posts.metaTitle: Why Replace Crane Wheels in Matched Pairs?
posts.metaDescription: Why driven crane wheels must be closely matched in diameter, what happens when they are not, and how to plan wheel replacement to prevent skewing.
posts.excerpt: Replacing a single worn driven wheel can create a new problem. Here is why crane wheels should be replaced — and manufactured — in matched sets.
posts.imageAlt: Warehouse interior with material handling equipment
posts.html:
When one crane wheel wears out, it can be tempting to replace only that wheel. On idler wheels that may be acceptable. On driven wheels it often creates a new problem: unequal wheel diameters that make the crane skew.

The geometry of the problem

A driven wheel travels a distance equal to its circumference on every revolution. If two driven wheels on opposite sides of a bridge turn at the same speed but have different diameters, the larger wheel travels further. The bridge turns slightly with every revolution, forcing the crane to skew until flanges correct it — with friction, noise and wear.

Even small diameter differences matter because the effect accumulates over every metre the crane travels.

Common drive arrangements

Common drive (line shaft)

One motor drives wheels on both sides through a shaft. Both wheels turn at exactly the same speed, so diameter differences translate directly into skewing.

Separate drives

Each end carriage has its own motor. Speeds are similar but not identical, and diameter differences still cause the crane to drift. Modern drive controls can partly compensate, but matched wheels remain important.

Why mismatched wheels make wear worse

  1. A new wheel is larger than the worn wheel opposite.
  2. The crane skews towards the smaller wheel.
  3. Flanges press against rails, wearing both.
  4. Wear increases diameter differences further.
  5. The cycle accelerates.

Best practice for wheel replacement

Situation Recommended approach
One driven wheel worn Replace the driven wheels on that drive line together
Common drive arrangement Replace driven wheels as a matched set
Idler wheel worn Can often be replaced individually, check overall alignment
Severe flange wear Investigate alignment before replacing

How tight is "matched"?

Driven wheels in a set should be manufactured to closely controlled diameters. Your crane manufacturer or wheel supplier can specify an appropriate tolerance for the crane's design and speed. When ordering, request that driven wheels are supplied as a matched set with measured diameters recorded on the inspection report.

Plan replacements in advance

Wheels wear gradually. By measuring wheel diameters during routine inspections, you can:

  • predict when wheels will reach their limits;
  • order matched sets with time to manufacture;
  • replace wheels during planned shutdowns.

Keep records

Record the measured diameter of every wheel at installation and at each inspection. This simple data reveals uneven wear early and helps diagnose skewing.

Don't forget the cause

If wheels have worn unevenly or quickly, correct the cause — misalignment, drive imbalance, brake problems or runway defects — before fitting new wheels. Otherwise, the new matched set will soon become mismatched.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does "matched pair" mean for crane wheels?

It means driven wheels manufactured and measured so their tread diameters are within a tight tolerance of each other. Because each revolution moves the crane a distance equal to the wheel's circumference, matched diameters ensure both sides of the bridge travel the same distance. Ask your supplier to record the measured diameter of each wheel on the inspection report so you can verify the match.

Can I replace idler wheels one at a time?

Often yes, because idler wheels do not drive the crane and small diameter differences have less effect on tracking. However, a single worn idler can indicate a wider problem such as misalignment or a damaged end carriage, so check the overall wear pattern before replacing it in isolation.

How close do driven wheel diameters need to be?

The acceptable difference depends on the crane design, span, speed and drive arrangement, so it should come from the crane manufacturer or an experienced wheel supplier. As a rule, the tighter the match the better, especially on common drives where both wheels turn at exactly the same speed.

Why do diameter differences matter more on common drives?

With a common (line-shaft) drive, both driven wheels rotate at identical speed. Any diameter difference means one side covers more distance every revolution, so the crane steadily skews until flanges force it back. On separate drives the effect still exists but can be partly offset by the drive control.

How can I plan wheel replacements to avoid breakdowns?

Measure tread diameters and flange thickness at regular inspections and record them. Plotting wear over time shows when wheels will reach their limits, giving enough notice to order a matched set and replace it during a planned shutdown rather than after a failure.

posts.title: Crane Travel Drives: Gearboxes, Motors and Couplings
posts.metaTitle: Crane Travel Drives: Gearboxes, Motors and Couplings
posts.metaDescription: How crane long-travel and cross-travel drives work, common gearbox, motor, coupling and brake problems, and maintenance practices for reliable crane travel.
posts.excerpt: Travel drives move the crane and trolley along their rails. Keeping gearboxes, motors and couplings healthy prevents breakdowns and protects wheels and rails.
posts.imageAlt: Technician maintaining a mechanical drive system
posts.html:
Every overhead and gantry crane uses travel drives to move the bridge along the runway (long travel) and the trolley across the bridge (cross travel). These drives include motors, gearboxes, couplings, brakes and controls. Their condition affects not only whether the crane moves, but how smoothly — and how fast wheels and rails wear.

Drive arrangements

Geared motors on each end carriage

Modern cranes typically use a geared motor mounted directly on each driven wheel or end carriage. This arrangement is compact and easy to maintain.

Central drive with line shafts

Older cranes may use a single motor and gearbox driving wheels on both sides via long shafts and couplings.

Trolley drives

Trolleys use similar arrangements on a smaller scale.

Key components and common problems

Motors

Problems include overheating, bearing failures and insulation breakdown. Frequent starting, inching and plugging place heavy demands on travel motors.

Gearboxes

Gearboxes reduce motor speed and increase torque. Common issues include:

  • oil leaks from seals;
  • low or degraded oil;
  • bearing wear and noise;
  • gear tooth wear or damage from shock loads.

Couplings

Couplings connect motors, gearboxes and shafts while allowing small misalignments. Flexible elements wear and need periodic replacement. Gear couplings require lubrication. Worn couplings cause noise, backlash and shock loading of gearboxes.

Brakes

Travel brakes stop the crane and trolley. Uneven brake performance between sides contributes to skewing.

Controls

Older cranes may use contactor control with resistors; modern cranes use variable frequency drives (VFDs) for smooth acceleration and deceleration.

Maintenance checklist

Isolate the crane and follow safe access procedures before work.

  • Check gearbox oil levels and condition; change oil at recommended intervals.
  • Inspect for oil leaks and replace seals.
  • Listen for noise and feel for heat on gearboxes and motors.
  • Inspect coupling elements for wear and check alignment.
  • Check brake linings and air gaps.
  • Inspect motor terminal boxes and cables.
  • Check mounting bolts and torque arms.
  • Review drive fault logs on VFD-controlled cranes.

Diagnostic quick reference

Symptom Possible causes
Clunk on starting or stopping Coupling wear, gear backlash, loose mounting
Overheating motor Excessive inching, brake dragging, overload
Noisy gearbox Low oil, bearing wear, tooth damage
Crane skews on start Unequal drives or brake timing
Oil on rails or brakes Gearbox seal leaks

Upgrading to VFD control

Retrofitting VFDs to older cranes offers:

  • smoother acceleration and braking;
  • reduced shock on gearboxes and couplings;
  • less load swing;
  • reduced wheel and rail wear;
  • better positioning control.

Upgrades should be engineered to suit the existing motors, brakes and structure.

Spare parts for drives

For critical cranes, consider holding spare coupling elements, brake parts, seals and, for the most critical drives, a complete spare geared motor.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should crane gearbox oil be changed?

Follow the gearbox manufacturer's interval, which is typically based on operating hours and oil type, and shorten it for hot, dusty or heavy-duty conditions. Oil analysis can extend or shorten intervals based on actual condition and also reveals wear metals that indicate developing bearing or gear damage. Always check oil levels during routine inspections, because low oil is a common cause of gearbox failures.

What causes a clunk when the crane starts or stops?

Typical causes are worn coupling elements, excessive gear backlash, loose gearbox mounting bolts or worn torque arms. These problems create shock loads every time the crane accelerates or brakes, which accelerates wear on gears and bearings and can loosen structural connections. Inspect and replace worn parts promptly.

Is it worth upgrading an older crane to VFD control?

On busy cranes it often is. Variable frequency drives give smooth acceleration and deceleration, reduce load swing, improve positioning and reduce mechanical shock on gearboxes, couplings, wheels and structures. The upgrade must be engineered to suit the existing motors, brakes and control system, and may require motor or brake changes on very old cranes.

Why do travel motors overheat?

Frequent inching, brakes that drag or release late, overloading, incorrect control settings and high ambient temperatures are common causes. Replacing an overheated motor without finding the cause usually leads to a repeat failure, so check brakes, operating practice and drive settings first.

Which drive spare parts are worth keeping?

Coupling elements, brake linings and coils, gearbox seals and contactors are inexpensive and commonly needed. For cranes that would stop production if a drive failed, a complete spare geared motor or gearbox can turn a multi-day breakdown into a few hours of work.

posts.title: CNC Machining for Hydraulic Components: Why Precision Matters
posts.metaTitle: CNC Machining for Hydraulic Components: Why It Matters
posts.metaDescription: How CNC turning and milling produce accurate, repeatable hydraulic components — pistons, glands, rods and manifolds — and why tolerances and finishes matter.
posts.excerpt: Hydraulic components only work when clearances, finishes and geometry are right. CNC machining delivers the precision and repeatability they need.
posts.imageAlt: Technician operating CNC machinery on a production floor
posts.html:
Hydraulic components depend on precision. A piston must fit its bore with a controlled clearance, a gland must locate a seal in exactly the right groove, and a manifold must route oil through intersecting drillings without leaks. Small dimensional errors lead to leakage, seal failure and lost performance. This is why CNC machining is central to modern hydraulic manufacturing.

What CNC machining brings

Computer numerical control (CNC) machines follow programmed toolpaths with high accuracy. For hydraulic components, this provides:

  • Accuracy: dimensions and geometry held within tight tolerances.
  • Repeatability: the hundredth part matches the first.
  • Complex geometry: multi-axis machining of grooves, ports and contours.
  • Surface finish control: consistent finishes for sealing surfaces.
  • Efficiency: shorter cycle times for batch and repeat work.

Typical CNC-machined hydraulic parts

Component Key machined features
Pistons Seal and wear-ring grooves, bore for rod, concentricity
Glands Rod seal, wiper and O-ring grooves, threads
Piston rods Threads, shoulders, mounting features before plating
End caps and clevises Bores, pin holes, ports, threads
Manifolds Valve cavities, cross-drillings, port threads
Shafts and couplings Keyways, splines, bearing seats

Why tolerances matter

Seal grooves

Seal manufacturers specify groove dimensions and tolerances. A groove that is too deep allows the seal to move and leak; too shallow and the seal is over-compressed, increasing friction and wear.

Concentricity

Pistons, glands and rods must be concentric. Eccentricity loads seals unevenly and causes uneven wear.

Clearances

Clearance gaps behind seals affect extrusion resistance at high pressure. Too large a gap lets the seal extrude and fail.

Threads

Gland threads and port threads must be accurate and clean to seal correctly and carry load.

Surface finish

Sealing surfaces need specific finishes. Too rough and seals wear; too smooth and lubrication suffers. CNC machining combined with appropriate finishing processes — grinding, honing, polishing or burnishing — produces the right finish for each surface.

Deburring and cleanliness

Sharp edges and burrs cut seals during assembly and can break off into the oil as contamination. Thorough deburring and edge-breaking, followed by cleaning, are essential steps in hydraulic manufacturing.

Inspection

Machining is only as good as its verification. Typical inspection methods include:

  • calipers, micrometers and bore gauges for critical dimensions;
  • thread gauges for ports and gland threads;
  • surface roughness measurement on sealing surfaces;
  • first-article inspection for new parts and periodic checks during batches.

Inspection results should be recorded, especially for safety-critical and customer-specified dimensions.

CNC and reverse engineering

CNC machining makes reverse engineering practical. Once a worn part is measured and a drawing approved, CNC programs reproduce the component accurately — and the program can be reused for future orders, guaranteeing consistency.

Choosing a machining partner

Look for:

  • appropriate machine capacity for your part sizes;
  • understanding of hydraulic sealing requirements;
  • documented inspection processes;
  • the ability to combine machining with heat treatment, plating and assembly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do hydraulic parts need such tight tolerances?

Seals are designed for specific groove dimensions and clearances. A groove that is slightly too deep or wide lets the seal move and leak; one that is too shallow over-compresses it, increasing friction and wear. Clearances behind seals control extrusion at high pressure. Concentricity between pistons, rods and glands keeps seals evenly loaded. Small dimensional errors therefore have large effects on reliability.

Can CNC machining reproduce old or obsolete parts?

Yes. Once a worn part has been measured and an approved drawing produced, CNC machining can reproduce it accurately, and the program can be stored so future orders match exactly. This makes CNC machining central to reverse engineering and to keeping older machines running.

What surface finish do sealing surfaces need?

Seal manufacturers specify roughness ranges for dynamic and static sealing surfaces. Too rough a surface wears seals like sandpaper; too smooth may not hold an adequate oil film. Finishing processes such as grinding, honing, polishing or roller burnishing are used to achieve the specified finish, which should be shown on the drawing.

Why is deburring so important for hydraulic parts?

Burrs and sharp edges on ports, cross-drillings and grooves cut seals during assembly and can break off later as metal contamination inside the system. Thorough deburring, edge-breaking and cleaning after machining protect both the seals and every downstream component.

What inspection should machined parts receive?

At minimum, critical dimensions, threads and sealing surface finishes should be checked and recorded. First-article inspection confirms a new program is correct, and periodic checks during batch production ensure consistency. For customer-critical parts, request a dimensional inspection report.

posts.title: Honing Hydraulic Cylinder Tubes: Surface Finish and Tolerances
posts.metaTitle: Honing Hydraulic Cylinder Tubes: Finish & Tolerances
posts.metaDescription: Why hydraulic cylinder barrels are honed, how honing creates the right bore geometry and surface finish for seals, and when worn tubes can be re-honed.
posts.excerpt: The inside of a cylinder barrel is a precision sealing surface. Honing gives it the geometry and finish that seals need to perform and last.
posts.imageAlt: Welder fabricating steel components in a workshop
posts.html:
The bore of a hydraulic cylinder barrel is where the piston seals do their work. Its diameter, straightness, roundness and surface finish all affect how well the cylinder seals and how long the seals last. Honing is the finishing process that gives the bore these properties.

What is honing?

Honing uses abrasive stones mounted on a rotating, reciprocating tool. As the tool moves through the bore, the stones remove small amounts of material, correcting geometry and producing a controlled surface texture with a characteristic cross-hatch pattern.

Many cylinder tubes are supplied pre-finished — for example, skived and roller-burnished tubes — which achieve excellent finishes efficiently. Honing is used both in manufacturing and in repair to correct and refinish bores.

Why bore finish matters

Seal life

A bore that is too rough acts like an abrasive, wearing seals quickly. A bore that is too smooth may not hold an adequate lubricating film, causing friction, heat and stick-slip.

Leakage

Scratches and scoring along the bore create leak paths past the piston seal, causing drift and loss of force.

Wear rings and guidance

Accurate bore geometry keeps the piston centred and wear rings evenly loaded.

Geometry as well as finish

Honing corrects:

  • diameter to the specified tolerance;
  • roundness (ovality);
  • straightness and taper along the length.

These geometric properties matter as much as surface roughness. An out-of-round bore cannot be sealed properly, regardless of finish.

Typical bore defects in repair work

Defect Common cause
Longitudinal scoring Contaminated oil, failed wear rings
Localised pitting Water in oil, corrosion during storage
Bell-mouthing at ends Side loads, wear at stroke ends
Barrel bulging Overpressure, shock loads
Ovality Side loads, clamping damage, thin walls

Can a worn tube be re-honed?

Re-honing can restore a bore with light scoring or minor corrosion. Each hone removes material, increasing the bore diameter. The questions are:

  1. Will the bore remain within the tolerance required by the piston seal?
  2. Will the wall thickness remain sufficient for the working pressure?
  3. Can defects be fully removed without excessive enlargement?

If the bore would become oversize, options include fitting an oversize piston and seals (where appropriate and safe) or replacing the tube.

Bulged barrels should not be honed back into service. Bulging indicates the barrel has been overstressed and should be replaced.

Inspection after honing

  • Bore diameter measured at several points along the length and around the circumference.
  • Surface roughness measurement.
  • Visual inspection under good lighting for remaining defects.
  • Cleaning to remove all abrasive residue before assembly — honing grit left in a cylinder is severe contamination.

Preventing bore damage

  • Keep oil clean with effective filtration.
  • Maintain wear rings so pistons do not contact the bore.
  • Remove water from oil and store cylinders properly.
  • Avoid side loads through good alignment and mounting design.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the purpose of the cross-hatch pattern?

The fine cross-hatch left by honing stones creates a controlled surface texture that holds a thin film of oil. That film lubricates the piston seals and wear rings, reducing friction and wear while still allowing the seals to seal effectively. The angle and depth of the pattern are controlled by the honing process.

How much material does re-honing remove?

Only as much as needed to remove defects and restore geometry, but every hone enlarges the bore slightly. Before honing, the repairer measures the bore and wall thickness to confirm it will remain within the seal manufacturer's tolerance and the pressure rating. If defects are too deep, the tube must be replaced or an oversize solution engineered.

Can a bulged cylinder barrel be repaired?

No. A bulged barrel has been permanently deformed by overpressure or shock and the material has been overstressed. Honing would remove the visible bulge but not the damage, so bulged barrels should always be replaced and the cause of the overpressure investigated.

Why must honing residue be removed completely?

Honing produces fine abrasive and metal particles. If any remain in the barrel, they act as grinding paste on new seals and spread through the hydraulic system. Thorough washing, flushing and inspection after honing are essential parts of a quality cylinder repair.

What is the difference between honing and skiving and roller burnishing?

Skiving and roller burnishing cut the bore to size and then roll it smooth, producing an excellent finish quickly — a common method for new cylinder tubes. Honing uses abrasive stones to correct geometry and create a controlled finish, and is particularly useful for repairs and for correcting ovality or taper.

posts.title: Induction Hardening Explained for Heavy Engineering Parts
posts.metaTitle: Induction Hardening Explained for Heavy Engineering Parts
posts.metaDescription: How induction hardening creates a hard, wear-resistant surface on shafts, rods, pins and crane wheels while keeping a tough core — and what buyers should specify.
posts.excerpt: Induction hardening gives components a hard, wear-resistant surface and a tough core. Here is how it works and why it is used on rods, pins and wheels.
posts.imageAlt: Sparks from metalworking in an engineering workshop
posts.html:
Many heavy engineering components need two conflicting properties: a surface hard enough to resist wear and a core tough enough to absorb shocks without cracking. Induction hardening delivers both. It is widely used on piston rods, pins, shafts, gears and crane wheels.

How induction hardening works

  1. Heating: an alternating current passes through a copper coil (inductor) around or near the part. This induces electrical currents in the surface of the steel, heating it rapidly above its transformation temperature.
  2. Quenching: the heated surface is immediately cooled, usually with a water-based quenchant, forming a hard martensitic layer.
  3. Tempering: the part is often tempered at a lower temperature to relieve stresses and adjust hardness and toughness.

Because heating is concentrated at the surface, the core remains relatively unaffected and keeps its toughness.

Key benefits

  • High surface hardness for wear resistance.
  • Tough core for impact and fatigue resistance.
  • Improved fatigue strength due to beneficial compressive stresses in the surface layer.
  • Selective hardening: only the areas that need it are hardened.
  • Speed and repeatability for production work.
  • Less distortion than through-hardening large parts.

Typical applications

Component Why induction hardening is used
Piston rods Hard base under chrome resists dents and wear
Pins and bushes Wear resistance at bearing surfaces
Shafts Wear resistance at bearing and seal seats, fatigue strength
Gears Hard, wear-resistant teeth with tough cores
Crane wheels Hard treads and flanges with tough wheel bodies

What to specify

When ordering induction-hardened components, specify:

  • Surface hardness range.
  • Effective case depth: the depth at which hardness drops to a specified value. Case depth must suit the loads and allow for wear and any finish grinding.
  • Hardened zones: which areas must be hardened and which must remain soft (for example, threads or areas to be welded).
  • Material grade: the steel must contain sufficient carbon and alloying elements to respond to induction hardening.

Material selection matters

Induction hardening works best on medium-carbon and suitable alloy steels. Low-carbon steels do not harden significantly. The material must also be clean and free of defects to avoid cracking during quenching.

Quality control

  • Hardness testing on the surface and, where required, on sections or test pieces to confirm case depth.
  • Crack detection using magnetic particle inspection for critical parts.
  • Dimensional checks after heat treatment and finishing.

Common problems and causes

Problem Possible cause
Low surface hardness Wrong material, insufficient heating, poor quench
Cracking Excessive hardness, sharp corners, material defects
Insufficient case depth Process parameters, coil design
Distortion Uneven heating or quenching

Good design helps: generous radii instead of sharp corners, uniform sections and avoiding holes near hardened zones reduce cracking risk.

Induction hardening in repair and reverse engineering

When reverse-engineering worn parts, hardness testing often shows that the original part was surface-hardened. Specifying the correct hardening in the replacement is essential for achieving the original — or better — service life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which steels can be induction hardened?

Medium-carbon steels and suitable alloy steels respond well because they contain enough carbon to form a hard structure when quenched. Low-carbon structural steels do not harden significantly. Material selection and heat treatment should therefore be specified together, and the drawing should state the required hardness and case depth.

Does induction hardening cause distortion?

It can cause some distortion, although usually less than through-hardening a large part because only the surface is heated. Long shafts and thin sections are most affected. Manufacturers often leave a small allowance for straightening or finish grinding after hardening to achieve final dimensions.

How is hardened case depth checked?

Case depth is usually verified by hardness testing across a sectioned sample or test piece made with the same process parameters. Surface hardness can be checked on every part with portable testers. Drawings should define how case depth is measured so results are consistent.

Can induction-hardened areas be welded?

Welding on or near hardened zones can create brittle structures and cracks. If a part must be welded — for example, a rod end — the drawing should specify which areas remain soft. Welding procedures for hardened parts must be carefully controlled and are best avoided where possible.

Why is tempering done after hardening?

Freshly quenched steel is very hard but can be brittle and highly stressed. Tempering at a lower temperature relieves some of these stresses and improves toughness, reducing the risk of cracking in service while retaining most of the hardness.

posts.title: Welding Quality in Heavy Fabrication: What Buyers Should Ask
posts.metaTitle: Welding Quality in Heavy Fabrication: Questions to Ask
posts.metaDescription: What determines weld quality in heavy fabrication, common weld defects, inspection methods and the questions buyers should ask fabricators.
posts.excerpt: Welds carry the loads in cylinders, brackets and crane structures. Knowing how weld quality is controlled helps you choose fabricators you can trust.
posts.imageAlt: Welder working on a heavy steel fabrication
posts.html:
Welded joints hold together cylinder end caps, mounting brackets, crane girders and countless other load-bearing components. A poor weld may look acceptable on the surface yet contain defects that lead to cracks and failures under load. For buyers of fabricated components, understanding how weld quality is controlled is essential.

What determines weld quality?

Qualified procedures

A welding procedure specification (WPS) defines how a weld is made: process, materials, preheat, filler metal, parameters and technique. Procedures are typically qualified by testing sample welds to prove they meet required properties, following recognised welding standards.

Qualified welders

Welders demonstrate their competence by passing tests for the specific processes, positions and materials they weld.

Correct materials and filler

Filler metals must match the base material and service requirements. Using the wrong consumable can produce brittle or weak welds.

Preheat and heat control

Thicker sections and higher-strength steels may need preheating to avoid cracking. Controlling heat input also limits distortion and protects material properties.

Joint preparation and fit-up

Clean, correctly prepared joints with proper fit-up are the foundation of sound welds.

Post-weld treatment

Some components need stress relieving after welding to reduce residual stresses and improve dimensional stability and fatigue performance.

Common weld defects

Defect Description Risk
Porosity Gas pores in the weld Reduced strength, leak paths
Lack of fusion Weld not fused with base metal Serious weakness
Incomplete penetration Weld not through the joint thickness Crack initiation, reduced strength
Cracks Hot or cold cracking Unacceptable; can propagate to failure
Undercut Groove melted into base metal at weld toe Stress concentration, fatigue
Slag inclusions Trapped slag Weakness, crack initiation
Excessive distortion Warping from heat Misalignment, fit problems

Inspection methods

  • Visual inspection: the first and most important check, by trained inspectors.
  • Dye penetrant testing: reveals surface cracks.
  • Magnetic particle inspection: detects surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steels.
  • Ultrasonic testing: finds internal defects in thicker sections.
  • Radiographic testing: imaging of internal weld quality in suitable joints.
  • Pressure testing: for pressure-containing welds such as cylinder end caps and manifold blocks.

The extent of testing should reflect the criticality of the component and any applicable standards.

Welding in hydraulic components

Hydraulic cylinders contain highly stressed welds, such as the joint between the barrel and end cap and the attachment of ports and mountings. These welds experience pressure cycles and fatigue. Correct joint design, full penetration where required, controlled procedures and pressure testing are essential.

Questions buyers should ask

  1. Are your welding procedures qualified, and to which standards?
  2. Are your welders qualified for this process and material?
  3. How do you control preheat and heat input?
  4. What inspection and NDT will be performed, and will I receive reports?
  5. Will the component be pressure tested (for hydraulic parts)?
  6. Is stress relieving required, and will it be carried out?
  7. How do you ensure traceability of materials?

Red flags

  • No documented procedures or welder qualifications.
  • Reluctance to provide inspection records.
  • Welding on load-bearing parts such as hooks or forged components that should not be welded.
  • Cosmetic grinding that hides weld defects.

Repairs by welding

Welding repairs to load-bearing crane parts and pressure components must be assessed carefully. Some components — such as forged hooks — should never be weld-repaired. Others may be repairable with approved procedures and inspection.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a welding procedure specification (WPS)?

A WPS documents exactly how a weld should be made: process, base and filler materials, joint preparation, preheat, welding parameters and technique. Procedures are qualified by welding and testing samples, proving that welds made this way achieve the required strength and toughness. Welders follow the WPS so results are consistent.

Why is preheating sometimes required?

Thick sections and higher-strength steels cool quickly after welding, which can trap hydrogen and form hard, brittle structures that crack. Preheating slows cooling and reduces this risk. The required preheat depends on material, thickness and welding process, and is specified in the welding procedure.

Which NDT methods are used on welds?

Visual inspection is always the first step. Dye penetrant and magnetic particle testing find surface and near-surface cracks, while ultrasonic and radiographic testing detect internal defects such as lack of fusion and inclusions. The methods and extent of testing should match the criticality of the component and any applicable standard.

Can all weld defects be found visually?

No. Visual inspection finds surface problems such as undercut, surface porosity and obvious cracks, but internal defects require volumetric methods like ultrasonic or radiographic testing. For critical load-bearing or pressure-containing welds, specify appropriate NDT.

Should I ask suppliers for welding records?

For critical fabrications — lifting equipment, pressure components, structural parts — yes. Welding procedures, welder qualifications and NDT reports demonstrate that welding was controlled and provide traceability if questions arise later.
