posts.title: Pressure Testing Hydraulic Components: Methods and Records
posts.metaTitle: Pressure Testing Hydraulic Components: Methods & Records
posts.metaDescription: Why hydraulic cylinders, manifolds and power units are pressure tested, common test methods, safety precautions and what a good test record contains.
posts.excerpt: Pressure testing proves a hydraulic component holds pressure without leaks before it reaches your machine. Here is how it is done and what records to expect.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer reviewing test data on a computer
posts.html:
Pressure testing is the final proof that a hydraulic component is fit for service. It verifies that the component holds pressure, does not leak and functions correctly before it is installed. For cylinders, manifolds and power units — new or repaired — a documented pressure test is a key quality checkpoint.

Why pressure testing matters

  • Detects leaks from seals, welds, threads and porosity.
  • Confirms structural integrity of welds and pressure-containing parts.
  • Verifies function, such as full stroke, smooth movement and cushioning.
  • Provides documented evidence of quality for customers and audits.

Common test types

Proof pressure test

The component is pressurised above its normal working pressure for a defined time, according to the design standard or specification, to confirm it can withstand pressure without permanent deformation or leakage. Test pressures should be defined by the design specification and must never exceed what the component is designed to withstand.

Internal leakage test

For cylinders, pressure is applied to one side of the piston while the other port is monitored for leakage. This confirms the piston seal is sealing properly.

External leakage test

Visual inspection of rod seals, static seals, welds and fittings while under pressure.

Function test

The cylinder or unit is cycled through its full stroke to confirm smooth operation, correct stroke length and cushioning performance. Power units are tested for flow, pressure settings, valve operation and temperature.

Low-pressure test

Some seal designs can leak at low pressure even if they seal well at high pressure. A low-pressure test checks for this.

Safety during pressure testing

Pressure testing involves stored energy and must be carried out with strict safety precautions:

  • use dedicated test benches with suitable guards and enclosures;
  • bleed air from the component before pressurising — compressed air stores far more energy than oil;
  • use calibrated gauges and pressure relief protection on the test rig;
  • never stand in line with fittings, plugs or end caps under pressure;
  • never tighten fittings while under pressure;
  • release pressure fully before disconnecting.

What a good test record contains

Item Example
Component identification Part number, serial number, drawing revision
Test date and technician Date, name or ID
Test pressure and duration Specified values
Test medium and temperature Hydraulic oil type, temperature
Results Internal leakage, external leakage, function
Gauge identification Calibrated gauge reference
Pass/fail and signature Inspector sign-off

Records should be kept and supplied with the component when requested.

Testing after repair

A repaired cylinder should be tested just like a new one. Testing after repair confirms that seals are correctly installed, that honing and rod repairs are effective and that no damage occurred during assembly.

Power unit testing

Power packs are typically flushed to remove contamination, then tested for:

  • pump flow and pressure;
  • relief and pressure valve settings;
  • directional valve operation;
  • leak-free connections;
  • temperature rise during a run test;
  • electrical functions and safety devices.

Ask for the test report

When buying hydraulic components, ask whether testing is standard and request test records. A supplier that tests and documents every unit gives you confidence and traceability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What pressure should a component be tested at?

The test pressure must come from the design specification or applicable standard for that component, and must never exceed what the component and test equipment are designed to withstand. Proof tests are typically above normal working pressure, while function tests may be performed at working pressure. Ask your supplier what pressure they use and why.

Why is trapped air dangerous during pressure tests?

Air is compressible and stores far more energy than oil at the same pressure. If a component fails while air is trapped inside, that energy is released violently, potentially ejecting parts or fittings. Bleeding air completely before pressurising and testing behind guards are basic safety requirements.

What does an internal leakage test show?

By pressurising one side of a cylinder piston and monitoring the opposite port, the test shows whether oil is passing the piston seal. Excessive leakage indicates a damaged or incorrectly installed seal, a scored barrel or other internal faults that would cause drift or loss of force in service.

Do repaired components need pressure testing?

Yes. A repair involves dismantling, machining and reassembly, any of which can introduce problems. Testing after repair confirms seals are correctly installed, surfaces are sealing and the component functions properly before it is fitted to a machine.

What should a pressure test record include?

Component identification, drawing revision, test pressure and duration, test medium and temperature, internal and external leakage results, function check results, gauge identification and calibration reference, the technician's name and date, and a clear pass/fail statement.

Every hydraulic cylinder and power pack we manufacture or repair is pressure and function tested with documented results. Learn more about our quality process.

posts.title: Understanding Engineering Drawings: Tolerances and Fits for Buyers
posts.metaTitle: Engineering Drawings, Tolerances & Fits — A Buyer's Guide
posts.metaDescription: A practical guide for maintenance and purchasing teams to engineering drawings: dimensions, tolerances, fits, surface finish symbols and notes.
posts.excerpt: You do not need to be a design engineer to understand a drawing. Knowing the basics of tolerances, fits and finishes helps you order the right part first time.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer reviewing technical component drawings
posts.html:
Engineering drawings are the language of manufacturing. They tell the manufacturer exactly what to make, to what accuracy and from what material. Buyers and maintenance teams who understand the basics can spot missing information, ask better questions and avoid costly mistakes.

The main parts of a drawing

Title block

Contains the part name, drawing number, revision, material, scale, units, general tolerances and approval information. Always check that you are using the latest revision.

Views

Orthographic views show the part from different directions. Section views cut through the part to show internal features such as bores and grooves.

Dimensions

Dimensions define sizes and positions. Critical dimensions usually carry specific tolerances.

Notes

Notes specify requirements that are not shown graphically: heat treatment, surface treatment, deburring, inspection or testing requirements.

Understanding tolerances

No part can be made to an exact size. A tolerance defines the acceptable range.

  • Bilateral tolerance: 50.00 ±0.05 means 49.95 to 50.05.
  • Unilateral tolerance: 50.00 +0.05/-0.00 means 50.00 to 50.05.
  • Limit dimensions: 49.95–50.05 states the range directly.
  • General tolerances: apply to dimensions without specific tolerances, usually defined in the title block by reference to a standard.

Tighter tolerances increase manufacturing cost. Good drawings apply tight tolerances only where function requires them.

Fits between mating parts

Fits describe how two parts go together, such as a shaft in a hole.

Fit type Description Example use
Clearance fit Always a gap Pins that must rotate, sliding parts
Transition fit May have small gap or interference Locating parts, gears on shafts
Interference fit Always overlap; parts pressed or shrunk together Bearings on shafts, bushes in housings

Fits are often specified using the ISO system of limits and fits (for example, H7 for a hole and g6 or k6 for a shaft). The letter indicates the position of the tolerance zone and the number its size.

Geometric tolerances

Some drawings include geometric tolerancing — symbols in boxes specifying requirements such as:

  • straightness and flatness;
  • roundness and cylindricity;
  • concentricity or runout relative to a datum;
  • perpendicularity and parallelism;
  • position of holes and features.

For hydraulic and rotating parts, runout and concentricity are often critical.

Surface finish

Surface finish symbols specify roughness, typically as an Ra value. Sealing surfaces, bearing seats and sliding surfaces have specific finish requirements. A missing finish callout on a seal groove or rod surface can lead to early seal failure.

Common drawing problems when ordering spares

  • Outdated revision.
  • Missing material or heat treatment information.
  • Dimensions taken from worn parts without correction.
  • No tolerances on critical features.
  • Missing thread specifications.
  • Unclear surface finish or coating requirements.

Before you send a drawing for quotation

  1. Check the revision is current.
  2. Confirm material and heat treatment are specified.
  3. Identify critical dimensions and fits.
  4. Add quantity and required documentation (inspection report, material certificate).
  5. Include mating part information if the drawing is incomplete.

If you do not have drawings, a manufacturer can create them by reverse engineering, with your approval before production.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a general tolerance?

A general tolerance applies to every dimension on the drawing that does not carry its own tolerance. It is usually stated in the title block, often by reference to a standard tolerance class. This avoids cluttering the drawing while still defining acceptable variation for non-critical features.

What does a fit like H7/g6 mean?

It is a notation from the ISO system of limits and fits. The capital letter and number describe the hole's tolerance zone and the lowercase letter and number describe the shaft's. H7/g6, for example, gives a close clearance fit commonly used for precise sliding or rotating parts. Other combinations produce transition or interference fits.

Why is the drawing revision so important?

Designs change over time to fix problems or improve parts. Manufacturing from an outdated revision can produce parts that do not fit, use the wrong material or repeat a known failure. Always check and state the current revision when ordering.

What is geometric tolerancing?

Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing controls the form, orientation and location of features — for example straightness, roundness, perpendicularity, runout and position. These controls are essential for rotating and sealing parts where size alone does not guarantee function.

What if I do not have a drawing for a part?

A manufacturer can reverse-engineer the part from a sample, produce a drawing for your approval and then manufacture it. Keep the approved drawing on file so future orders are fast and you are not dependent on a single source.

posts.title: Material Selection for Heavy-Duty Components: A Practical Overview
posts.metaTitle: Material Selection for Heavy-Duty Industrial Components
posts.metaDescription: A practical overview of steels and other materials used for shafts, pins, rods, wheels, bushes and fabrications, and how to choose the right one.
posts.excerpt: Choosing the right material is the foundation of a long-lasting component. Here is a practical overview of materials used in heavy engineering parts.
posts.imageAlt: Steel components being machined in a workshop
posts.html:
A component's material decides how strong it is, how well it resists wear and corrosion, and how it responds to machining, welding and heat treatment. Choosing well avoids premature failures; choosing poorly can make even a perfectly machined part fail early.

Start with the demands

Before choosing a material, define what the component must withstand:

  • Loads: static, cyclic (fatigue) and impact.
  • Wear: sliding, rolling or abrasive contact.
  • Environment: corrosion, temperature, chemicals.
  • Manufacturing: machining, welding and heat treatment requirements.
  • Cost and availability.

Common material families

Low-carbon structural steels

Easy to weld and fabricate; used for frames, brackets, base plates and general structures. They have moderate strength and are not significantly hardenable by heat treatment.

Medium-carbon steels

Higher strength and hardenability. Widely used for shafts, pins, axles and piston rods, often with induction hardening or quench-and-temper treatment.

Alloy steels

Contain alloying elements such as chromium, molybdenum and nickel. They offer higher strength, toughness and hardenability for highly stressed parts like heavily loaded shafts, gears and crane wheels.

Stainless steels

Used where corrosion resistance is essential, such as marine and chemical environments. Grades vary widely in strength, corrosion resistance and machinability.

Cast irons and cast steels

Used for housings, large wheels and complex shapes. Cast iron offers good machinability and vibration damping; cast steel offers higher toughness.

Bronzes and bearing materials

Used for bushes, bearings and wear components that slide against steel, offering good wear resistance and compatibility with lubricants.

Engineering plastics

Used for wear rings, guide strips and some bushes, offering low friction and corrosion resistance.

Matching materials to components

Component Typical material approach
Fabricated frames and brackets Weldable structural steel
Piston rods Medium-carbon or alloy steel, induction hardened and chrome plated
Pins and axles Medium-carbon or alloy steel, hardened as required
Crane wheels Forged or cast steel with hardened treads
Cylinder barrels Seamless or cold-drawn tubes suited to honing
Bushes Bronze, hardened steel or engineering plastics
Gears Alloy steels, through or surface hardened
Marine components Stainless steels or coated carbon steels

Heat treatment changes everything

The same steel can behave very differently depending on heat treatment. Normalising refines grain structure; quenching and tempering increases strength and toughness; induction hardening produces hard surfaces with tough cores. Always specify heat treatment together with the material.

Weldability

Higher carbon and alloy content generally makes steel harder to weld without cracking. Parts that must be welded may need lower-carbon grades or carefully controlled welding procedures, including preheat.

Corrosion resistance

Options for corrosive environments include stainless steels, protective coatings, plating and paint systems. The choice depends on the severity of the environment, the required strength and the cost.

Material certificates and traceability

For critical components, request material test certificates from the steel supplier. These document chemical composition and mechanical properties and support traceability.

When reverse-engineering parts

Determine the original material through hardness testing and, where necessary, material analysis. Consider upgrading if the original part failed by wear or fatigue — a better material or heat treatment can significantly extend life.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a material test certificate?

It is a document issued by the steel mill or supplier recording the chemical composition and mechanical properties of a specific batch of material. It provides traceability and evidence that the material meets the specified grade — important for load-bearing and safety-critical parts.

Is stainless steel always the best choice for durability?

Not necessarily. Stainless steels resist corrosion, but many grades have lower strength or wear resistance than heat-treated alloy steels and can be more expensive and harder to machine. They are the right choice where corrosion is the dominant problem; elsewhere, alloy steels with suitable coatings may perform better.

Why does heat treatment matter as much as the steel grade?

The same steel can be soft and tough, or hard and wear-resistant, depending on how it is heat-treated. A part made from the correct steel but with the wrong heat treatment can wear quickly or crack. Always specify heat treatment and target hardness together with the material.

What materials are used for bushes and bearings?

Bronze is common for sliding bushes because it works well against steel with lubrication. Hardened steel bushes suit high loads and abrasive conditions, while engineering plastics offer low friction and corrosion resistance. The choice depends on load, speed, lubrication and environment.

Can I upgrade materials when ordering replacements?

Yes, and it is often worthwhile when the original part wore or failed early. However, changes to load-bearing components should be reviewed by a qualified engineer to make sure the new material and heat treatment are suitable for the loads and do not create new problems.

posts.title: Surface Treatments for Corrosion Protection in Industrial Equipment
posts.metaTitle: Surface Treatments for Corrosion Protection
posts.metaDescription: Compare painting, galvanising, plating, chemical blackening and specialist coatings for protecting industrial components from corrosion and wear.
posts.excerpt: Corrosion quietly shortens the life of industrial equipment. The right surface treatment can extend component life dramatically in harsh environments.
posts.imageAlt: Industrial plant building with large process ducts
posts.html:
Corrosion costs industry enormous amounts every year in replacement parts, downtime and safety risks. Ports, mines, chemical plants and outdoor installations are particularly harsh environments. Selecting the right surface treatment for each component is one of the most effective ways to extend equipment life.

How corrosion attacks components

  • General corrosion: uniform rusting of exposed steel surfaces.
  • Pitting: localised attack creating deep pits, especially damaging on piston rods and sealing surfaces.
  • Crevice corrosion: in gaps between parts where moisture is trapped.
  • Galvanic corrosion: when dissimilar metals are in contact in the presence of moisture.
  • Corrosion fatigue: cracking accelerated by the combination of cyclic stress and corrosion.

Common surface treatments

Paint systems

Multi-layer paint systems with suitable primers, intermediate coats and topcoats protect structures and fabricated parts. Surface preparation, such as abrasive blasting, is critical for adhesion and durability.

Hot-dip galvanising

Steel is coated with zinc by immersion in molten zinc. Galvanising provides robust protection for structural steel, walkways and brackets, and the zinc protects the steel sacrificially even where scratched.

Zinc and zinc-alloy plating

Electroplated zinc provides corrosion protection for fasteners and small parts, often with additional passivation layers.

Hard chrome plating

Provides a hard, wear-resistant and corrosion-resistant surface for piston rods and wear surfaces. In very aggressive environments, standard chrome may need to be supplemented by other solutions.

Electroless nickel

Deposits a uniform nickel layer, even on complex shapes and internal surfaces. Offers good corrosion and wear resistance.

Chemical blackening and phosphating

Provide mild corrosion resistance and a base for oils or paints. Common on machined parts and fasteners.

Thermal spray and cladding

Thermal spray coatings and weld or laser cladding apply corrosion- and wear-resistant materials to surfaces, used for rods, shafts and wear areas in severe service.

Choosing a treatment

Component Typical treatment options
Structural frames Blasting and multi-coat paint, or galvanising
Fasteners Zinc plating, galvanising, stainless steel
Piston rods Hard chrome; upgraded coatings for marine/chemical environments
Machined parts (internal) Oiling, phosphating, blackening
Wear surfaces in corrosive environments Electroless nickel, thermal spray, cladding

Design for corrosion resistance

Good design reduces corrosion risk:

  • avoid water traps and crevices;
  • provide drainage holes in structures;
  • avoid contact between dissimilar metals or isolate them;
  • allow access for inspection and maintenance;
  • specify sealing of joints exposed to weather.

Maintenance matters

Coatings need maintenance. Inspect paintwork for damage and touch up promptly. Clean salt and chemical deposits from equipment regularly. Protect exposed rods and machined surfaces during storage.

Coatings and hydraulic seals

For hydraulic rods, any coating must be compatible with the seals and achieve the required surface finish. Not all corrosion-resistant coatings are suitable for dynamic sealing surfaces, so coating choice should be discussed with the cylinder manufacturer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is hot-dip galvanising better than painting?

Galvanising provides a thick, tough zinc coating that protects steel sacrificially even when scratched, making it excellent for structures, walkways and brackets outdoors. Paint systems offer colour choice and can be applied to assembled equipment and maintained on site. The best choice depends on the environment, component size, design and maintenance plans — and some structures use both (duplex systems).

Do chrome-plated hydraulic rods corrode?

They can. Chrome plating contains microscopic cracks, and in salty, humid or chemical environments moisture can reach the steel beneath, causing pitting, especially on rods left extended. For harsh environments, consider upgraded coatings or stainless rods and protect rods during storage.

What is galvanic corrosion and how is it prevented?

Galvanic corrosion occurs when two different metals are in electrical contact in the presence of moisture; the less noble metal corrodes faster. It is prevented by choosing compatible materials, isolating dissimilar metals with non-conductive washers or sleeves, and protecting joints from moisture.

How often should protective coatings be inspected?

Inspect coatings during routine equipment inspections and more often in severe environments such as ports and chemical plants. Repair chips, scratches and failed areas promptly, because corrosion spreads under damaged coatings and becomes much more expensive to fix later.

Do coatings affect hydraulic seals?

Coatings on dynamic sealing surfaces — such as piston rods — must be compatible with seal materials and achieve the correct surface finish. Not every corrosion-resistant coating is suitable for a sliding seal surface, so coating changes should be agreed with the cylinder manufacturer.

posts.title: From Prototype to Production: The Custom Component Manufacturing Process
posts.metaTitle: Custom Component Manufacturing: Prototype to Production
posts.metaDescription: How custom industrial components move from enquiry and design review through prototyping, testing and production — and how buyers can speed up the process.
posts.excerpt: Custom components follow a predictable path from enquiry to production. Understanding each step helps you plan, avoid delays and get the part you actually need.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer drafting a custom component design
posts.html:
Not every part can be bought from a catalogue. Special machines, obsolete equipment and demanding applications often need custom components — a cylinder with an unusual mounting, a manifold for a specific circuit, or a replacement part with no available drawing. Understanding how custom manufacturing works helps you plan projects and avoid surprises.

Step 1: Enquiry and requirements

Everything starts with clear requirements. A good enquiry includes:

  • drawings, sketches, samples or photos;
  • the function of the component and how it is used;
  • loads, pressures, speeds and duty cycle;
  • environment and any special conditions;
  • quantities, now and in future;
  • required documentation and testing;
  • target delivery date.

The more information provided, the faster and more accurate the quotation.

Step 2: Engineering review

Engineers review the requirements and identify:

  • missing information;
  • manufacturability issues;
  • opportunities to simplify or improve the design;
  • standard components that can reduce cost and lead time;
  • risks, such as tight tolerances or unusual materials.

This is often where the most value is added. Small design changes can cut cost or improve reliability significantly.

Step 3: Design and drawings

For new designs or reverse-engineered parts, drawings are prepared with dimensions, tolerances, materials, heat treatment and finishes. For complete hydraulic systems, a circuit diagram and component list are prepared.

Step 4: Customer approval

The customer reviews and approves the drawings or design before manufacturing begins. This step prevents costly misunderstandings.

Step 5: Prototype or first article

For new designs, a prototype or first article is manufactured and fully inspected. It may be tested on a rig or fitted to the machine for trial. Feedback leads to adjustments before production.

Step 6: Testing and validation

Depending on the component, testing may include pressure tests, function tests, load tests, hardness checks and dimensional inspection. Results are documented.

Step 7: Production

Once the design is validated, components are produced in the required quantities, with in-process and final inspection. CNC programs, fixtures and inspection plans developed during prototyping make repeat production consistent.

Step 8: Documentation and delivery

Deliveries include inspection reports, test records, material certificates and drawings as agreed.

Typical timeline factors

Factor Impact on lead time
Complete, clear information at enquiry Shortens quotation and design time
Approval turnaround Delays waiting for approval add directly to lead time
Special materials or bought-in components May add procurement time
Heat treatment, plating and coatings Add processing time
Testing requirements Add time but reduce risk

How buyers can speed things up

  1. Provide complete information and samples early.
  2. Nominate a technical contact who can answer questions quickly.
  3. Approve drawings promptly.
  4. Agree documentation requirements at the start.
  5. Order spares at the same time as the first units.

Why it is worth it

Custom components fit the application exactly, solve problems standard parts cannot and can outperform originals when improvements are built in. With approved drawings on file, future orders become fast and simple.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I speed up a custom manufacturing project?

Provide complete information at the start — drawings or samples, operating conditions, quantities and documentation requirements — nominate a technical contact who can answer questions quickly, approve drawings promptly and agree to order long-lead materials or bought-in components early. These steps often save more time than any change in the workshop.

Why do suppliers ask for drawing approval?

Approval confirms that the design matches your requirements before money and time are spent on manufacturing. It catches misunderstandings about dimensions, mountings, materials or interfaces, which are far cheaper to correct on paper than on finished parts.

Is a prototype always required?

No. Exact replacements made to an existing approved drawing usually go straight into production. New designs, significant modifications and critical components benefit from a prototype or first article that can be inspected, tested and trialled before full production.

What documentation should come with custom components?

Typically an approved drawing, dimensional inspection report and, depending on the component, test records, hardness results and material certificates. For complete hydraulic systems, circuit diagrams, parts lists and operating instructions should also be supplied. Agree requirements at the order stage.

Are repeat orders faster?

Yes. With an approved drawing, proven CNC programs, fixtures and an inspection plan already in place, repeat orders skip engineering and approval and benefit from experience gained on the first batch.

posts.title: Hydraulics in Construction Equipment: Applications and Challenges
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulics in Construction Equipment: Key Challenges
posts.metaDescription: Where hydraulics power construction equipment, the challenges of dust, shock loads and weather, and how to keep cylinders and systems reliable on site.
posts.excerpt: Construction sites are tough on hydraulics: dust, mud, shock loads and weather. Here is how hydraulic systems are used on site and how to keep them reliable.
posts.imageAlt: Construction workers on a building site with steel reinforcement
posts.html:
From excavators and loaders to tower cranes and concrete pumps, construction equipment relies on hydraulics for power and control. Hydraulic systems deliver large forces in compact packages, which makes them ideal for mobile machines. But construction sites are among the harshest environments for hydraulic components.

Where hydraulics are used on construction sites

  • Excavators: boom, arm and bucket cylinders; swing and travel motors.
  • Wheel loaders and backhoes: lift, tilt and steering cylinders.
  • Mobile and crawler cranes: boom luffing, telescoping, outriggers, winches and slewing.
  • Tower cranes: climbing systems and some slewing and hoist drives.
  • Concrete pumps: pumping cylinders and boom cylinders.
  • Piling rigs and drilling equipment: rotary drives, pull-down and mast cylinders.
  • Dump trucks and tippers: telescopic tipping cylinders.
  • Aerial work platforms: lifting and steering functions.

The challenges

Contamination

Dust, mud, cement and grit attack rod seals and enter systems during maintenance. Contamination is the leading cause of hydraulic failure on construction equipment.

Shock loads

Digging, breaking and lifting create sudden pressure spikes and impacts that stress cylinders, pins and structures.

Weather and temperature

Equipment works in heat, cold, rain and dust. Cold starts thicken oil; hot days push systems towards overheating.

Rod damage

Exposed cylinder rods are struck by rocks, debris and tools, damaging chrome and seals.

Operator practices

Running cylinders hard against end stops, overloading and rough operation accelerate wear.

Time pressure

Projects run on tight schedules, so breakdowns are costly and maintenance windows short.

Keeping hydraulics reliable on site

Area Good practice
Daily checks Look for leaks, damaged hoses, rod damage and oil level
Cleanliness Clean around fittings before opening; cap hoses; filter new oil
Rod protection Use guards on vulnerable cylinders; retract rods when parked
Filters Change on schedule and inspect indicators
Pins and bushes Grease regularly; replace worn pins before they cause misalignment
Temperature Keep coolers clean; warm up machines in cold weather
Operator training Avoid shock loading and bottoming out cylinders

Cylinder repair on construction equipment

Construction machines often have custom cylinders with long lead times from original manufacturers. Local cylinder repair and manufacturing can return machines to work faster: rods re-chromed or replaced, barrels honed, seals upgraded and cylinders pressure-tested. When cylinders fail repeatedly, upgrades such as larger rods, improved seals or better rod coatings can help.

Planning for uptime

  • Keep spare seal kits for critical cylinders.
  • Maintain a stock of high-wear hoses.
  • Identify cylinders with long lead times and consider spares.
  • Use oil analysis on high-value machines to catch wear early.

Lifting equipment on site

Cranes and lifting equipment are subject to strict inspection and certification requirements in most regions. Hydraulic components on lifting equipment — luffing and telescoping cylinders, load-holding valves and winches — are safety-critical and must be maintained and repaired by competent people to the manufacturer's specifications.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do hydraulic cylinders fail more often on construction sites?

Construction sites combine almost every condition that damages hydraulics: abrasive dust and cement, mud and water, impacts from rocks and debris, shock loads from digging and breaking, and maintenance that often happens outdoors under time pressure. Exposed cylinder rods are particularly vulnerable. Protecting rods, keeping wipers and filters in good condition, and cleaning fittings before opening the system make a noticeable difference to cylinder life.

How can I protect cylinder rods on site?

Retract rods whenever machines are parked, fit rod guards or bellows on cylinders exposed to falling debris, clean off cement and mud regularly, and protect rods when welding nearby. Inspect rods during daily walk-arounds and arrange repairs quickly when damage appears, because a nicked rod will quickly destroy the rod seal and let contamination into the system.

How often should hydraulic oil be changed on construction equipment?

Follow the machine manufacturer's recommended interval, and shorten it if equipment works in extremely dusty, hot or wet conditions. Oil analysis is the best way to decide: it shows contamination, water content and oil condition, so you change oil when it is actually needed rather than too early or too late. Always filter new oil when filling.

Can a local workshop repair cylinders from branded construction machines?

In most cases, yes. Experienced cylinder shops can dismantle, inspect, repair and test cylinders from all major equipment brands, often faster than waiting for original replacement units. They can also manufacture replacement parts such as rods, glands and pistons. For machines under warranty, check the manufacturer's warranty conditions first.

What should be included in a daily hydraulic check?

Look for leaks around cylinders, hoses and fittings; check hoses for abrasion, kinks and bulges; inspect rods for damage; check the oil level and filter indicators; and note any unusual noises, slow movement or drift. Report problems immediately — catching a damaged hose or rod early prevents bigger failures and safety risks.

posts.title: Hydraulic Components for Mining: Designing for Harsh Conditions
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Components for Mining: Built for Harsh Conditions
posts.metaDescription: How mining environments damage hydraulic cylinders and systems, and the design, material and maintenance choices that improve reliability in mines and quarries.
posts.excerpt: Abrasive dust, heavy shock loads and continuous operation make mining the ultimate test for hydraulics. Here is how components are designed and maintained to survive.
posts.imageAlt: Excavators and bulldozers working in an open-pit mine
posts.html:
Mining equipment works harder than almost any other machinery. Haul trucks, excavators, loaders, drills and crushers operate around the clock, in abrasive dust and mud, with heavy shock loads and limited time for maintenance. Hydraulic components must be designed, specified and maintained for these conditions.

Where hydraulics are used in mining

  • Excavators and shovels: boom, stick and bucket cylinders, swing drives.
  • Haul trucks: steering, hoist (tipping) and suspension systems.
  • Wheel loaders and dozers: lift, tilt, blade and ripper cylinders.
  • Drill rigs: feed, rotation and positioning functions.
  • Crushers and screens: adjustment and clearing cylinders, tramp release systems.
  • Underground equipment: roof supports, loaders and bolting rigs.

The challenges

Abrasive contamination

Fine rock dust is highly abrasive. It wears rod seals and, once inside the system, damages pumps, valves and cylinders.

Shock and overload

Digging into rock and handling heavy loads create pressure spikes and impact loads far above normal working conditions.

Continuous operation

High utilisation means wear accumulates quickly and downtime is expensive.

Corrosion

Water, acidic mine water and chemicals attack rods and structures.

Heat

High ambient temperatures and continuous operation challenge cooling systems.

Design features for mining duty

Feature Benefit
Heavy-wall barrels Resist bulging and damage from impacts
Larger rod diameters Resist buckling and bending
Upgraded rod coatings Better corrosion and wear resistance
Heavy-duty wipers and seal systems Keep abrasive dust out
Robust mountings and spherical bearings Accommodate misalignment and shock
Cushioning Reduce impact at end of stroke
Rod guards or bellows Protect exposed rods

Maintenance practices

  • Inspect rods daily for damage; damaged rods destroy seals quickly.
  • Keep breathers and filters in good condition and change elements on condition.
  • Use oil analysis to detect contamination and wear early.
  • Clean equipment before maintenance and keep hydraulic openings sealed.
  • Grease pins and bushes frequently; worn pins cause misalignment and side loading.
  • Track component life and replace cylinders proactively on critical machines.

Exchange cylinder programmes

Many mines use exchange programmes: a reconditioned spare cylinder is fitted immediately when one fails or reaches its planned life, and the removed unit is sent for overhaul. This minimises downtime and allows thorough repairs without time pressure.

Repair findings drive improvement

Each overhauled cylinder tells a story: scored barrels point to contamination, uneven bushing wear to side loads, bent rods to overload or buckling. Tracking these findings across a fleet helps identify improvements in design, maintenance or operation.

Safety in mining hydraulics

Mining equipment carries large stored energies in hydraulic systems and suspended loads. Isolation procedures, support of raised components and safe release of pressure — including accumulators — are critical whenever maintenance is performed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes mining hydraulics different from other industries?

Mining combines continuous high-utilisation operation, heavy shock loads, abrasive dust and corrosive water. Components accumulate wear far faster than in most industrial settings, and downtime is very expensive. As a result, mining cylinders often use heavier walls, larger rods, upgraded seals and coatings, and mines frequently plan replacements based on component life rather than waiting for failure.

What is a component exchange programme?

An exchange programme keeps reconditioned spare components — cylinders, pumps or motors — ready to fit. When a unit fails or reaches its planned life, the spare is installed immediately and the removed unit is sent for overhaul. This keeps machines working and allows thorough repairs without production pressure.

How can repair reports improve reliability?

Each overhaul report records what failed and why: scored barrels, bent rods, uneven bushing wear, contamination or seal damage. Tracking these findings across a fleet reveals patterns, such as recurring contamination or side loading. Addressing these root causes through better filtration, design upgrades or operating practices reduces future failures.

Are rod bellows effective in mining?

Rod bellows and guards can protect exposed rods from impacts and abrasive material in suitable applications. They must be durable, correctly sized and maintained, because a torn bellow can trap debris against the rod. In some applications, robust rod coatings and heavy-duty wipers are more practical.

What safety precautions apply to mining hydraulics?

Hydraulic systems on mining equipment store large energies in pressurised oil, accumulators and raised components such as buckets and truck bodies. Maintenance must follow strict isolation procedures: lower or mechanically support raised parts, relieve pressure, discharge accumulators and verify zero energy before work begins.

posts.title: Port Cranes and Container Handling: Keeping Equipment Running 24/7
posts.metaTitle: Port Crane Maintenance: Keeping Equipment Running 24/7
posts.metaDescription: The maintenance challenges of ship-to-shore cranes, RTGs and port handling equipment — continuous duty, corrosion and wind — and how to manage them.
posts.excerpt: Ports run around the clock, and every crane stoppage delays ships. Here is how port equipment is maintained for continuous operation in a corrosive environment.
posts.imageAlt: Aerial view of a container port with ship-to-shore cranes
posts.html:
Container terminals and bulk ports operate continuously. Ship-to-shore cranes, rubber-tyred and rail-mounted gantry cranes, reach stackers and straddle carriers move containers day and night. When a crane stops, vessel schedules slip, trucks queue and costs mount. Port equipment maintenance is about maximising availability in one of the harshest environments for machinery.

Equipment in a typical port

  • Ship-to-shore (STS) cranes: load and unload vessels.
  • Rail-mounted gantry (RMG) cranes: stack containers in yards.
  • Rubber-tyred gantry (RTG) cranes: flexible yard stacking.
  • Mobile harbour cranes: multi-purpose cargo handling.
  • Reach stackers and straddle carriers: container movement.
  • Bulk handling equipment: grab cranes, ship loaders and conveyors.

The challenges

Continuous duty

Port cranes often fall into high duty classes. Wheels, ropes, brakes and drives accumulate wear quickly.

Salt and corrosion

Salt-laden air corrodes structures, fasteners, electrical connections and exposed machined surfaces.

Wind

High winds can affect crane stability. Storm protection systems, rail clamps and anchors are critical.

Scale and height

Inspecting large structures at height requires planning, access equipment and safe working procedures.

Time pressure

Maintenance windows must fit around vessel schedules.

Key maintenance areas

Area Focus
Wheels and rails Wear monitoring, alignment, matched wheel replacement
Wire ropes and sheaves Regular inspection, lubrication, planned replacement
Brakes Hoist, trolley, gantry and storm brakes — testing and adjustment
Spreaders Twistlocks, hydraulics and electrical systems
Hydraulics Spreader, boom hoist and brake systems
Structures Corrosion and fatigue crack inspection
Electrical Cable reels, slip rings, drives and enclosures

Wheels: a frequent consumable

Gantry and trolley wheels on port cranes work hard. Matching driven wheels, maintaining rail alignment and choosing hardened wheels suited to the duty significantly extend wheel life. Holding spare wheel assemblies allows quick exchanges during short maintenance windows.

Corrosion management

  • Maintain paint systems on structures and repair damage promptly.
  • Use corrosion-resistant fasteners where appropriate.
  • Seal electrical enclosures and inspect regularly.
  • Protect hydraulic cylinder rods with suitable coatings.
  • Wash down equipment to remove salt deposits where practical.

Planning for availability

  1. Criticality ranking of each crane and component.
  2. Condition monitoring: rope inspection, wheel wear, oil analysis, thermography.
  3. Critical spares on site: wheels, brake components, spreader parts, hydraulic components.
  4. Planned maintenance windows coordinated with operations.
  5. Root cause analysis for repeat failures.

Spreaders and hydraulics

Container spreaders rely on hydraulic and electrical systems for twistlocks, telescoping and flippers. They take constant impacts, so hydraulic cylinders, hoses and valves on spreaders need frequent inspection and fast replacement.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do port cranes need special maintenance planning?

Port cranes operate continuously, often in high duty classes, in salty, corrosive air and exposed to wind. Maintenance windows must fit around vessel schedules. This makes condition monitoring, critical spares and carefully planned maintenance windows essential to keep cranes available.

How can corrosion on port cranes be controlled?

Maintain protective coatings and repair damage promptly, use corrosion-resistant fasteners and enclosures where appropriate, wash salt deposits from accessible areas, protect hydraulic cylinder rods with suitable coatings and inspect structures regularly for corrosion and fatigue cracks. Corrosion control is ongoing work rather than a one-time task.

Which spares are most important for port cranes?

Typical critical spares include wheel assemblies, brake components, wire rope or reliable rope supply, spreader parts such as twistlocks and hydraulic components, drive components and key electrical items. The exact list depends on crane type, duty and supplier lead times.

How are port cranes protected from wind?

Storm brakes, rail clamps, anchors and tie-downs secure cranes against high winds, while anemometers and alarms warn operators. These systems must be inspected and tested regularly, and operators must follow procedures for securing cranes when wind limits are approached.

Why do spreaders need frequent attention?

Spreaders take repeated impacts as they lock onto containers, and their hydraulic and electrical systems operate constantly. Twistlocks, cylinders, hoses and sensors should be inspected frequently, and spare spreader components held so faults can be fixed quickly.

posts.title: Material Handling in Warehouses: Crane and Hoist Reliability
posts.metaTitle: Warehouse Crane & Hoist Reliability: A Practical Guide
posts.metaDescription: How to keep overhead cranes, hoists and lifting equipment reliable in warehouses and distribution centres, from inspections to operator practices.
posts.excerpt: In busy warehouses, a stopped crane blocks the flow of goods. Here is how to keep cranes and hoists reliable in high-cycle material handling.
posts.imageAlt: High-bay warehouse racking with stored goods
posts.html:
Warehouses, distribution centres and stockyards rely on overhead cranes, hoists and lifting equipment to move heavy goods quickly. Unlike some industrial cranes that work occasionally, material handling cranes often run continuous cycles across multiple shifts. Reliability depends on matching equipment to duty, consistent maintenance and good operating practices.

Typical lifting equipment in warehouses

  • Overhead EOT cranes for heavy coils, plates and machinery.
  • Single-girder cranes with wire rope or chain hoists.
  • Jib cranes at loading bays and workstations.
  • Monorail hoists for production and dispatch lines.
  • Vacuum and magnet lifters for specialised loads.

What wears fastest in high-cycle handling

Component Why it wears
Hoist brakes Frequent starts, stops and inching
Wire ropes and chains Bending cycles and load cycles
Travel wheels Continuous travel, especially with skewing
Contactors and controls High switching frequency
Collectors and festoons Constant movement
Hooks and attachments Contact with slings and loads

Match the crane to the duty

A crane selected for occasional use will wear out quickly if utilisation increases. Warning signs that the duty has outgrown the crane include overheating motors, frequent brake adjustments and rapid wheel wear. Reviewing crane duty when operations change helps avoid persistent failures.

Maintenance priorities

  1. Daily pre-use checks by operators: controls, limits, brakes, hooks and ropes.
  2. Frequent brake inspection and adjustment on high-cycle hoists.
  3. Rope and chain inspection with replacement based on criteria.
  4. Wheel and rail monitoring to catch alignment issues early.
  5. Electrical maintenance of contactors, collectors and festoon systems.
  6. Periodic thorough examination by a competent person as required by regulations.

Operating practices that extend life

  • Use smooth acceleration and deceleration; avoid excessive inching.
  • Lift loads vertically — avoid side pulls and dragging.
  • Never exceed rated capacity, including the weight of attachments.
  • Report defects immediately and take faulty cranes out of service.
  • Keep travel paths clear and avoid collisions with end stops and other cranes.

Upgrades that improve reliability

  • Variable frequency drives for smoother motion, reduced swing and less mechanical shock.
  • Radio remote controls that allow operators to stand clear and see loads better.
  • Overload protection and load monitoring.
  • Anti-collision systems where multiple cranes share a runway.
  • Upgraded wheels and brakes for higher duty.

Spares for warehouse cranes

Keep brake parts, contactors, limit switches, pendant controls, rope or chain, and wheel assemblies for the most critical cranes. For older cranes with obsolete parts, plan reverse-engineered replacements before failures occur.

Safety culture

Lifting equipment safety depends on trained operators, competent inspectors and clear procedures for lifting operations. A strong safety culture also supports reliability: defects are reported early and fixed before they cause breakdowns.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do hoist brakes wear quickly in warehouses?

High-cycle operations involve frequent starts, stops and inching movements. Each stop uses the brake and generates heat. Inching in particular causes rapid wear. Operator training, smooth controls such as variable frequency drives and regular brake adjustment extend brake life.

What is the difference between a chain hoist and a wire rope hoist?

Chain hoists are compact and economical for lighter loads and shorter lifts. Wire rope hoists suit heavier loads, longer lifts and higher speeds, and are common on overhead cranes. The choice depends on capacity, lift height, duty and space.

How can I tell if a crane is overworked for its duty?

Signs include overheating motors, rapid wear of brakes, wheels and ropes, frequent electrical faults and structural cracking. If operations have increased since the crane was installed, review whether the crane's duty classification still matches its use.

Are radio remote controls safer than pendants?

Radio remotes allow operators to stand away from the load and choose the best viewing position, which can improve safety. They must be properly maintained, tested and used according to procedures, with clear rules for who controls the crane.

What maintenance records should be kept for warehouse cranes?

Keep pre-use check records, inspection and thorough examination reports, repair and parts records, and any load test certificates. These records demonstrate compliance and help identify recurring issues.

posts.title: Hydraulic Presses in Manufacturing Plants: Maintenance Essentials
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Press Maintenance Essentials for Manufacturing
posts.metaDescription: Practical hydraulic press maintenance: oil cleanliness, cylinder and seal care, valve maintenance, temperature control and safety system checks.
posts.excerpt: Hydraulic presses combine high forces with precise control. A focused maintenance routine keeps them accurate, productive and safe.
posts.imageAlt: Robotic assembly line in a manufacturing plant
posts.html:
Hydraulic presses are used for forming, stamping, moulding, assembly, straightening and compacting. They deliver very high forces with controllable speed and pressure, making them versatile and productive. They also concentrate large amounts of energy in one machine, so maintenance must cover both performance and safety.

Key systems in a hydraulic press

  • Main cylinder(s): deliver the pressing force.
  • Power unit: pump, motor, reservoir, filtration and cooling.
  • Valves: directional, pressure and flow control, often proportional for precise control.
  • Prefill valves: allow fast approach by filling large cylinders from the tank.
  • Guiding system: slides and gibs keep the ram aligned.
  • Safety systems: guards, light curtains, two-hand controls, safety valves and monitoring.

Common press problems

Symptom Possible causes
Ram drifts down Internal leakage in cylinder or valves, counterbalance problems
Slow approach or return Pump wear, prefill valve problems, flow settings
Inconsistent force Pressure control faults, worn pump, sensor issues
Overheating Running over relief, worn components, cooler fouling
Uneven ram movement Guide wear, misalignment, multiple-cylinder imbalance
Shock on decompression Incorrect decompression settings or valve faults

Maintenance essentials

Keep oil clean and cool

Presses often use proportional valves sensitive to contamination. Maintain fine filtration, monitor filter indicators and use oil analysis. Keep coolers clean and monitor temperature — overheating degrades oil and seals.

Maintain cylinders

Inspect the main cylinder for leaks and drift. Rod and gland seals in large press cylinders are expensive to replace, so preventing contamination and side loading is essential. Check guide alignment to avoid side loads on the cylinder.

Valve maintenance

Valves should be checked for correct settings and response. Prefill and decompression valves are critical to smooth operation; faults can cause shock and damage.

Guides and gibs

Worn guides allow the ram to tilt, loading the cylinder sideways and affecting part quality. Check clearances and lubricate as specified.

Electrical and sensors

Pressure transducers, position sensors and controls should be checked and calibrated to ensure accurate force and position control.

Safety systems

Presses can cause serious injuries. Safety systems must be inspected and tested regularly according to the manufacturer's instructions and applicable regulations:

  • guards and interlocks;
  • light curtains and safety mats;
  • two-hand controls;
  • safety valves that prevent unintended ram descent;
  • emergency stops.

Never bypass safety devices, and ensure maintenance is performed under proper isolation procedures — including mechanical blocking of the ram before working underneath it.

Planning for uptime

  • Keep seal kits for main cylinders and critical valves in stock.
  • Record pressures, temperatures and cycle times to spot trends.
  • Plan cylinder resealing during shutdowns rather than waiting for failure.

Upgrades and rebuilds

Older presses can be upgraded with modern power units, proportional control, energy-efficient pumps and improved safety systems. Cylinder rebuilds can restore performance and reduce leakage.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does a hydraulic press ram drift down?

Drift is usually caused by internal leakage in the main cylinder or valves, or problems with counterbalance or safety valves. Because presses can be dangerous, the cause should be diagnosed promptly by trained personnel and the ram mechanically supported during work.

What is a prefill valve?

A prefill valve allows large press cylinders to fill quickly from the reservoir during the fast approach stroke, using minimal pump flow. During the pressing stroke it closes so the pump can build pressure. Faulty prefill valves can cause slow approach, poor pressing or shock.

How important is oil cleanliness for presses?

Very important, particularly for presses with proportional or servo valves. Contamination causes valve sticking, poor control and seal wear. Fine filtration, clean oil handling and oil analysis are key parts of press maintenance.

Should press safety systems be tested regularly?

Yes. Guards, interlocks, light curtains, two-hand controls, safety valves and emergency stops must be inspected and tested according to the manufacturer's instructions and applicable regulations. Never bypass safety devices.

Can old presses be upgraded?

Yes. Older presses can be upgraded with modern power units, proportional control, energy-efficient pumps and improved safety systems. Upgrades should be engineered to match the press structure and intended use.

posts.title: Hydraulic Systems in Steel Plants and Foundries: Heat and Contamination
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulics in Steel Plants & Foundries: Heat and Dirt
posts.metaDescription: How heat, scale, dust and fire risk affect hydraulic systems in steel plants and foundries, and the design and maintenance choices that improve reliability.
posts.excerpt: Steel plants and foundries combine extreme heat, scale, dust and fire risk. Hydraulic systems here need special attention to stay safe and reliable.
posts.imageAlt: Sparks and heat in a metalworking facility
posts.html:
Steel plants, rolling mills and foundries depend heavily on hydraulics — for roll gap control, furnace doors, ladle handling, continuous casting, coilers, shears and cranes. They are also among the most demanding environments for hydraulic equipment: radiant heat, scale, dust, water and the risk of fire.

Where hydraulics are used

  • Rolling mills: roll gap control (AGC), roll changing, bending and balancing cylinders.
  • Continuous casting: segment clamping, mould oscillation, withdrawal units.
  • Furnaces: door cylinders, tilting mechanisms, charging equipment.
  • Coilers and shears: clamping, cutting and handling cylinders.
  • Ladle and crane equipment: heavy-duty cranes with high duty classes.
  • Foundries: moulding machines, shake-outs and casting handling.

The challenges

Heat

Radiant heat from furnaces and hot steel can push hydraulic oil and seals beyond their limits. Hoses and cylinders near heat sources are particularly vulnerable.

Scale, dust and water

Mill scale and dust are abrasive. Cooling water sprays create humid, wet conditions that introduce water into hydraulic systems.

Fire risk

A hydraulic leak spraying onto hot metal can ignite. This is why many plants use fire-resistant fluids in high-risk areas, along with protective measures.

Heavy, continuous duty

Mills run continuously, and equipment experiences heavy loads and shock.

Design measures

Challenge Typical measures
Radiant heat Heat shields, high-temperature seals, hose sleeves, relocation of components
Fire risk Fire-resistant fluids, hose protection, leak containment, routing away from ignition sources
Scale and dust Heavy-duty wipers, rod protection, sealed reservoirs, fine filtration
Water ingress Desiccant breathers, water removal, good seal selection
Shock loads Robust cylinders, cushioning, accumulators

Fire-resistant fluids considerations

Changing to a fire-resistant fluid affects the whole system. Seal materials, hose types, filters, paints and pumps must be compatible, and maintenance practices such as monitoring water content may change. Conversion requires careful planning and thorough flushing.

Maintenance priorities

  • Monitor oil temperature and keep coolers working effectively.
  • Inspect hoses frequently for heat damage; replace proactively near hot zones.
  • Check rod and seal condition on cylinders exposed to scale.
  • Use oil analysis to monitor contamination, water and fluid condition.
  • Maintain leak-free systems, especially near ignition sources.
  • Plan cylinder overhauls during scheduled mill shutdowns.

High-precision systems

Roll gap control systems use servo or high-response proportional valves that require very clean oil. Contamination control is critical to maintaining product quality.

Safety

Hydraulic failures in steel plants can lead to fires, dropped loads and uncontrolled movements. Isolation procedures, support of loads and safe release of stored energy are essential for maintenance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are fire-resistant hydraulic fluids used in steel plants?

A hydraulic leak spraying onto molten metal, hot slabs or furnace surfaces can ignite. Fire-resistant fluids are much less likely to sustain a fire, reducing that risk in high-hazard areas. Switching fluid type is a significant change: seals, hoses, filters, paints and sometimes pumps must be compatible, the system usually needs thorough flushing, and maintenance practices such as monitoring water content may change. A risk assessment should decide where fire-resistant fluids are needed.

How can hydraulic hoses be protected from radiant heat?

Route hoses away from heat sources wherever possible, add heat shields between hot equipment and hydraulic lines, use heat-resistant protective sleeves and select hoses rated for the temperatures involved. Hoses in hot zones age faster than elsewhere, so inspect them more often and replace them proactively rather than waiting for leaks.

Where does water contamination come from in mill hydraulics?

Cooling water sprays, steam, humid air drawn in through breathers, leaking heat exchangers and washing all introduce water. Water causes corrosion, degrades oil and damages pumps and valves. Desiccant breathers, good rod wipers and seals, cooler maintenance and regular oil analysis to measure water content help keep it under control.

Why do roll gap control systems need exceptionally clean oil?

Roll gap and other precision systems use servo or high-response proportional valves with very small internal clearances. Particles cause sticking, drifting and erratic control, which directly affects product thickness and quality. Fine pressure filtration, offline filtration and strict cleanliness targets are standard for these systems.

How can hydraulic downtime in steel plants be reduced?

Plan cylinder and valve overhauls during scheduled mill shutdowns, hold spares for critical actuators, monitor oil condition and temperatures, and investigate every repeat failure for root causes such as heat, scale ingress or misalignment. Exchange cylinders that can be fitted quickly are particularly valuable on mill equipment.

posts.title: Mobile Crane Hydraulic Systems: An Overview
posts.metaTitle: Mobile Crane Hydraulic Systems: How They Work
posts.metaDescription: An overview of mobile crane hydraulics: luffing and telescoping cylinders, outriggers, winches, slewing, load-holding valves and maintenance priorities.
posts.excerpt: Mobile cranes rely on hydraulics for nearly every movement. Understanding the main circuits helps maintenance teams keep them safe and productive.
posts.imageAlt: Large cranes lifting at an industrial site
posts.html:
Truck-mounted, all-terrain, rough-terrain and crawler cranes depend on hydraulics for almost every motion: setting up outriggers, raising and extending the boom, hoisting loads and slewing. Because these cranes lift heavy loads over people and property, their hydraulic systems are safety-critical and must be maintained with care.

Main hydraulic functions

Outriggers

Hydraulic cylinders extend beams and jacks to level and stabilise the crane. Each jack cylinder carries a large share of the crane's weight and load, so load-holding valves are fitted to prevent collapse if a hose fails.

Boom luffing

Large luffing (derricking) cylinders raise and lower the boom. They operate at high pressures and are equipped with counterbalance valves to control lowering speed and hold the boom safely.

Boom telescoping

Telescopic booms are extended using internal cylinders and, in many designs, rope or locking systems. Telescoping cylinders may be very long and require careful design against buckling.

Hoisting

Hydraulic motors drive winches through gearboxes, with spring-applied brakes and counterbalance or brake valves controlling the load.

Slewing

Hydraulic motors and gearboxes rotate the superstructure, with brakes holding position.

Steering and suspension

Many mobile cranes also use hydraulics for steering and suspension.

Safety-critical components

Component Role
Counterbalance valves Control lowering and hold loads on cylinders and winches
Pilot-operated check valves Hold outrigger jacks and cylinders if hoses fail
Winch brakes Hold suspended loads
Relief valves Limit system pressure
Load moment indicator sensors Provide data for safe operation, often including hydraulic pressure transducers

These components must be maintained and adjusted only by competent personnel according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Common problems

  • Boom drift from cylinder internal leakage or valve faults.
  • Outrigger jacks creeping from check valve or seal problems.
  • Jerky telescoping from air, contamination or seal friction.
  • Hydraulic leaks from hoses, fittings and cylinder seals.
  • Overheating during long working periods.

Maintenance priorities

  1. Daily checks: leaks, hose damage, oil level, outrigger and boom function.
  2. Rod inspection: luffing and outrigger cylinder rods are exposed and easily damaged.
  3. Filter changes and oil analysis.
  4. Hose replacement based on condition and age.
  5. Valve testing for load-holding devices during periodic inspections.
  6. Cylinder overhauls at intervals or when drift exceeds acceptable limits.
  7. Statutory inspections as required by local lifting equipment regulations.

Repairing crane cylinders

Mobile crane cylinders are high-value, safety-critical components. Repairs should include full inspection, rod and barrel repair as required, correct seal kits, and pressure and function testing with documented results. Load-holding valves should be checked or replaced as part of the repair.

Working practices

  • Always set up on firm, level ground with outriggers fully deployed as required by the load chart.
  • Never exceed rated capacities.
  • Avoid shock loading and sudden control movements.
  • Report any drift, leaks or unusual behaviour immediately.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does a counterbalance valve do on a mobile crane?

A counterbalance valve sits between the control valve and the cylinder or winch motor. It holds the load in position when the control is released and controls the speed of lowering so the load cannot run away. If a hose bursts, it helps prevent the load from dropping. Because it is safety-critical, it must only be adjusted, repaired or replaced according to the crane manufacturer's instructions.

Why do outrigger jacks slowly creep?

Creep is usually caused by internal leakage across the jack cylinder's piston seal or by leakage in the pilot-operated check valve that holds the jack. Since outriggers carry a large share of the crane's weight and load, any creep should be investigated before the crane is used again.

Can mobile crane cylinders be repaired by a local workshop?

Yes, if the workshop has experience with crane cylinders and follows the manufacturer's specifications. A proper repair includes inspection and measurement of all parts, correct seal kits, rod and barrel repairs where needed, pressure and function testing with documented results, and checking or replacing the load-holding valves.

What causes jerky boom telescoping?

Typical causes include air in the hydraulic system, contamination, worn seals or guide bearings in the telescopic cylinder, and dry or worn slide pads between boom sections. Jerky motion affects load control and can indicate developing damage, so it should be diagnosed promptly.

Are hydraulic components covered in crane inspections?

Yes. Periodic inspections and thorough examinations required by lifting equipment regulations typically include hydraulic cylinders, hoses, fittings, load-holding valves and associated safety systems such as load moment indicators. Keep records of hydraulic repairs alongside the crane's inspection history.

posts.title: Retrofitting Older Industrial Equipment with Modern Hydraulics
posts.metaTitle: Retrofitting Older Equipment with Modern Hydraulics
posts.metaDescription: When and how to retrofit older industrial machines with modern hydraulic power units, valves and controls to improve efficiency, reliability and safety.
posts.excerpt: Older machines are often mechanically sound but held back by outdated hydraulics. A targeted retrofit can add years of reliable, efficient service.
posts.imageAlt: Manufacturing plant with automated equipment
posts.html:
Many industrial machines are built to last decades. Their frames, structures and mechanical components may still be in good condition, while their hydraulic systems have become unreliable, inefficient or impossible to maintain due to obsolete parts. Retrofitting modern hydraulics can be far cheaper than replacing the whole machine.

Signs a retrofit makes sense

  • Frequent hydraulic breakdowns and leaks.
  • Obsolete pumps, valves or controls with no available spares.
  • High energy consumption and overheating.
  • Poor control accuracy affecting product quality.
  • Safety systems that do not meet current expectations.
  • Increased production demands the existing system cannot meet.

What a retrofit can include

New power unit

A modern power pack with efficient pumps, proper filtration, cooling and monitoring. Variable displacement pumps or variable speed drives can significantly reduce energy use.

Updated valves and controls

Replacing manual or old solenoid valves with modern directional, proportional or servo valves improves control, repeatability and diagnostics. Integration with PLC controls allows recipes, monitoring and fault reporting.

Cylinder upgrades

Cylinders can be rebuilt with modern seals, upgraded rods or redesigned for new loads. Position sensors can be integrated for closed-loop control.

Piping and hoses

Replacing leaking threaded pipework with properly designed tubing, flanges and modern fittings reduces leaks and contamination.

Safety improvements

Load-holding valves, safety valves, monitored valves and pressure monitoring improve safety, along with guarding and control upgrades as appropriate.

Benefits

Benefit How it is achieved
Energy savings Variable pumps, VFDs, accumulators, efficient circuits
Reliability New components, better filtration and cooling
Productivity Faster, more consistent cycles
Quality Precise control of force, speed and position
Maintainability Standard, available components and documentation
Safety Modern safety valves and monitoring

The retrofit process

  1. Survey: document the existing system, measure performance and identify problems.
  2. Requirements: define what the machine must achieve now and in future.
  3. Design: create a new circuit, select components and plan integration.
  4. Manufacture and test: build and test the power unit and assemblies before installation.
  5. Installation: plan installation during a shutdown to minimise downtime.
  6. Commissioning: flush, set up and verify performance.
  7. Documentation and training: provide circuit diagrams, parts lists and operator training.

Minimising downtime

Pre-building and testing the new power unit off-site, preparing hoses and pipework in advance and planning the installation carefully allows many retrofits to be completed in a short shutdown.

Is retrofit always the answer?

If the machine's structure is worn out or the process has fundamentally changed, a new machine may be better. A survey helps make that decision with facts rather than assumptions.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I decide between a retrofit and a new machine?

If the machine's frame, structure and mechanical components are sound and only the hydraulics and controls are outdated or unreliable, a retrofit is usually more economical and faster than replacing the machine. If the structure is worn out, the machine cannot meet new process requirements, or safety upgrades would be impractical, a new machine may be better. A survey of the existing equipment provides the facts to make this decision.

How long does a hydraulic retrofit take?

Engineering, manufacturing and testing the new power unit and assemblies happen off-site while the machine keeps running. Installation can often be completed during a planned shutdown because hoses, pipework and wiring are prepared in advance. The exact duration depends on the machine size and complexity.

Can a retrofit really reduce energy costs?

On machines that run long hours, yes. Replacing fixed pumps that dump excess flow over relief valves with variable displacement pumps or variable speed drives, adding accumulators and reducing throttling losses can cut energy consumption and heat generation substantially. Lower oil temperatures also extend seal and oil life.

What documentation should I receive after a retrofit?

Updated hydraulic circuit diagrams, electrical drawings, parts lists, pressure and flow settings, commissioning records and operating and maintenance instructions. Good documentation makes future troubleshooting faster and reduces dependence on the original installer.

Can safety be improved as part of a retrofit?

Yes. Retrofits are an ideal opportunity to add load-holding valves, monitored safety valves, pressure monitoring, accumulator safety blocks and modern control functions, alongside guarding and control system upgrades required by current safety expectations.

posts.title: Tipper and Dump Truck Hydraulic Cylinders: Care and Troubleshooting
posts.metaTitle: Tipper & Dump Truck Hydraulic Cylinders: Care and Fixes
posts.metaDescription: How tipper and dump truck hydraulic systems work, common telescopic cylinder problems, safe tipping practices and maintenance to prevent failures.
posts.excerpt: Tipper cylinders work hard in dirty conditions with heavy, uneven loads. Good care and safe tipping practice prevent most failures.
posts.imageAlt: Heavy truck on an open road
posts.html:
Tipper trucks and dump trailers rely on hydraulic cylinders — usually telescopic — to raise their bodies and discharge loads. These cylinders work in dusty, muddy conditions with heavy and sometimes uneven loads. They are also involved in some of the most serious accidents in road haulage when tipping goes wrong.

How a tipper hydraulic system works

  1. A power take-off (PTO) from the truck gearbox drives a hydraulic pump.
  2. A tipping valve directs oil to the cylinder to raise the body, holds it, and allows oil to return to lower it.
  3. A telescopic cylinder — usually single-acting — extends in stages to raise the body. Gravity lowers it.
  4. Safety features include relief valves, stroke limiters and, on many systems, controls that prevent overextension.

Common problems

Symptom Possible causes
Body will not raise fully Low oil, pump wear, relief setting, internal leakage
Body raises slowly PTO or pump problems, low engine speed, restriction
Body drops or creeps when raised Valve or seal leakage
Jerky or uneven staging Air, contamination, worn stage bearings
External leaks between stages Worn or damaged stage seals, scored stages
Bent cylinder stages Side loading from tipping on uneven ground or sticky loads

Safe tipping practices

Many tipper accidents — including overturns — are caused by unsafe tipping conditions rather than equipment faults. Safe practice includes:

  • Tip only on firm, level ground.
  • Check for overhead hazards such as power lines before raising the body.
  • Ensure loads discharge freely; sticky loads such as wet clay or asphalt can hold weight high in the body and destabilise the vehicle.
  • Keep the tailgate open and properly secured before tipping.
  • Never drive with the body raised.
  • Never work under a raised body without a suitable mechanical prop correctly in place.
  • Keep people clear during tipping.

Maintenance checklist

  • Check oil level with the body lowered.
  • Inspect the cylinder stages for damage, scoring and leaks when extended for checks.
  • Clean mud and debris from stages and mountings.
  • Grease mounting pivots and trunnions.
  • Inspect hoses and fittings for damage and leaks.
  • Check the PTO and pump mountings and operation.
  • Change filters and oil at recommended intervals.
  • Test safety devices such as stroke limiters and alarms.

Repairing telescopic tipper cylinders

Reconditioning typically includes resealing all stages, replacing stage bearings and stop rings, repairing or re-plating damaged stages and pressure testing. Bent stages usually need replacement rather than straightening.

When ordering repairs or replacements, provide:

  • number of stages;
  • retracted and extended lengths;
  • largest stage diameter;
  • mounting types;
  • working pressure;
  • body capacity and typical loads.

Prevent repeat failures

If cylinders bend or fail repeatedly, look at tipping practices, loading, ground conditions and whether the cylinder size suits the body and load. Upgrading to a heavier cylinder may be appropriate for demanding applications.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do tipper trucks tip over during unloading?

Overturning usually happens when the body is raised on uneven or soft ground, when sticky material stays high in the body instead of sliding out, when loads are unevenly distributed, or in strong crosswinds. Each of these shifts the centre of gravity sideways as the body rises. Tipping only on firm, level ground and confirming the load discharges freely are the most important precautions.

Is it safe to work under a raised tipper body?

Only when the body is held by a suitable mechanical body prop, correctly positioned and secured. Hydraulics alone must never be trusted to hold a raised body during maintenance, because valves can leak, seals can fail and hoses can burst.

Why does a raised tipper body slowly lower by itself?

Drift is typically caused by leakage in the tipping control valve or by internal leakage in the cylinder stages. It can worsen over time and may indicate seals or valves near the end of their life, so investigate and repair it promptly.

How often should tipper cylinders be serviced?

Follow the vehicle or cylinder manufacturer's recommendations and inspect cylinders regularly for leaks, damaged stages and worn mountings. Tippers working in quarries, construction and demolition sites, or carrying sticky and abrasive loads, generally need more frequent attention than those carrying free-flowing materials.

Can a tipper cylinder be upgraded for heavier work?

Yes. Heavier-duty cylinders with larger stages, improved bearings and upgraded seals are available for demanding applications. The replacement must suit the body design, mounting geometry, load and vehicle, so discuss the application with the cylinder manufacturer before upgrading.
