posts.title: How to Write a Clear RFQ for Hydraulic Components
posts.metaTitle: How to Write a Clear RFQ for Hydraulic Components
posts.metaDescription: A practical template for writing requests for quotation (RFQs) for hydraulic cylinders, power packs and custom components that get accurate quotes fast.
posts.excerpt: A clear request for quotation gets you accurate prices faster and avoids surprises later. Use this structure for hydraulic and custom engineering RFQs.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer and colleague reviewing technical drawings
posts.html:
A vague request for quotation (RFQ) produces vague quotations — or a long chain of questions that delays your project. A clear RFQ lets suppliers quote accurately and quickly, makes quotations easier to compare, and reduces the risk of receiving a part that does not fit or perform.

Here is a practical structure for RFQs for hydraulic cylinders, power packs and custom engineered components.

1. Basic information

  • Company name and contact person (with phone and email).
  • Project or equipment name.
  • Delivery location.
  • Required delivery date and whether it is firm.
  • Quotation deadline.

2. What you need

Describe the item clearly:

  • Type: cylinder, power pack, manifold, spare part, repair service.
  • Quantity: initial order and expected annual quantities.
  • New manufacture, repair or both.
  • Drawings or part numbers, including revision.
  • Samples or photos if drawings are not available.

3. Technical requirements

For hydraulic cylinders

Information Example
Bore / rod / stroke 100 / 56 / 600 mm
Retracted centres 920 mm
Mountings Clevis both ends, 40 mm pins
Ports 3/4" BSP, orientation as drawing
Working / maximum pressure 200 / 250 bar
Fluid Mineral hydraulic oil
Environment Outdoor, dusty
Special requirements Cushioning on extend, position sensor

For power packs

  • Actuators and their required forces/speeds.
  • Flow and pressure requirements, duty cycle.
  • Control method (manual, solenoid, proportional, PLC).
  • Power supply (voltage, frequency).
  • Reservoir size constraints and installation space.
  • Ambient conditions and noise limits.

For machined or crane parts

  • Material and heat treatment.
  • Critical dimensions and tolerances.
  • Surface finish and coatings.
  • Crane or machine details for context.

4. Quality and documentation

State the documentation you need:

  • dimensional inspection report;
  • material certificates;
  • hardness test results;
  • pressure test records;
  • circuit diagrams and manuals;
  • compliance with any specified standards.

Requesting documentation at the RFQ stage ensures it is included in the price.

5. Commercial requirements

  • Packaging and delivery terms.
  • Payment terms.
  • Warranty expectations.
  • Whether partial deliveries are acceptable.
  • Spare parts to be quoted at the same time.

6. Background information

Explain why you need the item:

  • Is this a replacement for a failed part? How did it fail?
  • Is the equipment being upgraded?
  • Is downtime driving urgency?

This context helps suppliers recommend improvements and prioritise urgent work.

Common RFQ mistakes

  • Sending only a part number from an obsolete machine.
  • Omitting pressure, load or duty information.
  • Forgetting mounting details or port orientations.
  • Requesting documentation after the order is placed.
  • Comparing quotes that are based on different assumptions.

Comparing quotations

When quotes arrive, check that each one:

  • meets the full specification;
  • includes required testing and documentation;
  • states lead time realistically;
  • clarifies warranty terms;
  • highlights any assumptions or exceptions.

The lowest price is not always the lowest cost if it excludes testing or arrives too late.

Make it easy

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the single most important part of an RFQ?

Clear technical requirements. Suppliers need dimensions or drawings, pressures, loads, speeds, operating conditions, quantities and documentation needs to quote accurately. Missing technical information is the most common reason quotes are delayed, vary widely between suppliers, or lead to parts that do not fit or perform as expected.

Should I include photos with my RFQ?

Yes. Photos of the part, its installation, mountings, port orientations and any nameplates help suppliers understand the requirement quickly and reduce questions — especially when drawings are missing. Include a tape measure or ruler in shots for scale where possible.

How do I compare quotations fairly?

Check that each quote meets the full specification, includes the testing and documentation you requested, states a realistic lead time and warranty, and lists any assumptions or exclusions. Put the quotes side by side on these points before comparing price. A cheaper quote that excludes testing or arrives weeks later may cost more overall.

Should spare parts be quoted in the same RFQ?

Yes. Asking for seal kits, wear parts or a complete spare unit at the same time often reduces cost, because the supplier can manufacture or order them alongside the main item. It also ensures spares are available when you need them.

What if I do not know all the technical details?

Send what you have — photos, partial dimensions, the machine type and a description of how the part is used. A capable supplier will help you complete the specification, measure the part or reverse-engineer it. It is better to start the conversation early than wait for perfect information.

posts.title: Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Hydraulic Cylinder Manufacturer
posts.metaTitle: Choosing a Hydraulic Cylinder Manufacturer: Key Questions
posts.metaDescription: The questions to ask when choosing a hydraulic cylinder manufacturer or repairer — engineering support, in-house processes, testing, documentation and lead times.
posts.excerpt: Not all cylinder suppliers are equal. These questions help you separate capable manufacturing partners from simple traders.
posts.imageAlt: Precision machining in a hydraulic manufacturing workshop
posts.html:
Hydraulic cylinders are critical to the machines they power. A poorly designed or badly made cylinder leads to leaks, drift, downtime and, in lifting applications, safety risks. Choosing the right manufacturer or repairer matters as much as the specification itself.

Here are the questions worth asking before you place an order.

1. Do you design or just assemble?

Some suppliers build only to drawings; others offer engineering support. If your application is new, or the original cylinder failed, you need a supplier who can review loads, buckling, mountings, seals and materials — and suggest improvements.

2. Which processes are done in-house?

In-house machining, honing, welding, assembly and testing give better control over quality and lead time. Outsourced processes are not necessarily a problem, but ask how they are controlled.

Process Why it matters
CNC machining Accuracy of pistons, glands, grooves and threads
Tube honing / finishing Bore finish and geometry for seal life
Rod processing Hardening, chrome plating and finish quality
Welding Strength and integrity of end caps and mountings
Assembly Clean assembly prevents early contamination
Testing Proves the cylinder before delivery

3. How do you select seals?

A good manufacturer selects seals for the actual pressure, speed, temperature, fluid and environment — not simply the cheapest kit. Ask which seal suppliers they use and whether they can offer upgrades for harsh conditions.

4. What testing do you perform?

Every cylinder should be pressure and function tested. Ask what is tested — internal leakage, external leakage, full stroke, cushioning — and whether you will receive a test record.

5. What documentation do you provide?

Typical documentation includes drawings, inspection reports, test records and, where needed, material certificates. For repairs, ask for a findings report explaining what was found and why the cylinder failed.

6. How do you handle repairs?

Ask whether the repairer:

  • inspects and measures all components;
  • explains repair options and costs before work;
  • replaces all seals, not just the leaking one;
  • tests after repair;
  • provides a warranty.

7. What are your realistic lead times?

Ask for lead times for new cylinders, repairs and urgent breakdown work. A supplier who quotes a realistic date and meets it is more valuable than one who promises a fast date and misses it.

8. Can you reverse-engineer obsolete cylinders?

If your equipment is old, you will eventually need cylinders that are no longer available. Ask whether the supplier can measure, draw and manufacture replacements, and whether they will share the approved drawing with you.

9. What industries and applications do you serve?

Experience with similar applications — cranes, mining, presses, mobile equipment — means the supplier understands your conditions and common failure modes.

10. Can I visit?

A workshop visit tells you a lot: cleanliness, equipment, organisation and the people you will work with.

Red flags

  • No testing, or testing "on request only".
  • Vague answers about seal brands or materials.
  • No inspection or findings reports.
  • Lowest price with no explanation of what is included.
  • Reluctance to discuss failures or warranties.

Build a partnership

The best results come from long-term relationships. A manufacturer who knows your equipment can keep drawings on file, hold critical spares and respond quickly when breakdowns happen.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does it matter whether a manufacturer works in-house?

Machining, honing, welding, assembly and testing done in-house give the manufacturer direct control over quality and lead times. Outsourced processes can still work well, but they add handovers and scheduling dependencies, so ask how they are controlled and inspected.

Should every cylinder be pressure tested before delivery?

Yes. Pressure and function testing confirms that seals are correctly installed, welds and threads hold pressure, and the cylinder strokes and cushions properly. A documented test record should be available for every unit, new or repaired.

What warranty should I expect from a cylinder supplier?

Terms vary, so ask what is covered, for how long and under what conditions. Warranties usually exclude damage from contamination, overload, misalignment or improper installation. A supplier confident in their work will explain the terms clearly and investigate any failures openly.

Can a manufacturer improve on my existing cylinder design?

A manufacturer with engineering capability can review how and why the existing cylinder failed and recommend improvements — a larger rod to resist buckling, better seals for heat or speed, harder rod coatings for corrosive environments, or improved mountings to tolerate misalignment.

Is it worth visiting a supplier before ordering?

For significant or ongoing business, yes. A visit shows you the workshop's equipment, cleanliness, organisation, testing facilities and the people you will work with — all strong indicators of the quality you can expect.

posts.title: OEM vs Aftermarket Crane Parts: Making the Right Choice
posts.metaTitle: OEM vs Aftermarket Crane Parts: How to Choose
posts.metaDescription: Compare OEM and aftermarket crane parts on fit, quality, documentation, cost and lead time, and learn how to evaluate aftermarket suppliers safely.
posts.excerpt: OEM parts are not always available or fast, and aftermarket parts are not all equal. Here is how to decide what is right for your crane.
posts.imageAlt: Assorted crane spare parts and mechanical components
posts.html:
When a crane part wears out, buyers often face a choice: order from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) or buy from an aftermarket supplier who manufactures equivalent parts. Both options can be right — depending on the part, the crane and the supplier.

What are OEM parts?

OEM parts are supplied by the crane's original manufacturer or its authorised suppliers. They are made to the original design specifications.

Advantages

  • Known fit and specification.
  • Direct compatibility with warranty and service agreements.
  • Clear part numbers and documentation.

Limitations

  • Can be expensive.
  • Lead times may be long, particularly for older models.
  • Parts may be obsolete for older cranes or unavailable if the OEM has ceased trading.

What are aftermarket parts?

Aftermarket parts are manufactured by independent suppliers, either to OEM drawings supplied by the customer, by reverse engineering, or to equivalent catalogue designs.

Advantages

  • Often shorter lead times, especially from local manufacturers.
  • Cost savings.
  • Availability for obsolete equipment.
  • Opportunity to improve on the original design or material.

Limitations

  • Quality varies widely between suppliers.
  • Documentation may be limited unless requested.
  • May affect warranty terms on newer cranes.

Comparison

Factor OEM Quality aftermarket
Fit Assured Assured when made to drawing or carefully reverse-engineered
Lead time Variable, often long for older cranes Often shorter
Cost Higher Often lower
Availability for old cranes Limited Good
Improvements Rare Possible
Documentation Standard Request inspection reports and certificates

Which parts suit aftermarket supply?

Many mechanical parts are well suited to quality aftermarket manufacture:

  • wheels, axles and bearing housings;
  • pins, bushes and shafts;
  • sheaves and drums;
  • couplings and brake drums;
  • fabricated brackets and guards.

For proprietary electronic systems, safety devices and certified components such as hooks and rated lifting accessories, OEM or certified equivalents are usually the appropriate choice.

How to evaluate an aftermarket supplier

  1. Engineering capability: can they measure, draw and specify materials and heat treatment correctly?
  2. Manufacturing control: in-house machining, heat treatment control and inspection.
  3. Documentation: dimensional reports, hardness results and material certificates.
  4. Experience: familiarity with cranes and their duty classes.
  5. Drawing approval: do they provide drawings for your approval and records?
  6. References: other crane users they supply.

Warranty and compliance considerations

For cranes under warranty or service contracts, check whether non-OEM parts are permitted. For any load-bearing component, ensure the replacement meets or exceeds the original specification and that significant changes are reviewed by qualified engineers.

A balanced strategy

Many maintenance teams use both: OEM parts for proprietary electronics and newer cranes, and quality aftermarket parts for mechanical wear components and obsolete equipment. Keeping approved drawings for aftermarket parts builds independence and reduces future lead times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are aftermarket crane parts safe to use?

Quality aftermarket parts made to the correct specification — with appropriate materials, heat treatment and inspection — can perform as well as or better than original parts. Quality varies between suppliers, so choose experienced manufacturers, request documentation, and ensure load-bearing parts meet or exceed the original specification.

Will aftermarket parts affect my crane's warranty?

They may. For cranes still under warranty or a service agreement, check the terms before fitting non-OEM parts. For older cranes outside warranty, aftermarket parts are widely used for mechanical wear components.

Which crane parts should always be OEM or certified?

Certified lifting components such as hooks and rated lifting accessories, some safety devices, and proprietary electronic controls are usually best sourced from the OEM or as certified equivalents. Mechanical parts such as wheels, pins, sheaves and couplings are commonly sourced from quality aftermarket manufacturers.

How can I check the quality of aftermarket parts?

Request dimensional inspection reports, hardness test results and material certificates; ask about the supplier's engineering and manufacturing processes; and, for new suppliers, consider a workshop visit or references from other crane users.

Why keep drawings for aftermarket parts?

Approved drawings let you reorder quickly, compare suppliers, and avoid repeating reverse engineering every time a part wears out. They also provide a record of specifications for audits and future maintenance.

posts.title: Total Cost of Ownership for Hydraulic Equipment
posts.keyword: total cost of ownership hydraulic equipment
posts.metaTitle: Total Cost of Ownership for Hydraulic Equipment
posts.metaDescription: Why purchase price is only a fraction of hydraulic equipment cost, and how to compare options using energy, maintenance, downtime and service life.
posts.excerpt: The cheapest hydraulic component is rarely the cheapest to own. Total cost of ownership reveals the real cost over the equipment's life.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer analysing data on a computer workstation
posts.html:
When comparing quotations for hydraulic equipment, it is natural to focus on the purchase price. But for most hydraulic systems, the purchase price is a small part of the total cost over the equipment's life. Energy, maintenance, repairs and downtime usually cost far more. Total cost of ownership (TCO) puts all these costs on the table.

The components of TCO

1. Purchase and installation

The initial price of the equipment, plus installation, commissioning and any modifications to fit it.

2. Energy

Hydraulic power units can consume significant electricity, especially on machines that run many hours. Inefficient pumps, throttling losses and heat generation all add up.

3. Maintenance

Filters, oil, seals, inspections and labour over the life of the equipment.

4. Repairs and spare parts

The cost of repairing failures, including parts and labour.

5. Downtime

Lost production while equipment is broken or under maintenance. For critical equipment, downtime is often the largest cost of all.

6. End of life

Disposal, replacement or refurbishment at the end of service life.

An illustrative comparison

Consider two power units for the same machine, operating many hours a year:

Cost element Option A (low price) Option B (efficient design)
Purchase price Lower Higher
Pump type Fixed displacement Variable displacement
Energy use Higher (excess flow to heat) Lower (flow matched to demand)
Cooling Larger cooler needed Smaller cooler
Oil and seal life Shorter (higher temperatures) Longer
Downtime risk Higher Lower

On machines with high utilisation, the energy and reliability savings of the more efficient design can exceed the difference in purchase price over the equipment's life. The exact figures depend on operating hours, electricity prices and duty cycle — which is why a TCO comparison should use your own data.

Where TCO decisions matter most

  • Power units on machines running multiple shifts.
  • Pumps where variable displacement or variable speed drives reduce energy use.
  • Cylinders on critical equipment, where reliability prevents downtime.
  • Filtration, where better contamination control extends component life.
  • Crane wheels and wear parts, where better materials reduce replacement frequency.

How to estimate TCO

  1. Estimate operating hours per year and equipment life.
  2. Estimate energy use from motor power and duty cycle.
  3. List maintenance items and their frequencies.
  4. Estimate failure frequency and repair costs based on experience.
  5. Value downtime per hour for the affected process.
  6. Compare options over the same period.

Even rough estimates often reveal that higher-quality options pay back.

Ways to reduce TCO

  • Choose efficient pump and control strategies.
  • Specify appropriate filtration and cooling.
  • Select durable materials and seals for the actual conditions.
  • Standardise components to simplify spares.
  • Plan maintenance based on condition monitoring.
  • Hold critical spares to reduce downtime.

Ask suppliers for TCO information

Suppliers can often provide information on energy consumption, expected service intervals and component life. Asking for this information encourages quotations based on value rather than lowest price.

Frequently Asked Questions

What costs make up total cost of ownership?

Purchase and installation, energy consumption, routine maintenance (filters, oil, seals, labour), repairs and spare parts, production losses during downtime, and end-of-life disposal or refurbishment. For many hydraulic systems, energy and downtime together far exceed the purchase price.

Why is energy often the biggest running cost?

Hydraulic power units on machines running many hours consume significant electricity, and inefficient circuits waste much of it as heat. That heat then requires coolers and shortens oil and seal life — adding further cost. Efficient pump and control choices reduce both energy and maintenance costs.

How should I put a value on downtime?

Estimate what an hour or day of stoppage costs for the affected process: lost output or margin, idle labour, overtime to catch up, late-delivery penalties and knock-on effects on other operations. Even a rough figure usually shows that reliability improvements pay back quickly on critical equipment.

Do efficient hydraulic systems always cost more to buy?

Often they cost more upfront because variable pumps, better valves and controls are more expensive than basic components. On high-utilisation machines, energy savings and improved reliability commonly recover that difference over the equipment's life.

Can suppliers help me compare total cost of ownership?

Yes. Ask suppliers for expected energy consumption, maintenance intervals, component life and spare parts costs. This information lets you compare options on lifetime value rather than purchase price alone.

posts.title: Lead Times for Custom Components: What Affects Them
posts.metaTitle: Lead Times for Custom Components: What Affects Them
posts.metaDescription: What determines lead times for custom hydraulic and crane components — design, materials, processes and approvals — and how buyers can shorten them.
posts.excerpt: Lead times for custom parts are rarely random. Understanding what drives them helps you plan, avoid delays and get urgent parts faster.
posts.imageAlt: Technician working on an industrial installation
posts.html:
"When can you deliver?" is often the first question buyers ask. For custom hydraulic and crane components, the answer depends on several factors — some controlled by the manufacturer, others by the buyer. Understanding them helps you plan better and shorten lead times when it matters.

What drives lead time

1. Information completeness

Missing information is the most common cause of delay. Every question that needs answering before design or manufacturing can start adds days.

2. Engineering and drawings

New designs and reverse-engineered parts need engineering time for measurements, drawings and calculations. Repeat orders with approved drawings skip this step.

3. Customer approval

Drawings and specifications usually need customer approval. Approval delays add directly to lead time.

4. Materials

Standard steel grades and sizes are usually available quickly. Special alloys, large forgings, specific tube sizes and chrome bars may need to be ordered, adding significant time.

5. Bought-in components

Seals, pumps, valves, motors, sensors and bearings come from external suppliers. Their lead times can dominate the overall schedule.

6. Processes

Heat treatment, plating, coating and specialised finishing often involve external processors or batch scheduling.

7. Testing and documentation

Pressure testing, inspection and documentation add time but reduce the risk of problems after delivery.

8. Workshop capacity

Current workload affects when work can start.

Typical timeline structure

Stage Factors
Quotation Completeness of enquiry
Engineering and approval Design complexity, approval speed
Procurement Materials and bought-in components
Manufacture Machining, welding, heat treatment, coatings
Assembly and testing Complexity, test requirements
Dispatch Packaging, documentation, transport

How buyers can shorten lead times

  1. Provide complete information at the enquiry stage: drawings, samples, specifications and documentation requirements.
  2. Approve drawings quickly and nominate a decision-maker.
  3. Keep approved drawings on file for future repeat orders.
  4. Order long-lead items early, such as pumps and special materials, even before final details are fixed.
  5. Accept equivalent standard components where the original is hard to obtain.
  6. Plan replacements using condition monitoring rather than waiting for failure.
  7. Hold critical spares for components with long lead times.

Handling breakdowns

When a breakdown occurs, ask the manufacturer about:

  • repairing the existing part rather than making a new one;
  • temporary solutions to restore operation;
  • prioritised manufacturing for critical components;
  • partial deliveries — for example, one urgent unit, with spares following later.

Clear communication about the cost of downtime helps suppliers prioritise effectively.

Realistic promises

Be wary of unrealistically short lead times. A supplier who commits to an achievable date and keeps you informed is more valuable than one who promises a fast delivery and misses it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do custom components take longer than catalogue parts?

Catalogue parts may be in stock, while custom components require engineering, drawing approval, material procurement, machining, heat treatment or coatings, assembly and testing. Each stage takes time, and bought-in items such as pumps or special steels can add their own lead times.

How can I get an urgent part faster?

Send complete information immediately, ask whether repairing the existing part is faster than making a new one, accept equivalent standard components where suitable, approve drawings quickly and explain the cost of downtime so the supplier can prioritise. Partial deliveries — one urgent unit first — can also help.

Do approval delays really affect delivery dates?

Yes. Manufacturing usually cannot start until drawings are approved, so every day spent waiting adds directly to the lead time. Nominate someone with authority to review and approve drawings promptly.

Should I hold spares for components with long lead times?

For critical equipment, holding spares for long-lead components — custom cylinders, special pumps, matched crane wheels — is often the most effective way to prevent long shutdowns. The cost of the spare is usually small compared with weeks of downtime.

Are very short promised lead times reliable?

Not always. Ask how the supplier will meet the date, which materials and components they already have, and how they will keep you updated. A realistic date that is kept is more valuable than an optimistic one that slips.

posts.title: Inspection Documentation to Request from Your Supplier
posts.metaTitle: Inspection Documentation to Request from Suppliers
posts.metaDescription: Which inspection reports, test records and certificates to request for hydraulic and crane components, and how documentation supports quality and traceability.
posts.excerpt: Good documentation proves a component was made and tested correctly. Here is what to request — and why it matters long after delivery.
posts.imageAlt: Engineers reviewing technical documentation together
posts.html:
A component can look perfect and still be wrong. Documentation provides evidence that dimensions, materials, heat treatment and performance meet requirements. It also creates a record that helps future maintenance, repairs and audits. Knowing what to request — and requesting it before the order — is part of good purchasing.

Common types of documentation

Dimensional inspection report

Records measured dimensions against drawing requirements, typically for critical dimensions and tolerances. Essential for machined parts, wheels, pins, shafts and reverse-engineered components.

Material test certificate

Issued by the steel mill or supplier, documenting chemical composition and mechanical properties of the material. Important for load-bearing and safety-critical components.

Hardness test report

Confirms the results of heat treatment. For surface-hardened parts such as crane wheels and induction-hardened rods, the report may include surface hardness and, where specified, hardened depth.

Pressure and function test record

For hydraulic cylinders, manifolds and power units, documents test pressures, durations, leakage results and function checks.

Welding records

For critical fabrications: welding procedures, welder qualifications and NDT reports.

NDT reports

Results of non-destructive testing such as magnetic particle, dye penetrant or ultrasonic inspection.

Coating and plating reports

Thickness and adhesion results for paints, plating or chrome where specified.

Drawings, circuit diagrams and manuals

As-built drawings, hydraulic circuit diagrams, parts lists and operating and maintenance instructions — particularly for custom systems.

What to request for different products

Product Typical documentation
Hydraulic cylinder (new) Drawing, test record, inspection of key dimensions
Hydraulic cylinder (repair) Findings report, parts replaced, test record
Power pack Circuit diagram, parts list, test record, manual
Crane wheels Dimensional report, hardness report, material certificate
Pins and shafts Dimensional report, material certificate, hardness report if treated
Fabricated structures Dimensional report, welding and NDT records if specified

Why documentation matters

  • Quality assurance: confirms requirements were met.
  • Traceability: links components to materials and processes.
  • Maintenance: provides baseline data for future inspections.
  • Root cause analysis: helps investigate failures.
  • Compliance: supports audits and regulatory requirements.
  • Future orders: documentation and drawings make repeat orders faster and more consistent.

Request it at the start

Documentation takes time to produce and may require specific inspection steps during manufacturing. Include documentation requirements in your RFQ and purchase order so they are planned and priced from the start.

Store it properly

Keep documentation with equipment records in your maintenance system. When a component is replaced or repaired, the previous documentation is valuable reference.

A supplier who documents is a supplier who controls

Suppliers who readily provide inspection and test records usually have controlled processes. Reluctance to provide documentation is a warning sign.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should I ask suppliers for documentation?

At the RFQ stage. Some documentation — such as inspection reports, hardness tests or material certificates — requires specific steps during manufacturing and affects price. Requesting it after the order may be impossible or expensive.

What is a dimensional inspection report?

It is a record of measured dimensions compared with the drawing's requirements and tolerances, usually covering critical dimensions. It confirms the part was checked and is within tolerance, and provides baseline data for future wear measurements.

Why are material certificates important?

They document the chemical composition and mechanical properties of the material used, providing traceability back to the steel batch. For load-bearing and safety-critical components, they are key evidence that the correct material was used.

Should repaired components come with documentation?

Yes. A repair findings report explains what was found and why the component failed, and a test record confirms it was tested after repair. This information helps you prevent repeat failures and supports maintenance records.

How should documentation be stored?

Attach it to the equipment record in your maintenance management system or a well-organised file, linked to the machine and component. When a component is replaced or repaired, previous documentation becomes valuable reference for specifications and wear history.

Every component we manufacture or repair is supplied with appropriate inspection and test documentation. Learn more about our quality process or request a quote.

posts.title: Spare Parts Inventory Planning for Critical Equipment
posts.metaTitle: Spare Parts Inventory Planning for Critical Equipment
posts.metaDescription: How to plan spare parts inventory for cranes and hydraulic equipment using criticality, lead time and failure history — without tying up excess capital.
posts.excerpt: Too few spares and breakdowns become shutdowns; too many and capital sits idle on shelves. Here is a practical way to plan the right inventory.
posts.imageAlt: Warehouse shelving stocked with parts and materials
posts.html:
Every maintenance manager faces the same balancing act with spare parts. Hold too few, and a minor failure becomes a long shutdown while parts are sourced. Hold too many, and capital is tied up in parts that may never be used — or that become obsolete. A structured approach helps you stock the right parts in the right quantities.

Step 1: List your equipment and rank criticality

Start with the equipment, not the parts. Rank each machine or system by:

  • impact of failure on production and safety;
  • availability of backup equipment;
  • cost of downtime per hour or day.

Focus detailed spares planning on the most critical equipment first.

Step 2: Identify critical components

For each critical machine, identify components whose failure would stop it. For cranes and hydraulic systems, typical candidates include:

  • hydraulic cylinders, pumps and motors;
  • valves and solenoid coils;
  • crane wheels, brakes and couplings;
  • gearboxes and motors;
  • control and safety components;
  • wear parts such as seals, filters and brake linings.

Step 3: Assess lead time and availability

For each component, determine:

  • typical lead time from suppliers;
  • whether it is standard or custom;
  • whether it is obsolete or at risk of obsolescence;
  • whether it can be repaired quickly instead of replaced.

Step 4: Use a simple risk matrix

Short lead time Long lead time
High criticality Hold wear items; consider spares Hold spares
Low criticality Buy when needed Consider spares or repair plans

Components that are critical and slow to obtain are the strongest candidates for stock.

Step 5: Set stock levels

  • Wear parts: base quantities on consumption history and reorder points.
  • Insurance spares: usually one per group of identical machines.
  • Repairable spares: consider exchange units — fit the spare immediately and repair the failed part for the shelf.

Step 6: Standardise where possible

Standardising components across machines — seal sizes, valve types, pumps and fasteners — reduces the number of different spares needed. When replacing equipment, consider standardisation opportunities.

Step 7: Address obsolescence proactively

Older equipment often has parts that are no longer available. Identify these early and:

  • reverse-engineer components and keep approved drawings;
  • order spares before failures occur;
  • consider upgrades that replace obsolete subsystems.

Step 8: Store and maintain spares properly

Spares that deteriorate on the shelf are useless when needed:

  • protect machined surfaces from corrosion;
  • store seals and rubber parts away from heat, light and ozone;
  • store cylinders horizontally with ports capped and rods protected;
  • rotate shaft-mounted spares periodically where recommended;
  • label clearly with equipment and location.

Step 9: Review regularly

Review the spares list after breakdowns and at least annually. Add parts that caused unexpected downtime, reduce stock of items that never move, and remove parts for retired equipment.

Working with suppliers

Manufacturers can support your strategy by keeping drawings on file, holding customer-specific stock, offering exchange programmes and committing to priority lead times for breakdowns.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I identify which spare parts are critical?

Ask three questions for each component: does its failure stop production or create a safety risk, is there an alternative way to keep operating, and how long would a replacement take to obtain? Components that stop critical equipment and have long lead times are the strongest candidates for stock.

What is an insurance spare?

An insurance spare is a part that rarely fails but would cause a long, expensive shutdown if it did — for example, a gearbox, a custom cylinder or a matched set of crane wheels. It may sit on the shelf for years, but one avoided shutdown can justify its cost.

How do I stop spare parts deteriorating in storage?

Protect machined surfaces from corrosion, store seals and rubber parts away from heat, light and ozone, keep cylinders horizontal with ports capped and rods protected, rotate shafts periodically where recommended, and label everything clearly with the equipment it belongs to.

How often should the spares list be reviewed?

At least once a year and after every significant breakdown. Add parts that caused unexpected downtime, adjust quantities based on actual usage, and remove items for equipment that has been retired or replaced.

Can suppliers hold stock on my behalf?

Many manufacturers offer customer-specific stock, framework agreements or exchange programmes for critical components. These arrangements reduce your on-site inventory while guaranteeing availability when parts are needed.

posts.title: How to Prepare a Worn Part or Sample for Reverse Engineering
posts.metaTitle: Preparing a Worn Part for Reverse Engineering
posts.metaDescription: How to prepare and send a worn or failed part for reverse engineering: what to include, how to package it and what information speeds up the process.
posts.excerpt: Reverse engineering starts with the sample you send. A well-prepared part and good information mean a faster, more accurate replacement.
posts.imageAlt: Engineer measuring and drafting a component
posts.html:
When a part is obsolete or drawings are missing, reverse engineering can recreate it. The quality and speed of that process depend heavily on what you send to the manufacturer. A well-prepared sample with good supporting information can save days of back-and-forth.

What to send

The part itself

The actual worn or failed part is the most valuable reference. Where possible, send the complete component rather than fragments. If the part is broken, send all pieces.

Mating parts or their dimensions

A part's dimensions often depend on what it fits into or onto. For example:

  • a pin's diameter relates to the bushes or holes it fits;
  • a wheel's bore relates to the axle or bearing;
  • a gear relates to its mating gear and shaft.

Send mating parts if practical, or measure and record their dimensions.

An unworn example if available

If you have an unworn or less worn identical part — on another machine or in stock — it can show original dimensions more accurately.

Information to include

Information Why it helps
Machine make, model and serial number Context and possible original data
Location in the machine Function and loading
Quantity needed now and in future Planning and cost
How the part failed Opportunities to improve
Operating conditions Load, speed, temperature, environment
Photos of the part installed Orientation and interfaces
Required documentation Inspection reports, certificates

Preparing the part

  1. Do not clean aggressively. Remove loose dirt and oil, but avoid grinding, wire brushing or polishing that changes dimensions or removes evidence of wear patterns.
  2. Do not straighten or repair bent or damaged parts. The damage itself may reveal useful information.
  3. Label the part with your company name, contact person and reference.
  4. Mark orientation if relevant (for example, which side faced outward).
  5. Protect machined surfaces with a light oil or wrap to prevent corrosion in transit.

Packaging and shipping

  • Use sturdy packaging suitable for the weight.
  • Protect fragile features such as threads, gear teeth and sealing surfaces.
  • Include a copy of your information sheet inside the package.
  • Send photographs and information by email in advance so engineering review can start before the part arrives.

When you cannot send the part

If the part cannot be removed or must remain in service, a manufacturer may be able to measure it on site, or work from detailed photos and measurements. Complex parts or parts with critical fits are best measured directly.

What happens next

The manufacturer will typically:

  1. inspect and measure the part;
  2. assess material and hardness;
  3. produce a drawing for your approval;
  4. manufacture and inspect the replacement;
  5. return the original sample if requested.

Keep the drawing

Once approved, keep the drawing in your records. Future orders become simple and fast, and you are no longer dependent on a single supplier's knowledge.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I clean a part before sending it for reverse engineering?

Remove loose dirt and excess oil so the part can be handled safely, but avoid grinding, wire brushing or polishing. Aggressive cleaning can change critical dimensions and remove wear patterns that help engineers understand how the part failed.

Do I need to send the mating parts too?

If practical, yes. Mating parts show the fits and clearances the new part must achieve. If they cannot be removed, measure their key dimensions — bore and shaft diameters, thread sizes, mounting positions — and include those measurements with photos.

What if the part is broken into pieces?

Send all the pieces. The fracture surfaces often reveal how and why the part failed — fatigue, overload or material defects — which can guide improvements to material, heat treatment or design in the replacement.

Can a part be measured on site instead of sent away?

For parts that cannot be removed, or very large components, on-site measurement is possible. However, complex parts with precise fits are best measured in a workshop with proper equipment, so remove and send them if downtime allows.

Will my original part be returned?

Usually, if you request it. Agree this when sending the part, and label it clearly with your company name and reference so it can be identified and returned after the drawing has been completed.

We reverse-engineer crane spare parts, crane wheels and hydraulic components. Start a request and attach photos of your part.

posts.title: Hydraulic Safety Basics: Working Safely Around Pressurised Systems
posts.metaTitle: Hydraulic Safety Basics: Working Around Pressurised Systems
posts.metaDescription: Essential hydraulic safety practices: stored energy, isolation, injection injuries, hose safety, accumulators, suspended loads and safe maintenance procedures.
posts.excerpt: Hydraulic systems store enormous energy, even when switched off. These safety basics protect everyone who works on or near hydraulic equipment.
posts.imageAlt: Technician wearing a hard hat working on industrial equipment
posts.html:
Hydraulic systems make heavy work look easy. That same power makes them dangerous when something goes wrong or when maintenance is carried out unsafely. Many hydraulic injuries happen because people assume a stopped machine is safe. This guide covers the essential safety principles. It is not a substitute for your site's procedures, the equipment manufacturer's instructions or appropriate training.

Understand stored energy

A hydraulic system can hold energy long after the pump stops:

  • Trapped pressure in cylinders, hoses and valves held closed by check valves.
  • Accumulators, which store pressurised oil specifically to release it later.
  • Suspended loads held up by cylinders, which can fall if pressure is released.
  • Raised structures such as booms, tipper bodies and press rams.
  • Hot oil and components, which can cause burns.

Before any maintenance, all of these energy sources must be identified and controlled.

Isolation and lock-out

Follow your site's lock-out/tag-out procedures:

  1. Stop the machine and isolate power sources.
  2. Lower loads to the ground or support them mechanically with suitable blocks, props or stands.
  3. Relieve system pressure using the correct procedure.
  4. Discharge accumulators and verify with a gauge.
  5. Lock and tag isolation points.
  6. Verify zero energy before starting work.

Hydraulic injection injuries

High-pressure oil escaping from a pinhole leak can penetrate skin. These injuries may look minor at first but are medical emergencies requiring immediate specialist treatment.

  • Never use your hand to search for leaks. Use cardboard or wood, and wear appropriate protection.
  • Seek urgent medical attention for any suspected injection injury, and tell medical staff it involved hydraulic fluid.

Hose safety

Hoses fail through age, abrasion, kinking, incorrect assembly and over-pressurisation. A bursting hose can whip violently and spray hot oil.

  • Inspect hoses regularly and replace damaged or aged hoses.
  • Use hoses, fittings and assemblies rated for the system pressure.
  • Use hose restraints and guards where failure could injure people.
  • Route hoses to avoid abrasion, heat and pinch points.

Never work under unsupported loads

Hydraulic cylinders and valves can leak. A load held only by hydraulics can drift down or drop suddenly if a hose fails. Always use mechanical supports rated for the load before working under raised equipment.

Correct tools and procedures

  • Never loosen fittings under pressure.
  • Use calibrated gauges when testing.
  • Bleed air carefully.
  • Use the right tools for disassembly — cylinders may contain trapped pressure or spring forces.
  • Follow manufacturer procedures for adjusting relief and load-holding valves; incorrect settings can create dangerous conditions.

Personal protective equipment

Depending on the task: safety glasses or face shields, gloves, protective clothing and safety footwear. Hot oil and high-pressure sprays are real hazards.

Housekeeping and fire risk

Clean up oil spills promptly to prevent slips. Hydraulic oil leaking onto hot surfaces can ignite; fix leaks and keep ignition sources away from hydraulic equipment.

Training and competence

Hydraulic work should be carried out by trained, competent people. Operators should be trained to recognise warning signs — leaks, drift, unusual noise — and report them.

Quick safety checklist

Before work Done?
Loads lowered or mechanically supported ☐
Power isolated and locked out ☐
Pressure relieved and verified ☐
Accumulators discharged and verified ☐
PPE in place ☐
Correct tools and procedures available ☐

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a hydraulic injection injury?

It occurs when high-pressure fluid from a pinhole leak or failed fitting penetrates the skin. The wound may look small, but fluid can travel deep into tissue and cause severe damage. Treat any suspected injection injury as a medical emergency, seek specialist treatment immediately and tell medical staff the injury involved hydraulic fluid.

Is a hydraulic system safe once the pump is switched off?

Not necessarily. Pressure can remain trapped behind check valves and in cylinders, accumulators store pressurised oil by design, and raised loads held by cylinders can fall if pressure is released. Always relieve pressure, discharge accumulators, support loads mechanically and verify zero energy before starting work.

How should I look for hydraulic leaks safely?

Never use your hands. Pass a piece of cardboard or wood near suspected leaks while wearing eye protection and gloves, and keep your body out of line with fittings and hoses. If a leak is found, shut down and isolate the system before repairing it.

Why must loads be supported mechanically before maintenance?

Hydraulic cylinders and valves can leak internally, and hoses can fail without warning. A load held only by hydraulics can drift down or drop suddenly. Mechanical props, blocks or stands rated for the load protect anyone working beneath raised equipment.

What personal protective equipment is needed for hydraulic work?

Typical PPE includes safety glasses or a face shield, suitable gloves, protective clothing and safety footwear. Tasks involving hot oil, high-pressure testing or work at height may require additional protection. Follow your site's risk assessments for each task.
